ranking.title: Signed-Off v2: buy-and-build, AI-leveraged nuclear engineering house sold through the buyer co-op
Regional Partner Group: rollover-first anchor-and-fill consolidator of independent uniform and linen laundries
HCBS Operations Utility for Managed-LTSS Plans
Run-Base Shrinker v2: funded retirement of application run cost, paid per invoice line that drops
Stafette: Meister-partnered service hubs that absorb the customer books and crews of closing Handwerk firms (replaces Meisterwerk)
Level-1 Bench (refined from Overnight Yard Crews)
Qualified-challenger fiscal agent: buy the ticket in choice markets, bid the statewide auctions later
Root-Cause Contract: outcome-priced fixes for social housing's costliest homes
Outreach Partner Labs (rebuilt): open-book operating company for health systems that keep their outreach lab
Capped Outage: scope- and date-guaranteed gas-turbine overhauls for owners with no LTSA

decisive_factors: A's median case is a real cash-flowing business: it buys an existing nuclear boutique and earns about 15-17% EBITDA (about $4M, worth about $30M) even if AI delivers nothing. B's median is break-even after the team and carries inventory and price risk.

B's moat is a temporary shortage premium. Rystad says price and lead-time growth has stalled, and new OEM capacity lands in 2027-29. A's tailwind is multi-year: nuclear restarts, uprates and a hiring shortage, with a staffing-constrained incumbent set.

B's core gap, 'nobody holds stock', was found false. Several dealers already sell and ship units at the target size, and the likeliest single outcome is that B fails its own 2-week test. A's weak points are narrower and cheaper to test.

B has no unit-economics path to a good business. Realistic gross margin is 7-10% on pass-through units, which is a dealer spread. A's 8-15% discount, capped at half the measured hours saved, protects margin.
A fails soft. If AI productivity is unproven, A degrades to an ordinary boutique roll-up. If B's premium or supply fails, B has nothing left except brokering.
h2h:C10:C04:ab.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded, so the question is which failure is less likely and which floor is higher.

B's floor is poor. Its own refinement concedes no moat at launch. The median is $30M revenue at about 11-13% gross margin, and the critic puts realistic margin at 7-10%. That is break-even after a 25-person team, and it carries storage, warranty, liquidated-damages and mark-to-market risk. The premium that justifies the business is a function of a shortage that Rystad and Wood Mackenzie say is peaking. New OEM capacity arrives in 2027-29, and the cancelled-unit supply B relies on is itself a sign of softer demand. Supply, meaning whether OEMs will assign slots or transfer cancelled units to a newcomer, is untested and not covered by the test. The 'nobody holds stock' premise failed, since Maddox, JCL, Giga and Sunbelt Solomon already do this. The $120M upside is padded by roughly $10M of fees that contradict B's own pricing and is only 2-3% likely.

A is the consensus roll-up trade, and the critic gives its upside only 1-3%. But A buys EBITDA instead of hoping for a spread. At roughly 6.5x EBITDA, an $8M enterprise value platform with seller note gives a 15%-margin nuclear boutique that already holds an approved-supplier listing and a QA manual. Demand is durable: 6,900-7,400 in-house engineers growing to 9,200-10,400 by 2030, restarts, and uprates. The AI claim is optional upside. The discount rule (price cut at most half of hours saved) keeps margin positive even at 15% hours saved.

A's real gaps are the orphan supply (the evidence is one auctioned, distressed comp), change-of-control survival of the listing, and needing a credentialed nuclear QA co-founder. Those are serious, but they cap the downside at a modest-sized acquisition. B's downside is a stalled desk with no assets.
h2h:C10:C04:ab.a_biggest_risk: No supply of ASL-listed, 30-100 person nuclear boutiques at or below about 6.5x EBITDA outside the Pelican, Arlington and New Mountain processes, plus customers or the QA listing not surviving the ownership change. The AI productivity edge is unproven on calculation-grade work. The result is no deal, or an ordinary overpriced boutique.
h2h:C10:C04:ab.b_biggest_risk: There is no durable premium or access to supply. Dealers already ship units of the right size in weeks, OEMs have no reason to give a newcomer slots they can sell directly, and new capacity in 2027-29 compresses the shortage premium. This leaves a thin dealer spread of about 7-10% gross, and the likeliest outcome is failing the 2-week test.

decisive_factors: A's base case does not depend on its unproven AI claim. It is a purchased, cash-flowing nuclear engineering boutique, so revenue starts at close. B must create demand from nothing for a product no one is shown to buy.

B's core price assumption is contradicted by its own evidence. It needs a 93% staffing markup against a 35-45% norm, and LAUNCH implies about $34-39 bill rates. Its free-conversion and tenure mechanics push median EBITDA to roughly 0%, and the WIOA subsidy is likely ineligible. Two critics rated B fatal.

A has real sector tailwinds (restarts, uprates, engineer shortage, PE appetite) and an option-like structure. A stop-buying rule at month 12 and a roughly $10k bake-off cap the downside, and the median is a solid roughly $4M EBITDA business.

Both ideas have a low-single-digit chance of reaching the upside, so expected value turns on the median and the odds of reaching it. A's median is better ($25M revenue at about 17% margin, worth about $30M) than B's ($20M at 0-7% margin, worth about $5M at staffing multiples). A's odds are also higher: dossier base case 40-45% versus B's median being 'a failed pilot'.
h2h:C10:C06:ab.reasons:
Neither idea has a credible venture-scale upside. A's $110M case is about 1-3% likely, and B's $100M case is about 1-2%. The decision therefore rests on the median outcome and the probability of reaching it.

A's median is an ordinary but real business. One platform acquisition of about $8M EV plus a tuck-in gives about $4M EBITDA, worth about $30M, with revenue from day one. It sells into a sector with genuine demand growth. The AI productivity claim is upside, not a base-case requirement. The bear case is that no target clears the 6.5x cap or customers leave after the ownership change. The founder can stop at month 12 with limited capital sunk. The nuclear QA co-founder is a real gate, but the task assumes a capable team. Competition from Pelican and Arlington for deals and alliance lock-in are serious. They mostly cap the upside, though, and make good targets scarce. They do not remove the base case.

B is a greenfield staffing-plus-academy business with a load-bearing assumption nobody has validated: shops paying about $50 an hour for trainees they could hire direct at $24-28. The critics found the price anchor contradicted by LAUNCH's pricing. The tenure and conversion mechanics are internally inconsistent and push EBITDA to about zero. The WIOA subsidy is likely unavailable for hired-out staffing. Incumbents are PE-funded and could price-match or buy the entrant. The $500 test is cheap, but even a pass leaves a 5-7% margin staffing firm with no moat. That is worth far less than A's median.
h2h:C10:C06:ab.a_biggest_risk: No quality ASL-listed boutique can be bought at or below about 6.5x EBITDA. Pelican, Arlington and New Mountain are bidding and the evidence for 'orphan' supply is thin. If a target is bought, customers or the supplier listing may not survive the change of control. The company then becomes a plain roll-up with no edge, or never closes a deal.
h2h:C10:C06:ab.b_biggest_risk: Shops and dealers will not pay a bill rate of $50 or more an hour (a 93% markup) for six-week trainees they can hire directly at $24-28. Free conversion after about 1,000 hours, shorter tenure and an ineligible WIOA subsidy then push EBITDA to roughly zero. Nothing shows temp technicians are bought at scale.

decisive_factors: A's median case needs no AI breakthrough: it buys an existing approved-supplier boutique, so revenue and cash flow start at close. B starts from zero revenue and a demand test it has not yet passed.

B's first-round critics rated both customer demand and procurement/execution as fatal. Its own dossier says 'weak, leaning kill'. A's first-round critics rated all three objections serious, not fatal.

A's base case is a profitable roll-up (about $25M revenue, about $4M EBITDA, 40-45% by the dossier's own scenarios). B's median is conditional on clearing a data gate it gives about 30%, and it is mostly pass-through works at 8-12% EBITDA.

Both second-round critics put the upside at 1-3% or lower. A's bad outcome is a modest or break-even roll-up with tangible assets and a salvageable sale. B's bad outcome is zero revenue, with only the cheap first test limiting the loss.
h2h:C10:C15:ab.reasons:
Both ideas have weak upside cases, with critics putting the joint probability at 1-3% for A and under 1% for B. The decision therefore turns on the base case and the downside.

A's base case is an ordinary but real business. Buying a nuclear engineering boutique with 13-21% EBITDA margins gives immediate revenue, cash flow and an existing customer base, and the base case does not depend on AI productivity. It resembles a search-fund acquisition with a domain co-founder. The median is about $25M revenue and $4M EBITDA, worth roughly $30M, on modest equity because of seller notes. The dossier gives that base case 40-45%. Its serious objections (entrenched alliances, a consensus PE trade, insurance, change of control) mostly hit the upside and the AI edge. The refined plan already stops buying at a price cap and dilutes none of the core value if the bake-off shows no AI saving.

B has to create a category. Its first-round critics rated the customer and procurement objections fatal, and the dossier found no carve-out precedent and no evidence of a buyer. Buyers are bundling and insourcing. A newco fails the turnover and credit-score tests. Wates and Mears already sell adjacent products. The control-group pricing collides with Awaab's Law. The revenue is mostly low-margin works, and the equity story rests on a fund layer that does not exist. B's cheap first test is a real merit, but A's expected value is higher at both the median and the tail.
h2h:C10:C15:ab.a_biggest_risk: Sourcing and keeping the asset. No evidence shows five or more approved-supplier boutiques priced at or below 6.5x EBITDA outside the Pelican, Arlington and New Mountain processes. The supplier listing and customer acceptance could also fail to survive the ownership change and the new AI procedure. Either failure collapses the plan into no deal or a shrinking book.
h2h:C10:C15:ab.b_biggest_risk: Nobody may buy it. There is no precedent for a cohort carve-out, and landlords are bundling and insourcing. A newco cannot pass procurement turnover and credit tests. Primes such as Wates and Mears can add the same service inside existing contracts, so the realistic role is a low-margin subcontractor. The core premise (concentrated, persistent hot-spot costs) is also untested.

decisive_factors: A's floor is an ordinary profitable services business (15-17% EBITDA, ~$4M on $25M revenue, about $30M of value at 7-8x). B's median is 5-8% EBITDA and the critic computes 12-20x EBITDA actually paid, which is a capital loss at exit.

A's demand is strong: restarts, uprates, nuclear engineer headcount rising 6,900-7,400 to 9,200-10,400 by 2030, and incumbents capacity-constrained. B's sector loses money at competitive-bid prices (Wisconsin -12.5%) and faces federal and state fraud and cut pressure.

A's central bet, the AI productivity lift, can be tested in about 13 days for under $10k. A also fails soft: without the lift it is a plain roll-up with a stop-buying rule. B's central bet, a cheap seller supply, has no price evidence at all, and the pitch's own premise of a scarce qualification ticket is contradicted for Texas (free entry) and Colorado (closed contract).

Liability profile: A can cap liability at fees and degrade to T&M if E&O is unavailable. B carries 3504 joint-and-several payroll-tax exposure and Calderon-style wage-hour risk ($162M settlement) on a ~2% fee, in a thin spread business.
h2h:C10:C02:ab.reasons: Both ideas share a $25M median revenue, so expected outcome comes down to what that revenue earns, what it costs to buy, and how likely the thesis is to be fatally wrong. In A, the median is a buy-and-build nuclear engineering boutique at roughly 15-17% EBITDA. It is bought at a capped 6.5x EBITDA with at least 30% seller paper, in a market with real labor-shortage and restart/uprate tailwinds. Its worst realistic outcome is an ordinary, cash-generating roll-up or a no-buy at month 12, which costs little. The AI lift is upside, not the floor, and it can be tested cheaply. The serious objections (alliance lock-in, PE competition for targets, E&O insurability, change-of-control survival) hurt the upside much more than the median. The second-round critic's 1-3% upside probability is ugly, but the median is a normal services business. B's own critic shows the median case is effectively a bear case. The fee is about 2% of spend, the only public cost data shows the sector losing money, and the premium-price segment is unsized and partly mis-specified (Minnesota fees are participant-paid and tiered; Colorado is a closed award). The acquisition thesis rests on a seller price nobody has found, against H.I.G. and General Atlantic paying about 10x. B also adds political, fraud-crackdown and tax-liability tail risk, which A does not have in the same form. A is wounded but has a real floor, a cheap kill test, and growing demand. B has a thin, policy-exposed floor and a likely capital loss at the median.
h2h:C10:C02:ab.a_biggest_risk: Cannot source acquisitions at orphan prices (Arlington, Pelican and New Mountain bid up boutiques, and the evidence is one auctioned, distressed GSE sale), and without the AI productivity cut of 30% or more the business is just an undifferentiated roll-up that incumbents can undercut on narrow fixed-price scopes.
h2h:C10:C02:ab.b_biggest_risk: The "buy the qualification ticket cheaply" premise fails. Small fiscal agents either earn thin or negative margins at $68-120 per participant-month, or sell at multiples (about 10x for sponsor-backed assets, 12-20x effective at the median) that make the median case a capital loss, with no FMS deal price found to support the 1.0x revenue assumption.

decisive_factors: Failure mode: if the AI thesis fails, A degrades to an ordinary profitable boutique roll-up. If B's demand thesis fails, there is no business.

Demand evidence: A's customers already buy outsourced nuclear engineering, and the acquired book brings revenue on day one. B has no sign that any non-Elevance plan will pay a fixed fee, and its buyers are cutting costs and exiting markets.
Capital and time to first dollar: A's median needs one roughly $8M-EV deal with 30% seller paper. B needs $8-12M and 12-24 months of runway before a paid pilot, and $50-80M for the upside.

Risk of the stack: A's riskiest assumption, the AI hours cut, is testable for under $10k in 13 days. B's second assumption, a 10-15% R3 margin at 95% of in-house cost in a ratio-bound labor business, is asserted and only provable in a pilot.

Upside quality is similar (about $100M of revenue, roughly 1-3% chance on the critics' numbers, 5-8% on the authors'), so the median and the floor decide it. A's median is a real cash-generating asset and B's is likely under $5M.
h2h:C10:C03:ab.reasons:
Neither idea is strong, and on the critics' numbers both $100M cases are a 1-3% shot. So this comes down to the median, the floor, and which objections are more likely to be fatal.

A is a nuclear engineering roll-up with an AI cost lever. The critics are right that it is mostly a consensus private-equity trade: more than half the upside revenue is bought, and the AI productivity gain is unproven on calculation-grade work. But its structure degrades gracefully. The business starts at acquisition close with real customers, an approved-supplier listing and cash flow. The demand backdrop is real: restarts, uprates, and operating-plant engineers growing from about 7,000 to 9,000-10,400 by 2030. If the bake-off fails, it is still a roughly $25M-revenue, roughly $4M-EBITDA boutique worth about $30M. If no target clears the 6.5x cap, you stop buying and lose little. The median needs one small deal with seller paper, which is founder-scale capital. The key unknown is cheap to test.

B is a greenfield sale to health plans. Its own file says the key assumption is untested: that a plan will pay a fixed, non-contingent fee to an unaffiliated vendor. Rivals already buy CareBridge and the large plans insource. The buyers are shrinking and cutting costs, and cycles run 12-30 months with state sign-offs. The author's own odds are 55-60% of ending under $5M. The only margin that matters, R3 at 10-15% under a caseload ratio, is asserted, not derived. Even the $100M case yields only about $14M of EBITDA. B's call sprint is a good cheap kill test, but passing it still leaves $8-12M and two years of runway before any proof.

A's objections hurt its upside. B's objections hit demand, which is the thing that can kill it outright. I judge A's expected outcome higher.
h2h:C10:C03:ab.a_biggest_risk: That a first-time team cannot buy ASL-listed nuclear boutiques at the 6.5x or lower cap outside the Pelican, Arlington and New Mountain processes. If so, the idea has no sourcing edge, and without the AI hours cut it is just an ordinary roll-up at auction prices. Change-of-control survival of the supplier listing and customers is assumed, not shown.
h2h:C10:C03:ab.b_biggest_risk: That no non-Elevance, non-UnitedHealth Medicaid plan will pay a fixed, non-contingent fee to a neutral vendor. Plans would insource, buy from CareBridge, or insist on savings-only. There is no RFP or buyer statement in the dossier, so there would be no revenue base, and the R3 labor rung's thin margin is a second unproven assumption behind it.

decisive_factors: A's median case is a profitable, cash-generating nuclear engineering firm (about $25M revenue, about $4M EBITDA). B's own author calls its median 'the failure mode': a burning services company that breaks even around year 8-9.

Capital and downside shape. A buys an existing book of business for roughly $8M at the platform stage, with a stop-buying rule at month 12. B must fund engineering up front, with a $28M modelled burn (plan $45-60M) in the median case and contingent receivables that lenders treat like equity.

Demand realism. A sells to owners with real budgets and a structural capacity shortage, in a sector with regulatory friction and a restart and uprate tailwind. B's key assumption (owners actually release savings) has contrary evidence of 5-6% realized against 20% targeted, and a CFO can do the same work in-house or with Redress at about parity.

B's upside and odds are worse. B needs about 94 signings, bases of $80M, 9-11.5% verified reduction and a 28% share all at once, so its own sensitivity table shows any single miss sinks it, and its author puts the unconditional odds at about 2-4%. A's upside odds are also low (about 1-3%), but A's median still creates value.

Valuation. Contingent-fee revenue values low (PRGX about 1.2x revenue). Nuclear engineering boutiques are being bought at market multiples by Pelican, Arlington and New Mountain, which gives A a credible exit even if the AI thesis fails.
h2h:C10:C13:ab.reasons: Both ideas were wounded by their critics, and both are honest that their $100M-plus upside is a roughly 2-8% shot. So the call comes down to the median outcome and the capital required. A is a consensus roll-up with an AI cost lever bolted on. Even if the lever fails, a $10M-revenue nuclear boutique bought on disciplined terms is a real asset. It sells to customers with budgets and a documented capacity shortage, and strategic and PE buyers who pay up for such firms are visibly active. The author's median is about $25M revenue and about $4M EBITDA, worth about $30M from a modest equity cheque, with a hard stop if no target clears the price cap. The main weaknesses are that the 'orphan price' evidence is thin, insurance for AI-produced deliverables is uncertain, and the owners' alliances are hard to enter. These weaknesses mostly cap the upside. They don't make the business worthless. B's median is a cash-burning services company that, by its author's own words, is the failure mode. It must fund engineering for clients, wait 9-15 months for the first success-fee dollar, and then rely on CFOs paying 26-30% of savings for three years when the DIY and Redress alternatives are at parity. Its decisive unknown, owner follow-through, has contrary evidence (5-6% realized against 20% targeted). Its gating is cheap and honest, but the prize after the gates is a low-multiple contingent-fee business. Expected value favors A, clearly but not decisively, because A's acquisition supply is also unproven.
h2h:C10:C13:ab.a_biggest_risk: Failing to acquire boutiques at the orphan price (6.5x EBITDA or less, outside the Pelican, Arlington and New Mountain processes), or losing ASL status and customers after the ownership change. If so, there is no platform, and the AI thesis (30%+ fewer hours at 90%+ first-pass acceptance) is untested on calculation-grade work.
h2h:C10:C13:ab.b_biggest_risk: Business owners do not actually release the identified retirable run spend, so invoice lines do not fall. Realization of 5-6% against 20% targeted is the contrary evidence. Without a fee base, the funded engineering is a sunk cost and CFOs cap the share at 15-20% or choose Redress or in-house.

decisive_factors: Capital and survivability: A's median case needs about $8M of enterprise value (one platform plus a tuck-in) and still produces about $4M of EBITDA from a real, cash-generating acquired book. B needs $100-175M of other people's equity, and its own unconditional median is $0.

Evidence on the keystone behavior: A's pivotal assumption (AI cuts hours 30% or more on calculation-grade work) is unproven but testable in about 13 days for under $10k, with demand for a discount comparatively likely. B's keystone (an OEM prepays a non-incumbent owner) has no precedent found by the researcher or any of the three critics.

Value proposition: B's customer-side value is near nil, since an OEM can fund the same line by signing directly with the plant's current owner or with Doncasters/Howmet. A at least offers a measurable discount plus surge capacity into a market with a documented engineer shortage.

Quality of the downside: B's sources and uses do not close, its returns are mediocre (about 1.8-3.3x gross) even in the upside, and mid-size targets are being consolidated by better-capitalized buyers (CPP/GE, Arcline, Pursuit). A's failure mode is an ordinary small engineering firm with a floor, not a zero.
h2h:C10:C05:ab.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded roll-ups. The question is which has the higher expected outcome per unit of capital and time that a capable team can actually realize.

A's upside is a long shot (critic says 1-3%, author says 5-8%), and its AI edge is unproven. But its median case is a respectable small business: a $10M-revenue acquired nuclear engineering boutique growing to about $25M at 15-17% EBITDA, bought for roughly $8M of EV with seller paper. Even the dossier's bear case (stalls under $15M) leaves a real cash-flowing firm. A's key unknowns are cheap to test. The bake-off costs under $10k and has explicit pass and kill thresholds, and the broker, E&O and supplier-form checks run for free in parallel. Its objections (incumbent lock-in, co-op rebid cycles, insurability) mainly cap the upside, since the acquired book supplies revenue on day one.

B is a capital-allocation business that needs $100-175M of equity and a proven casting operator, and a first-time team brings neither. Its core mechanism (customer reservation payments funding a line at a non-incumbent owner) has zero precedent. The customer-side logic is also weak: if OEMs fund 60-80% of a line anyway, they can do it directly with the incumbent owner, so the sponsor mostly serves the seller. The round-two critic found that the sources and uses do not close, and the entry-price comp (Precicast) is gone. The upside case returns only about 1.8-3.3x gross. The honest unconditional median is $0, and the cycle (turbine orders peaking, overcapacity flagged) adds a second correlated risk. B's larger headline revenue does not offset a roughly 5% realistic hit rate on ten times the capital.
h2h:C10:C05:ab.a_biggest_risk: The AI productivity edge does not materialize (hours cut under about 15% on calculation-grade work), or no listed boutique can be bought below about 6.5x EBITDA outside the Arlington/Pelican/New Mountain auctions. Either failure leaves an undifferentiated roll-up with no price edge against entrenched, capacity-constrained incumbents and alliances that can match narrow fixed-price scopes.
h2h:C10:C05:ab.b_biggest_risk: No non-captive OEM will sign a funded multi-year reservation with make-whole to a non-incumbent-owned caster, because they can fund an incumbent directly or buy the supplier themselves. Without that customer money the capital stack does not close, and the equity return does not clear a hurdle rate.

decisive_factors: Floor and median: A's median is an owned, cash-generating boutique (about $25M revenue, about $4M EBITDA, roughly $30M enterprise value). C11's unconditional median is about $7-12M of mostly pass-through revenue at roughly breakeven EBITDA, with a 45% chance of never signing a second client.

Objection fatality: A's serious objections (incumbent lock-in, insurance, a consensus roll-up) mostly cap the upside, because the acquired book earns money whether or not AI works. C11's first-round critics rated competition, pricing and legal as fatal. The refined version patches the legal problem only by giving up the operator's equity, so consolidated test revenue goes away.

Demand evidence: A's customers already buy outsourced engineering at about $0.7-1.2B a year, and PE is paying real money for Enercon and Jensen Hughes. C11 has no US case of a health system choosing a startup operator over cash and then renewing. Its only comparable (PAML at Kootenai) ended in the hospital insourcing.

Price and cost logic: A's discount is a rule (half of measured hours saved) and the unit economics hold for any hours cut of 15% or more. C11's price needs the operator to be 17-24% cheaper than the hospital's own cost, and the 15-18% baseline cost is admittedly unbenchmarked.

Cost of being wrong: A can stop buying at month 12 and keeps an asset-backed business. C11 is cheaper to test, at under $2k, but it has no asset floor, and a successful operator tends to be bought by Labcorp or Quest.
h2h:C10:C11:ab.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded, and both upside cases ($110M revenue) have a joint probability of 1-5%, so the decision rests on the median, the downside and which objections are fatal.

A is, at worst, the consensus nuclear-services roll-up with a disciplined sourcing rule and an AI cost option. The AI option is unproven, but the thesis does not depend on it. The base case buys one boutique at about $8M enterprise value, adds a tuck-in and a small fixed-price lane, and ends with roughly $4M of EBITDA. Dossier odds put roughly 40-45% on that base case and 45-50% on stalling under $15M or being absorbed. A stalled boutique still has positive value. Discount-to-hours-saved economics are sound, and the stop rule at month 12 limits losses. The real obstacles are that Pelican, Arlington and New Mountain are bidding for the same targets, that the co-op and incumbent alliances shut some doors, and that errors-and-omissions cover for AI work is uncertain. The refinement already moves the plan to a time-and-materials fallback.

C11's survivable form has weak economics. Once the Medicare 1833(h)(5)(A) problem forced a 100% hospital-owned entity, the company became a vendor paid cost plus 10-12% at about 8% EBITDA. It needs an unbenchmarked cost advantage over the hospital's own commercial functions, and Quest or Labcorp can match it. Its only precedent, PAML at Kootenai, ended with the hospital firing the operator. The customer's real alternative is a cash check or an in-house build with Mayo or ARUP advice. The 45% chance of never signing a second client leaves little for investors even if the roughly $2k test passes. A's capital need and first-time-team problem are real. C11 is cheaper to start, but its expected payoff is lower and more likely to be zero.
h2h:C10:C11:ab.a_biggest_risk: Sourcing. The plan needs listed nuclear boutiques bought at or below 6.5x EBITDA, outside the Pelican, Arlington and New Mountain processes. Evidence for such orphan prices is two data points from one failed roll-up. Without a deal at that price there is no business. If a deal does close, the next risk is that the unproven 30% AI hours saving is what lets the discount pay for itself, and that incumbents can match fixed prices on narrow scopes.
h2h:C10:C11:ab.b_biggest_risk: Demand and price. A non-selling health system must sign a 5-year open-book contract with a startup at least 8% below its own commercial-function cost. The alternatives are doing it in-house, taking advisory help from Mayo, ARUP or Chi, or accepting a national's management offer. The cost advantage rests on an unbenchmarked estimate, no non-national operator has been shown to renew past year 3, and the billing-law and EKRA structure still needs counsel's approval.

decisive_factors: Value if it works: A's upside is about $110M revenue at 20%+ EBITDA, with a liquid strategic or sponsor exit (Arlington, Pelican and New Mountain are buyers). B's upside is about EUR 6M EBIT inside a steward-owned, capped-yield, no-exit structure, which is a small regional service group.

Median-case floor: A buys a profitable listed boutique, so it has revenue and EBITDA from day one (about $25M revenue, about $4M EBITDA, roughly $30M of value) without AI working. B's median is about EUR 0.8M EBIT, and its hub economics are invented (19% contribution, EUR 240k overhead) and negative below EUR 1.55M of revenue.

Tailwind and scarcity: nuclear engineering demand is rising (operating-plant engineers up about 30% by 2030, restarts, uprates) and approved-supplier status is scarce. B's market is shrinking (turnover -12%, orders -15%) and is crowded by HomeServe/Brookfield, VINCI, Konzmann, Builtech, MEISTEREHRE and GREENOX.

Fatal-objection quality: A's fatal risks (orphan supply, AI productivity, insurance) are each testable and mostly affect the upside, not the median. B's are structural: adverse selection among sellers who cannot sell, crew and customer attrition, unfundable hold-forever capital, and a sunk-overhead neighbour that can undercut the platform on every book.
h2h:C10:C09:ab.reasons:
Both ideas were left wounded, with upside probabilities of roughly 1-5%, so the call turns on value-if-works and on what the median outcome looks like.

A is, at worst, a plain nuclear-boutique roll-up. That is not exciting, but it is a real business. It buys an operating, ASL-listed firm with revenue and customers, in a sector with rising demand, scarce supplier status and active sponsors who pay for these assets. The critics' strongest points (incumbent lock-in, the USA co-op, AI-exclusion insurance, and orphan-price supply resting on one failed roll-up) mostly cap the upside rather than break the median. The AI cost edge is only the differentiator and is not needed for the base case. Capital is staged by a stop rule: no acquisition under the cap by month 12 means stop buying.

B's economics are thinner at every level, even if it works. The upside is about EUR 6M EBIT, held forever under capped-yield steward capital with no flip exit. The core model (19% contribution) is invented and reverse-fitted. Sellers are adversely selected, since owners who cannot sell have owner-dependent, consumer-heavy books. Crew retention is unmodelled. A neighbour with sunk overhead can outbid the platform. It also depends on LPs accepting a 7-10% no-exit yield that no one has identified. B's seller-ledger test is cheaper, but a pass would not show the business creates enough value.

A has the higher expected value and a better downside floor, so A wins. The margin is moderate because A's real execution risk is high.
h2h:C10:C09:ab.a_biggest_risk: The central acquisition thesis may not exist at the stated price. There may be no supply of ASL-listed 30-100 person nuclear boutiques at 6.5x EBITDA or less outside the Pelican, Arlington and New Mountain processes, and the AI-driven 30% hours cut that would justify a discount and a premium case is unmeasured. If quality assets cost 9-12x, the upside falls to $50-60M and the business becomes an ordinary, expensive roll-up.
h2h:C10:C09:ab.b_biggest_risk: Seller adverse selection combined with unproven contribution economics. The books available from closing owners with no alternative are likely owner-dependent, consumer-heavy and low-margin, so the assumed 70% retention and 19% contribution on absorbed crews may not exist. The hub then stays below its EUR 1.55M break-even, and with no identified LP for the no-exit tranches B and C the business stalls at a sub-scale, near-zero-margin regional group.

decisive_factors: Profit structure: A earns services margins on revenue it produces (15% baseline EBITDA, 20%+ if the discount rule holds). B's revenue is mostly pass-through, with 10-14% gross margin and $4-7M EBITDA even at $100M revenue. The 'prize' in B is far smaller than its revenue headline.

Downside floor: A's median case is ownership of a real, cash-flowing nuclear engineering firm, about $4M EBITDA worth roughly $30M, bought with seller paper and a small equity cheque. B's median is 'break-even to small loss', and B most likely dies at a gate (sponsor, surety, shop slots) before any revenue.

Internal contradiction in B: passing its own demand test (owner growth of 10% or more) selects the cases where the prime loses money. Costs come to about 0.87-0.90x OEM against 1.00x pricing, which leaves 3-4% margin before bonds. A's critics produced no equivalent defect in the unit economics; the discount rule gives a break-even price cut of 0.65 x hours cut.

Cost and speed of falsification: A's fatal unknown (hours cut of 30%+) is testable for under $10k in 13 days, and a failed test leaves a plain roll-up with a stop-buying rule at month 12. B needs a sponsor ($15-60M), a surety line, a reinsurer or stop-loss quote, unreferenced-entrant qualification and hardware slots, none of which a founder controls.

Tail risk asymmetry: A caps liability at fees on $10-50k deliverables and refuses lost-generation exposure. B sells fixed-price, date-guaranteed, bonded outages with retained as-found growth, and a casting squeeze or a bad early package (adverse selection) could wipe retained capital.
h2h:C10:C01:ab.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded, so the question is which wounds are more likely fatal and what remains if the main thesis fails.

A is, by its own admission, a consensus buy-and-build trade with a differentiated sourcing rule, which is a real weakness. But the weakness is priced in. Without any AI edge it is still an ordinary nuclear engineering boutique roll-up with real customers, real margins and a recurring-services base. Revenue starts at acquisition close, so there is no 33-month supplier-approval cycle. The median of about $25M revenue and about $4M EBITDA is a decent outcome for a small equity cheque. The cheap-to-test AI hypothesis only moves A between a plain roll-up and a better one. The incumbent and co-op objections mostly hit the fixed-price lane, which is the minority of A's revenue. The E&O gap is handled by degrading to time-and-materials.

B's critics were rated fatal in round one, and the rewrite concedes most of them. It keeps a thin intermediary position: no hardware, no references, no moat for four years, and Hanwha able to copy the cap in 18-24 months. Its own margin arithmetic undercuts the demand gate. The owners it says have growth to absorb are the ones where the prime loses money. The hard date has nothing behind it, because the hardware holders control the scarce slots. It needs an unfound sponsor and surety, and even success yields a low-profit pass-through business with a roughly 3% shot at the upside.

Expected profit favors A by a wide margin: more probability mass, higher margin per revenue dollar, and a real salvage value.
h2h:C10:C01:ab.a_biggest_risk: The productivity thesis and the sourcing thesis both fail together. Orphan boutiques at 6.5x EBITDA or less do not exist outside the Pelican, Arlington and New Mountain processes, and AI cuts hours by under 15%. That leaves a late entrant in a consensus PE roll-up, or no deal at all. Acquired customers or approved-supplier status could also be lost on change of control.
h2h:C10:C01:ab.b_biggest_risk: The unit economics do not work for an unreferenced neutral prime. A fixed price near 1.00x OEM against about 0.87-0.90x cost leaves 3-4% margin before bonds and bid costs, and the demand test selects for owners whose growth makes the prime lose money. It also lacks the sponsor, surety and shop slots to qualify or perform. Hanwha, which already holds the references and the hardware, can copy the cap.

decisive_factors: Durability of the revenue: A sells a substitution for a mandated, recurring plan cost under 3-year contracts with delegation switching costs. B sells one-off equipment resales whose premium comes from a shortage that Rystad and the OEM build-out schedule say is fading by 2027-29.

Median case: A's median (~$18M revenue, about 20k lives, ~50% likely conditional on a paid pilot) is a real contracted services company needing ~$8-12M to prove. B's median (~$30M revenue) is gross profit of $4-5M, roughly break-even after a 25-person team, and needs ~$20M plus warehouse debt.

Weak points of B that the test does not cover: the supply side (OEM slot access for a newcomer, assignability of cancelled units, spec fit), no moat at launch, and incumbents (JCL, Maddox to 160 MVA, Giga, Sunbelt Solomon) already working the same spread. B's own refinement says no power at launch.

Both have unevidenced demand and 2-3% to 8% odds of the upside, so the call is close. A's fatal objection (will anyone pay a fixed fee) is cheaply and cleanly falsifiable, and the wedge is a second source in a market where plans buy outsourced ops. B's window decays as the founder builds.
h2h:C03:C04:ab.reasons:
Neither idea survived its critics intact. Both refined pitches concede the original thesis is dead, both have a cheap two-week falsification test, and both put the upside case at roughly 2-8%. So the call turns on the median outcome and on which objection is more likely fatal.

A is now an operations-outsourcing business, not a neutral-risk-manager story. It replaces cost the plan already carries (missed-shift response, reconciliation, ratio-bound coordinators). Revenue would be contracted, recurring, with delegation and audit-trail switching costs. The business category exists (Maximus, Conduent, Evolent, CareBridge). The honest weaknesses are real: demand is unevidenced, buyers are cutting costs, sales cycles run 12-18 months, and the R3 labor margin is asserted rather than derived. Still, the $18M median and ~14% blended EBITDA at scale describe an actual company, and the $55-60M ceiling without R3 is a reasonable floor on ambition.

B has clearer present pain (128-160 week lead times, documented premiums), but the business captured is a dealer spread. The refined pitch admits no moat at launch, incumbents with stock to 160 MVA, an unevidenced supply side that the test never touches, and a premium that compresses as new OEM capacity lands in 2027-29. Its median is roughly break-even. Its upside needs about 36% share of its own reachable count. That is a bet on a transient scarcity rent. A's thesis is structural, so I give A a narrow edge.
h2h:C03:C04:ab.a_biggest_risk: No non-Elevance, non-UnitedHealth Medicaid plan will pay a fixed, non-contingent fee for outsourced HCBS operations or coordination. They will insource, buy from CareBridge at a discount, or insist on savings-only, and the R3 labor rung cannot clear a 10-15% margin at 95% of in-house cost. The sale is also slow and the buyers are shrinking.
h2h:C03:C04:ab.b_biggest_risk: The supply side fails and the premium decays. OEMs allocate slots to volume buyers rather than a newcomer's pooled deposits, cancelled units prove non-assignable or the wrong spec, and incumbent dealers (JCL, Maddox, Giga, Sunbelt Solomon) already deliver stock. As new OEM capacity lands in 2027-29 the speed premium compresses to a ~5% dealer spread and the business stays near break-even.

decisive_factors: B's customer and execution objections were rated fatal and are structural: no cohort carve-out precedent, buyers bundling and insourcing, and a newco excluded by turnover and D&B tests. A's three objections were all rated serious, none fatal.

A sells a substitution into an existing, large, well-understood outsourcing category (a $1.2-1.8B pool of plan spend, known buyers, fee-for-service). B needs to create a new contract category (control-indexed outcome pricing), and its upside rests on that category-creation step.

A gets its demand signal fast and cheaply: 12+ priced calls in 2 weeks, then a pilot priced at cost plus 10% by month 9-18. B's premise test (cost concentration) is also cheap, but its decisive causal read needs a full winter (about month 20), and capitation is not sold until then. Neither of B's cheap tests shows anyone will pay.

B carries stacked extra risks A lacks: regression-to-the-mean contamination of savings, randomized controls colliding with Awaab's Law, FSMA and indemnity exposure, a landlord who keeps the legal duty for a saving worth under 0.5% of turnover, and a UK-only buyer set of about 45-55 landlords.

Value if it works is similar (about $100M revenue, EBITDA about $14M for A and 8-12% for B, mostly pass-through works), so the probability of working decides it. A's chance of reaching a median-type outcome looks about twice B's.
h2h:C03:C15:ab.reasons:
Both ideas are long shots whose $100M cases the critics put at roughly 1-2% (A) and under 1% (B). The upside value is similar, so the decision rests on the chance of a real business and how fast the demand question gets answered.

A is a fixed-fee operations service sold to Medicaid plans that already carry the cost. Its objections are real: rivals already buy from CareBridge, plan budgets are shrinking, and the R3 coordination margin is asserted rather than derived. But none is fatal on the evidence. Outsourcing health-plan back-office and coordination work is a normal category. The pool is large, and the refined pitch needs no risk licence or plan equity. The 2-week priced-call test asks the right question, whether a plan will pay a fixed fee, and a negative answer kills it cheaply. If the test passes, A is a workable BPO business in the Maximus and Conduent mold. At median that is about $18M of revenue, a modest outcome, but a plausible one.

B has two critic-rated fatal problems that the rewrite only partly fixes. It has no precedent for a cohort carve-out, and a newco cannot clear procurement turnover and D&B tests, which leaves it subcontracting to the same primes it competes with. It also depends on three unproven links: cost concentration, a causal cut of 40% or more against a control, and the creation of a new contract type. Awaab's Law Phase 2 is a real forcing function for the cheap early rungs. But those rungs are a crowded remediation contracting business, and the outcome-priced capitation is where the value sits. Its 8-week data gate tests only the premise, not willingness to pay.

A ranks higher on odds of a viable business, speed of learning, market size and shots on goal.
h2h:C03:C15:ab.a_biggest_risk: No non-Elevance, non-UnitedHealth Medicaid plan will pay a fixed, non-contingent fee to an unaffiliated vendor. Plans instead insource, stay with CareBridge, or demand savings-only terms. Their budgets are also shrinking. The R3 labor rung's 10-15% margin at 95% of in-house cost is unproven, which caps the business at an R1-R2 boutique of roughly $55-60M at best.
h2h:C03:C15:ab.b_biggest_risk: There is no buyer for the product. Landlords are bundling disrepair work into whole-stock partners or insourcing. A newco cannot pass the procurement turnover and credit-score tests. The core premise (cost concentration that persists and is causally fixable by 40% or more) is unproven and exposed to regression to the mean. Together these leave a small remediation niche, not a capitated-contract business.

decisive_factors: Capital and feasibility: A can start on $8-12M of seed with no downstream risk and no plan money, and its keystone assumption can be falsified for $0-3k in two weeks. B needs $130-175M of equity, a proven casting operator and a first deal won against GE/CPP, Arcline, Pursuit and Doncasters.

Where each pitch is fatal: B's keystone, an OEM prepaying a line at a non-incumbent owner, has no precedent (none found by the researcher or any of the three critics). Its customer value proposition is also near nil, because the OEM could sign the same deal with the plant's current owner. A's keystone is merely unevidenced (will a sub-scale non-Elevance plan pay a fixed fee to replace admin spend it already carries), and the critics did not show it false.

Probability-weighted outcome: A's own odds are about 25-30% for $15M+ revenue and 5-8% for $100M. B's are about 12% at best for $100M and its unconditional median is $0. B's equity return even in the upside case is only about 1.8-3.3x gross, and the sources-and-uses math does not close at the low end.

Downside shape: if A fails, it fails early and cheaply (pilot gates at month 12 and 24). B's failure modes (no sellable asset at a sane price, anchors buy rather than fund, equity wants a proven operator CEO) hit before any value is created, and the founder is likely reduced to deal originator with a small stake.
h2h:C03:C05:ab.reasons:
Neither idea is strong, and the question is which has the higher probability-weighted outcome per unit of capital and time. B has the larger upside on paper: a real shortage, high OEM switching costs, and revenue bought on day one at 18-22% EBITDA. But the machinery that makes B work is mostly outside a founding team's control. It needs a proven casting operator, $130-175M of other people's equity, and a first-time sponsor beating GE/CPP, Arcline and Pursuit for a scarce qualified asset. Its own odds are 5-12% for $100M, and the unconditional median is $0. The core mechanism, customer money following a protective contract to a non-incumbent owner, has never been observed, and the unanswered critic point is decisive: if the customer funds the line anyway, it can do so with the plant's current owner, so the sponsor serves only the seller. Dossier and critics converge on "dead as a founder-led startup."

A is a modest business whose objections are more survivable. The refined version drops neutrality as the reason to buy and sells substitution of admin and coordination spend the plan already carries, at no more than 95% of in-house cost. It needs little capital before R4 and carries no downstream risk. The median of about $18M revenue and the $100M upside (about $14M EBITDA) are small, and R3 margin and demand are unproven. But the demand question can be answered in two weeks for under $3k, and failure is cheap and early. Expected value is thin but positive, and the downside is bounded. B has a bigger prize that is much less likely to be reached and costs far more to find out.
h2h:C03:C05:ab.a_biggest_risk: No unaffiliated Medicaid LTSS plan agrees to pay a fixed, non-contingent fee. Plans insource, buy from CareBridge/Carelon, or insist on savings-only, and the R3 labor rung cannot earn 10-15% margin under caseload ratios. The business then stalls as a thin-margin R1-R2 boutique capped near $55-60M, or lower.
h2h:C03:C05:ab.b_biggest_risk: The keystone, an OEM prepaying a capacity line at a non-incumbent-owned caster, has no precedent. Without it the capital stack does not close, and a sponsor with no operating edge buys qualified assets against deeper-pocketed bidders at cycle-peak prices.

decisive_factors: Median-case economics: A's median (about $18M revenue, fixed-fee, 34% gross margin, positive EBITDA) is a workable services business. B's own median ($16.6M at year 7) is still losing money, breaks even around year 8-9, and B's author calls it 'the failure mode'.

Downside shape and capital: A's R1/R2 rungs are non-contingent, low-capital, with a pilot priced at cost plus 10%, so the floor is a small regional ops business. B funds about $1M of engineering per client up front against back-ended, contingent, constrained-recognition receivables ($45-60M realistic need).

Clarity of 'why buy': A is substitution of mandated, ratio-bound work the plan already pays for, a familiar BPO purchase. B's 'why pay us' is unanswered because the CFO who backs the program already owns the missing ingredient and has cheaper alternatives (Redress, renegotiation, DIY).

Empirical realization risk: B's core fee base has contrary evidence (20% targeted vs 5-6% realized) and its price (about 1.1-1.3x a year's saving over the term for parity with DIY) is hard to defend. A's equivalent risk, willingness to pay, is a binary question that 12 priced calls can settle quickly.
h2h:C03:C13:ab.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded long shots with similar medians (about $17-18M revenue) and low odds of $100M (A: 5-8% by its author, 1-2% by its critic; B: 2-4% unconditional). The upside tail does not separate them. B's year-8 upside EBITDA (about $33M on $121M) beats A's (about $14M on $101M), but B needs signings, account size, reduction depth, share, tail and cheap financing all at once, and every single sensitivity breaks it. So the decision rests on the median and the downside.

A's median is a positive-margin fixed-fee services business with a moderate capital need. Its early rungs substitute for admin spend the plan already carries, at a price the plan can compare to its own cost. The buyer is under cost pressure, which tends to favor outsourcing mandated work over new spend. The real danger is that nobody buys: no demand evidence exists, buyers are shrinking, and cycles are long. That is a binary question that 12 priced calls can answer cheaply, and the fall-back is a small regional ops business.

B's median burns about $28M (realistically $45-60M) to reach roughly $17-20M of revenue at near-zero EBITDA, and contingent revenue is valued low (PRGX at roughly 1.2x). Its fee base depends on business owners actually releasing spend, which the evidence says rarely happens (5-6% realized against 20% targeted). It also sells execution to a CFO who already holds the missing ingredient and has cheaper alternatives. A's regulatory and concentration risks are real, but B's problem is more likely to be fatal because it undermines the revenue itself. The call is close.
h2h:C03:C13:ab.a_biggest_risk: No evidence that any non-Elevance, non-UnitedHealth Medicaid plan will pay a fixed, non-contingent fee to an unaffiliated vendor. Plans may insource (Centene has 338K LTSS lives in-house), buy from CareBridge, or insist on savings-only, while their Medicaid margins and budgets shrink. Cycles of 18-30 months and state delegation approvals could outrun the runway. The thin-margin, caseload-ratio-bound labor rung may not produce the 10-15% margin the pitch assumes.
h2h:C03:C13:ab.b_biggest_risk: Realization. Business owners do not release the identified spend (5-6% realized against 20% targeted in the cited health-system panel), so third-party invoice lines never fall and there is no fee base. This compounds with the unanswered 'why pay us' question: CFOs cap the share near 15-20% or choose Redress, renegotiation or in-house, so the company is left funding engineering for a lagged, contingent, low-valued revenue stream.

decisive_factors: B's key price assumption (about 6.5x EBITDA for $15-25M family laundries) matches the sponsor size-premium bands the critics cite, GF Data at roughly 5.9-6.7x. A's orphan-price assumption rests on two distressed data points in the hottest sector in energy, with Pelican, Arlington and nuclear-only funds all bidding.

B's failure mode is that nothing gets bought at the cap, which costs time and little capital. A's chain needs ASL and QA status to survive a change of control, owners to accept AI procedures, insurers to cover AI work, and a rare nuclear QA/licensing co-founder, so more links can break.

B's addressable supply is larger and more proven: 100-200 route-based targets, with ten-plus funded buyers showing the mechanism closes deals. A's pool of five ASL boutiques at orphan prices is not evidenced, and its demand side contradicts itself: the discount is only $1-7k per deliverable and owners keep the liability.

A's only differentiator is the unmeasured 30% AI productivity claim, and the dossier admits rivals can buy the same tools. B's lever is price discipline plus a size-premium multiple. That lever is weak but needs no unproven technology, and B's median ($45M revenue) and stated upside odds (about 10%) are somewhat higher than A's ($25M, 1-8%).
h2h:C10:C16:ab.reasons:
Both ideas are, once stripped of their claimed edges, buy-and-build roll-ups. Each has a median case of roughly 8-12% IRR and a low-probability upside that rests mostly on multiple expansion. So the question is which roll-up is more likely to be executable at all, and which fallback is better.

B wins narrowly, mainly on executability. Its central assumption, buying family laundries at about 6.5x, is untested for rollover deals. It is at least consistent with published size-premium bands, and the mechanism clearly works: Alsco, Wildman, Falcon, Surge, ImageFIRST and others close these deals regularly. A needs several unproven things to hold together: orphan ASL-listed nuclear boutiques that nobody else is bidding for, a QA listing that survives a change of control, owners awarding per-deliverable work outside alliances, E&O cover for AI-produced work, and a hard-to-find nuclear QA insider as co-founder. Hiring scarce nuclear engineers is also called "not fully fixable."

A has the better fallback sector: nuclear demand is growing and exits are hot. But that heat also bids up entry prices, which undercuts A's sourcing thesis. A's one real edge, AI hours cut, is unmeasured on calculation work, and its second-round critic put the upside at only 1-3%.

B's weakness is real: no moat, an 8% median IRR, and adverse selection among sellers. If sellers want 8x and strategic prints, B simply never buys, so it fails cheaply. I would not call this a clear win. It is close to even.
h2h:C10:C16:ab.a_biggest_risk: The target-supply and entry-price assumption fails: no ASL-listed nuclear boutique can be bought at or below 6.5x outside the Pelican, Arlington and New Mountain processes, or customers and QA status do not survive the ownership change. The business then either never starts or becomes an overpriced ordinary roll-up, with the AI-productivity edge unproven and copyable.
h2h:C10:C16:ab.b_biggest_risk: Sellers do not accept about 6.5x with 20-35% rollover from a new, unproven vehicle, because Alsco, Wildman and PE platforms offer higher prices and more certainty. Any seller who does accept is adversely selected, and the platform buys nothing or buys poor assets, leaving an 8% median IRR roll-up with no moat.

decisive_factors: B's own arithmetic makes the median case a capital loss: about $25M invested for $1.3-2M EBITDA, which is 12-20x paid. The real success probability is therefore the 8-10% upside only, and that upside returns only 1.4-2.1x on $60-75M.

B rests on a purchase price nobody has found, in a sector with thin and often negative margins (Wisconsin -12.5%). The premium-fee segment is unsized, and Texas has free entry, so acquired books are not sticky. H.I.G. and General Atlantic compete for the same small operators.

B's tail risks are structural: IRS 3504 joint-and-several tax liability, a $162M wage-hour settlement, DOJ and CMS enforcement, and state or federal cuts to paid-caregiver self-direction that the plan says it cannot fix. A's regulatory exposure is lighter, because R1-R3 carry no downstream risk and the plan keeps authorization decisions.

A has better economics at scale and a more credible scale story (a pooled 24/7 desk with a staffing floor). It also has a cheap staged path: about $8-12M to two paid pilots, with a kill gate at month 12 if there is no $1M paid pilot.

A's demand objection is first-order, but it matches an established category: plans already outsource operations to Maximus, Conduent and CareBridge. The refined offer sells substitution of an admin budget the plan already carries.
h2h:C03:C02:ab.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded and neither clears a venture-grade expected value. I lean to A narrowly, because its downside is cheaper and its economics are better if it works.

B is a PE-style roll-up that needs $60-75M of sponsor capital. By the critic's math from the pitch's own figures, the median outcome loses money: roughly $25M invested for $1.3-2M EBITDA. The upside is a joint event (premium fees of about $150 holding, 79k participants, two statewide wins, a New York slot opening). Even if it lands, it returns about 1.4-2.1x over seven years. The load-bearing assumption is that small operators earn 15-20% margins and will sell at about 1.0x revenue. No deal price has been found by me or by any critic, and the Wisconsin cost data shows the sector losing money at competitive prices. B also carries tail risks that can wipe out equity and that the plan itself calls unfixable: joint tax liability, wage-hour class actions, enforcement, and cuts to self-direction.

A's central objection is real. No non-Elevance plan has been shown to pay a fixed fee, and plans are shrinking and insourcing. But A now sells substitution of an admin budget the plan already carries, which fits how health plans buy outsourced operations. The first-stage capital is smaller ($8-12M), and kill gates sit at months 12 and 24. If R3 works, margins are better than B's. The weaknesses are R3's thin margin and an upside that is only about $14M EBITDA.

I rate this a close call. A's demand risk is existential but cheap to resolve, while B's economics look structurally poor even when it works.
h2h:C03:C02:ab.a_biggest_risk: No non-Elevance, non-UnitedHealth plan pays a fixed, non-contingent fee to an unaffiliated vendor. They insource, buy CareBridge, or demand savings-only terms. This lands while plan budgets are shrinking and sales cycles run 12-30 months.
h2h:C03:C02:ab.b_biggest_risk: Small fiscal agents with real 15-20% margins cannot be bought at about 1.0x revenue. Sponsor-backed H.I.G. and General Atlantic crowd out the buy side, so the only sellable assets are the money-losing ones. The median case then becomes a capital loss.

decisive_factors: Severity of objections: A's critics rated the objections 'serious' and the dossier called it 'wounded'. All three of B's critics rated theirs 'fatal' and B's dossier said 'weak, trending dead'. A's objections are about unproven demand. B's include a legal-structure problem and a pricing problem.

Pricing logic: A replaces admin and coordination spend the plan already carries, at or below 95% of in-house cost, with no risk licence and low capital. B needs the startup to run 17-24% cheaper than the hospital's own commercial functions, with no route density, no benchmark and a 5-year lock-in.

Market and moat: A has a larger pool (about 660k HCBS-using members, $1.2-1.8B of spend) and proven category demand (CareBridge, HHAX). B has about 160 target systems and a 'neutrality' edge that only 10-20% of stayers value. The hospital owns its own TIN and contracts, so B's switching costs are weak by design, and the nearest precedent (PAML/Kootenai) ended in the operator being acquired and fired.

Probability-weighted outcome: A's median is about $18M, with credible partial outcomes at R1-R2 (about $55-60M ceiling without the labor rung). B's honest unconditional median is about $7-8M. Its upside rests on a 33% win rate against Orion, TriCore, Mayo/ARUP/Chi and the nationals, with no US precedent, and its layers (hub, JV) undercut its own neutrality.

Cheap, falsifiable test: both can be tested for under $3k. A's pass or kill criteria are sharper and the risk is purely commercial. B also depends on counsel clearing Medicare billing, EKRA and 42 CFR 424.73.
h2h:C03:C11:ab.reasons:
I prefer A, with a clear margin, though neither is a great business.

Both have a thin-margin services core. A's $100M of revenue is about $14M of EBITDA. B's is about $8-9M, mostly pass-through, with an enterprise value of $80-130M. So venture-scale upside is about equal and both are long shots (A about 5-8%, B about 2-5%). The difference is in the base case and in what can kill each one.

A's biggest objection is that no non-Elevance plan has been shown to pay a fixed fee to an unaffiliated vendor. That is a commercial risk. The refinement already dropped the weak "neutral" thesis for a substitution-pricing thesis. It also removed the risk-licence exposure by putting risk last, and the product is an administrative subcontract. The market is large, the buyer has a budget line, and CareBridge's growth and HHAX's 180+ MCOs show plans buy this category. Even if only R1-R2 sells, the business reaches roughly $55-60M. Plans that insource or buy from Carelon would cap it, but they would not make it unviable.

B's objections are structural. After the rebuild it needs hospitals to sign a 5-year contract at a price that implies a 17-24% cost advantage no startup can have without density. Hospitals' alternatives are free or cheap (in-house, ARUP/Mayo advice, a national's management offer, a check from Labcorp). The only documented customer of the model (Kootenai) fired its operator. The legal fix (a 100% hospital-owned LLC) is unverified by counsel, and EKRA and 424.73 add friction. The hub and JV layers needed for scale contradict the neutrality moat.

A's cost of being wrong is a cheap, fast kill. B has more ways to fail, and several are outside the founders' control (regulators, national competitors, hospital preference for cash).
h2h:C03:C11:ab.a_biggest_risk: No evidence that a non-Elevance, non-UnitedHealth Medicaid LTSS plan will pay a fixed, non-contingent fee (about $40+ PMPM for operations, about $110+ PMPM for coordination) to an unaffiliated cold-entrant vendor instead of insourcing, buying from CareBridge, or insisting on savings-only. R3's 10-15% margin in a ratio-bound labor business is the second assumption.
h2h:C03:C11:ab.b_biggest_risk: Hospitals' best alternatives (in-house, ARUP/Mayo/Chi advice, a national's management deal, or a sale for cash) beat a startup's offer. The cost-plus price needs an unsupported 17-24% cost advantage with no route density. No US precedent exists of a non-national operator being chosen over those alternatives and renewed, and the legal structure is still unproven.

decisive_factors: Profit per revenue dollar and survivable downside: A reaches about 34% gross and 14% EBITDA at scale ($14M on $101M), with no risk capital until year 2+. B has 10-12% gross at best and 3-4% after the second critic's correction. B's upside is $4-7M EBITDA, and its median case is break-even.

Probability stack and capital at risk: A's odds are 5-8% for the upside and about 25-30% for $15M or more, on $8-12M of seed capital and a falsifiable cheap test. B is about 3% for the upside. It needs a sponsor, a surety line and supply slots before the first package, and one bad early loss (a rotor failure or casting inflation) can wipe out its retained capital.

Quality of the objections: all three of B's critics rated it fatal (the Hanwha copy risk, scored RFPs that reward references and bonds, an insurance wrap likely uninsurable under the NY fortuity opinion). A's were serious and mostly answered by the rewrite (no downstream risk, priced as substitution of existing admin spend, neutrality dropped as the pitch).

Demand mechanism: A sells a mandated, ratio-bound cost the buyer already carries, and plans are cutting admin. Its main unknown (will a non-Elevance plan pay a fixed fee) is open but plausible. B's demand test selects for cases where the prime loses money, and its customer segment (OEM-transactional buyers with no ISP alternative) is the least likely to award to an unreferenced newcomer.
h2h:C03:C01:ab.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded and neither is a clean venture-scale winner, so this comes down to which has the better expected outcome per dollar and year of founder effort. A wins on three counts.

First, economics. A's rungs R1-R2 are an ops-plus-software substitution sale at roughly 60%+ implied gross margin, with R3 labor as the thin layer. At the $101M upside it produces about $14M of EBITDA. B is pass-through revenue. Its own refined doc gets 10-12% gross at par pricing. The second-round critic's arithmetic puts the margin at 3-4% before bond premiums, bid costs and liquidated damages. Its $110M upside is $4-7M of EBITDA, and its median is break-even.

Second, risk structure. A carries no downstream insurance risk in R1-R3 and needs no plan equity. Its first 24 months cost $8-12M, and a two-week priced-offer sprint cheaply tests the single key assumption. B takes fixed-price scope-growth risk with no hardware, no references and no moat for 4+ years. It needs a sponsor, a surety line and slot reservations before it can win anything. Its insurance wrap hits an adverse New York ruling.

Third, the critic record. All three of B's critics were fatal. A's were serious, and the rewrite conceded the right points.

A's weaknesses are real: unevidenced demand, shrinking buyers, 12-18 month sales cycles, and an unproven R3 margin. Even so, A's median is more plausible and its probabilities are higher (5-8% vs about 3%). Rough expected value favors A by a wide margin.
h2h:C03:C01:ab.a_biggest_risk: No non-Elevance, non-UnitedHealth Medicaid plan will pay a fixed, non-contingent fee to an unaffiliated vendor. The plans that can afford it insource (Centene) or already buy CareBridge, and the rest insist on savings-only. The R3 margin (10-15% at 95% of in-house cost) is also unproven, and without R3 the ceiling is about $55-60M.
h2h:C03:C01:ab.b_biggest_risk: A no-reference, no-hardware startup cannot win the work or finance the risk. Buyers score references and demand 100% bonds. Hanwha and other ISPs can copy the cap. The margin that survives the demand test is about 3-4%, so the company is either unfinanceable (no sponsor, no surety, no slots) or loses money on its first few packages.

decisive_factors: The fatal objection to A is existence of demand. No plan has been shown to want this, rivals already buy CareBridge or insource, and buyers are shrinking. The fatal objection to B is price, and its sellers, buyers, lenders and deal flow are all evidenced.

At the median B is the larger, more tangible business: about $45M of bought revenue and roughly $6-7M of EBITDA, against A's about $18M and roughly $2-3M. At the upside B reaches about $26M of EBITDA against A's about $14M, and the stated odds are 10% for B against 5-8% for A (1-2% by A's own critic).

B buys existing cash-flowing route books deal by deal. If sellers will not accept 6.5x or less, the team walks away at near-zero cost, so B behaves like an option. A must burn $8-12M, with 12-18 months to a first paid pilot, before it learns whether anyone pays.

A's economics are weak even if it works. Its labour-bearing rung carries a thin, asserted margin, its price undercuts plans' in-house cost at scale, its upside arithmetic has a gap, and $100M of revenue is only about $14M of EBITDA on $50-80M of capital. B's weakness is mediocre median returns (about 8% IRR) and a thin edge, but that failure mode is ordinary returns rather than no sale at all.
h2h:C03:C16:ab.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded, so I compared how likely each is to die outright and what each pays if it lives.

Idea A is a build-from-zero fixed-fee services business sold to Medicaid plans. Three critics and the dossier found no evidence any non-Elevance plan wants it or will pay a non-contingent fee. Revealed behaviour points the other way: rivals buy CareBridge, big plans insource (Centene has 338K lives in-house), and savings-only is the market norm. Buyers are cutting costs and exiting states. Sales cycles run 12-24 months with state sign-off. The labour-bearing rung that carries the $100M case has a margin asserted rather than derived, and it conflicts with the caseload-ratio argument. Its price also exceeds a larger plan's in-house cost. Even the best case is about $14M of EBITDA on $50-80M of capital. The likely outcome is no paid pilot.

Idea B is a conventional roll-up with a thin edge. Its median return of about 8% IRR is mediocre, and strategics and PE platforms are strong, funded competitors. But the model is proven. Sellers exist, deals close monthly, and lenders and independent-sponsor capital are available. The whole thesis rests on one cheaply testable number, the entry multiple. Entry discipline (walk away above 7x) means failure usually looks like no deal or ordinary returns, not a burned seed round. Every acquisition buys real, recurring-contract cash flow. The median is a tangible $45M-revenue business, and the upside has more EBITDA than A's.

B's risks are adverse selection and a weak edge. A's risk is that there is no customer. I weigh a no-customer failure as more likely and more final. The margin is 2 rather than 3 because B's median returns are poor and its edge is nearly nil.
h2h:C03:C16:ab.a_biggest_risk: No non-Elevance, non-UnitedHealth Medicaid plan will pay a fixed, non-contingent fee to an unaffiliated vendor. Plans insource, buy from CareBridge, or insist on savings-only, and no one has shown demand for this product. Plans are also cutting budgets and exiting states.
h2h:C03:C16:ab.b_biggest_risk: Family laundries will not sell to a new, unproven vehicle at or below about 6.5x normalized EBITDA with rollover. Alsco, Wildman and PE platforms bid about 8x or more with more certainty. Entry at 7.5x cuts IRR to about 12.5%, and the median case to about 4%. The only sellers who accept would then be adversely selected.

decisive_factors: A's fatal objection (will a plan pay a fixed fee) is testable in two weeks and is a normal BPO sale into a real $1.2-1.8B budget line. B's fatal objections (invented 19% contribution, adverse-selected sellers, no-exit capital) can't be settled by its own test.

B's return is capped by design: hold-forever with a 6-8% preferred yield, a 6.6% hub EBIT even in the upside, and about EUR 0.8M EBIT in the median. A keeps ordinary equity upside (about $14M EBITDA at scale, strategic and PE exits) and has the better median.

B is a direct clone of better-capitalized players (HomeServe/Brookfield, VINCI, Konzmann, MEISTEREHRE) on the same channel, and its own marginal-economics logic says neighbours with spare capacity absorb closing books more cheaply. A's incumbents are adjacent, and rivals already buy outsourced HCBS ops.
B needs a German-speaking Handwerk-credible operator and EUR 28-30M of no-exit equity from a first-time team. A needs $50-80M but in stages, and its first rungs are low-capital admin subcontracts.
A's headwinds are real (shrinking Medicaid plans, insourcing, thin R3 labor margin, 5% buyer savings), so the call is close.
h2h:C03:C09:ab.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded long shots, and the critics put the upside case at 1-2% for each. The question is which is more likely to be killed by its objections, and what each is worth if it survives.

A's central risk is demand. Nobody has shown that a plan will pay a fixed fee. But the category exists: CareBridge scaled, rival plans subcontract outsourced HCBS operations, and the budget line is real. The kill test is a cheap, direct price test with 12 or more buyer calls over two weeks, and it hits the exact assumption that matters. If A fails, it fails early and cheaply. If it works, the ladder runs from admin subcontracts with software-like margins up to labor-bearing coordination. The upside is about $14M EBITDA with ordinary equity and a strategic or PE exit, and the median is a roughly $18M-revenue ops company. Its flaws are real: the R3 margin is asserted, the scale argument only holds for small plans, buyers are shrinking and insourcing, and the plan's saving is only about 5%.

B has a clearer seller-side story, since closing owners exist. But its economics are invented (19% contribution, EUR 240k overhead). Its sellers are adverse-selected. Its pitch is already run by better-capitalized rivals (Brookfield's HomeServe, VINCI, Konzmann). Its own marginal-economics logic favors neighbours with spare capacity. Its structure caps investor return at a 6-8% yield with no exit, which makes the EUR 28-30M raise by a first-time team very unlikely. The median is about EUR 0.8M EBIT. Even the upside is about EUR 6M EBIT, and the two-week test cannot validate the model.

A has the larger, more liquid payoff and a faster, cleaner falsification, so it edges out B.
h2h:C03:C09:ab.a_biggest_risk: No non-Elevance, non-UnitedHealth Medicaid LTSS plan pays a fixed, non-contingent fee for outsourced HCBS operations and coordination. Plans insource, buy from CareBridge/Carelon at a marginal discount, or insist on savings-only. The value to the plan is only about 5% of loaded cost, and the R3 labor margin is unproven.
h2h:C03:C09:ab.b_biggest_risk: The unit economics are unproven (19% contribution, 70% retention on books from owners who could not sell), and the structure cannot be financed. A first-time team would have to raise EUR 28-30M or more of no-exit, capped-yield equity against better-capitalized direct competitors (HomeServe/Brookfield, VINCI), so it likely stays a small regional service group.

decisive_factors: Demand evidence is much stronger for A: 128 to 160-week lead times, buyers visibly paying 3 to 15% for speed, and intermediaries such as Ayr (over $500M of orders on $25M raised), FluxCo and Giga already reaching scale. B's only demand evidence is a shortage of qualified technicians, and the dossier itself found no source showing shops buy temporary technicians at scale.

B's load-bearing price assumption is probably false. A 93% markup ($52 bill on a $27 wage) compares with a 35 to 45% staffing norm and an implied $34 to 39 bill from the existing LAUNCH temp-tech comp. Shops can hire direct at $24 to 28, and WIOA subsidies likely exclude hire-out staffing. The conversion fee also contradicts the tenure assumptions, which pushes median EBITDA to about 0%.

Both medians are weak, but A's upside is worth more and is somewhat likelier. A has a 2 to 3% chance of about $120M revenue and $8 to 12M EBITDA, an $80 to 150M exit, and a deal size of about $2M per unit. B has a 1 to 2% chance of $100M revenue at 7 to 16% EBITDA, a low-multiple staffing business.

A's downside is staged and asset-backed, with fee-only brokering first and at most $15M at risk in a matched book. Its main flaws are timing, since the premium may fade as new OEM capacity lands in 2028, and no moat. B's flaws are structural: a thin-margin staffing model facing workers' comp and liability exposure, PE-backed consolidators, and direct-hire substitutes.
h2h:C04:C06:ab.reasons:
I put A ahead by a narrow margin. Both ideas are rebuilt, wounded, low-moat intermediaries whose most likely outcome is failing the two-week test, so this is a ranking of weak options.

On expected value, A has the better evidence and the bigger payoff. The need is documented: lead times of 128 to 160 weeks, buyers paying 3.4% to 15% for speed, and startup intermediaries (Ayr, FluxCo, Giga) already taking real volume with tens of millions of capital. That shows the pain is real and a newcomer can capture orders. The risk is competition and supply access, not whether anyone wants the product. A also scales by ticket size. About $2M per unit means a handful of deals pays for a small team, and the upside case would be an $80 to 150M company. Its capital is heavy ($30M equity plus a warehouse line) but staged. The first 12 weeks are fee-only, and principal risk is capped at about $15M with title passing only against a PO or at 12% or more below replacement cost.

B's central assumption looks wrong. Shops are asked to pay about $52 an hour for six-week trainees. That is a 93% markup against a 35 to 45% norm, and the one temp-tech comp implies a bill rate of about $34 to 39 for experienced techs. The direct-hire substitute at $24 to 28 is cheap and common, and the WIOA subsidy likely excludes hire-out staffing. The free-conversion terms conflict with the assumed 1.7-year tenure, which takes median EBITDA to about zero. The demand figures measure a shortage of qualified technicians, not Level-1 slots, which are easy to fill. Even if the price holds, the business is a 5 to 10% margin staffing firm with brake and tire liability and well-funded roll-ups buying the same targets.

A's biggest weakness is that its supply side is unevidenced and the premium may compress in 2028. I rank that as less likely to be fatal than B's unproven willingness to pay.
h2h:C04:C06:ab.a_biggest_risk: Neither a newcomer's access to supply nor the speed premium is evidenced. No source shows OEMs will accept pooled-deposit reservations or that cancelled units are assignable. Established dealers (JCL, Maddox, Giga, Sunbelt Solomon) may already deliver in 20 weeks or less at a thin spread. New OEM capacity in 2028 would then compress the premium to a dealer spread of about 5%, leaving a break-even business with no moat.
h2h:C04:C06:ab.b_biggest_risk: Shops and dealers will not pay a staffing bill rate of $50 or more per hour (about 93% over wage) for six-week trainees when they can hire directly at $24 to 28. Nothing found shows temp-technician buying at scale. Breakeven is about $47.50, the closest comp implies a $34 to 39 bill, and the conversion terms and the WIOA subsidy assumption both undercut the model.

decisive_factors: A's demand is documented and acute. Lead times run 128-160+ weeks, buyers are paying premiums for speed, and intermediaries (Ayr, Giga, JCL) have reached $100M+ with tens of millions of capital. B has no existence proof of a funded, paid-per-invoice-drop shop at scale, and no RFP or contract was found.

B's own median case is a thin-margin services company with $17M revenue and about $28M of burn (planned at $45-60M), breaking even around year 8-9. A's median is roughly break-even after a rebuild that cut equity to about $30M, and its first 12 weeks need no inventory.

B's core 'why pay us' question is unanswered. The CFO already owns the capital and the authority, the comparators are 25%-once advisers or doing it in-house, and the stated edge is parity with DIY. B's fee base also depends on owners releasing spend, with 5-6% realized against 20% targeted. A's gap is narrower and testable, though competitive.
