Feedback speed and kill cost. A's 14-day test uses real dealer quotes and buyer calls with clear kill lines. B's test relies on friendly contacts handing over AP exports, and its pass metric is emailed intent, not an invoice line falling.
B has the higher ceiling ($100M revenue at about $20-33M EBITDA versus A's $8-12M), but both uppers sit at about 2-4%. That is not enough to offset B's negative median.
h2h:C04:C13:ab.reasons:
Both ideas survived their critics only as small, low-odds businesses, so this is close. The upside cases are similar: about 2-4% odds of $100-120M revenue. B's upside is richer, with $20-33M EBITDA against A's $8-12M. B's contingent-services revenue would be valued low, though, as the PRGX comp of about $195M suggests. The call therefore rests on the median and the downside.

A sells into a real, acute, documented shortage with proven willingness to pay and a large pool ($1.5-3B a year). The rebuild killed the fatal parts: the $0.7B fleet is gone, leaving about $30M of equity and matched-book guardrails. Its median is a small, roughly break-even dealer-financier. Its losses are capped by a 25% unsold-inventory limit and a 6-month hold limit. Its early steps are fee-only and carry no inventory risk. Its weaknesses are real. There is no moat, dealers can copy it, the supply side (assignable cancelled units, OEM slots for a newcomer) is unevidenced, and the premium compresses as OEM capacity lands in 2027-29.

B's median is the failure mode by its own admission: $17M of revenue, deep burn, break-even near year 8-9. Its fatal flaw is realization. Business owners must release spend, the evidence is 5-6% realized against 20% targeted, and the CFO already holds the capital and the authority the pitch sells. The fee, about 1.3 years of savings, is only at parity with doing it yourself. B also adds liability, E&O and AI-exclusion issues.

A's weaknesses are competitive and cyclical. B's are demand-side and behavioral, which is harder to fix.
h2h:C04:C13:ab.a_biggest_risk: No defensible edge or supply access. Dealers and funded intermediaries (Maddox, JCL, Giga, Ayr, FluxCo) already serve the same buyers at the same spreads. A newcomer has no OEM slot priority and no evidence that cancelled units can be assigned. As new OEM capacity lands in 2027-29, the speed premium compresses to a roughly 5% dealer spread.
h2h:C04:C13:ab.b_biggest_risk: Realization. Even with a CFO sponsor, business owners may not release the identified spend, so third-party invoice lines never fall and no fee base exists. The evidence is 5-6% realized against 20% targeted. CFOs also have little reason to pay 26-30% for three years plus a tail for capital and authority they already own, when Redress, in-house teams and renegotiation are the alternatives.

decisive_factors: Demand for A is proven and already monetised (Ayr, Giga, FluxCo, JCL and Maddox sell into the same shortage). Demand for B is unproven: no carve-out precedent, and buyers are bundling and insourcing.
A's failure mode is a thin dealer or broker margin, which still earns money. B's failure mode is that nobody buys and revenue is zero. A has a higher floor.
A can earn revenue within months through fee-only brokered deals. B needs about 20 months to get a causal result and does not ramp until year 3.

Upside profit pools are similar (A about $8-12M EBITDA, B about $9-13M), and both upside cases are rated heroic and not credible. So the probability of reaching a real median business decides it, and that favours A.

A sells into the hottest US capital-formation theme (data-center power) with strategic acquirers available. B is England-only, needs procurement-law expertise, and its fund layer depends on a standard nobody has adopted.
h2h:C04:C15:ab.reasons:
Both ideas are badly wounded, and neither upside case is believable (A about 2-3% unconditional, B under 1-3%). The choice therefore turns on which one is more likely to become a real, profitable median business and which has the less fatal objection.

A's objections are about margin and moat, not about whether anyone buys. The shortage is real, with 128-160 week lead times. Funded intermediaries (Ayr above $500M of orders, Giga above $150M of infrastructure sales) show buyers pay for speed. A newcomer broker or matched-book dealer working a 5-10% spread on $2M+ units can cover a small team on a handful of deals, and brokered fees need no inventory. The risks are real: dealers already exist, supply from cancelled slots is unevidenced, and the premium compresses once new OEM capacity lands in 2028-29. Even so, the realistic floor is a small profitable dealer or broker, and the exit options are strategic.

B's central objection is that no one has shown they will buy outcome-priced hot-spot cohorts. Landlords are bundling into whole-stock deals and insourcing. A newco cannot meet the turnover tests and D&B score, so it ends up subcontracting to incumbents (Wates Healthy Homes, Mears) at prime margins. Its premise (top 5% of homes carry 25% or more of spend, persistently) is unrun. Revenue starts in year 3, and fixes are mostly pass-through works. If the premise fails, the likely result is nothing.

B is cheaper to kill, but A's expected outcome is higher, so A wins narrowly.
h2h:C04:C15:ab.a_biggest_risk: No defensible supply or speed edge. OEMs allocate slots to volume buyers, and no source shows cancelled or in-production units can be assigned to a third party. Stocked dealers and funded startups already serve the same buyers, so the business shrinks to a thin-margin broker once new capacity lands in 2028-29.
h2h:C04:C15:ab.b_biggest_risk: No buyer exists for the product: landlords are bundling and insourcing, no cohort carve-out precedent was found, and a newco cannot pass procurement turnover tests. Even if the top-5% concentration test passes, outcome-priced capitation may never be bought, leaving only commodity fix-only subcontracting.

decisive_factors: B's central economics are contradicted by evidence and by its own model. The $52 bill rate is a 93% markup against a 35-45% norm, and the only comparable (LAUNCH, experienced techs) implies about $34-39. Break-even is about $47.50. Free conversion after about 1,000 hours pushes median EBITDA to roughly zero or negative once shops and workers act rationally. A's weak points (no demand evidence, asserted R3 margin) are unproven rather than contradicted.

Business quality if it works. A sells a mandated, ratio-bound cost line ($1.2-1.8B pool) on 3-year delegated contracts with real switching costs and a tech-enabled, AI-automatable desk (R1/R2). B sells a product consumed by its own conversion mechanism, with no moat, a direct-hire substitute that is cheaper than the all-in price, and PE-funded consolidators (Amerit, True North, Ryder) as competitors.

Revealed outsourcing behavior. Rivals have bought HCBS operations from third parties (CareBridge in Iowa, Centene with Cityblock), and the category produced a $2.7B exit. Nothing comparable shows shops buying trainee labor at scale, and the trade's big employers (Penske, Love's, Ryder) insource training.

B wins on capital, speed and cost of being wrong ($500 test, fast SMB sales cycles, favorable freight and shortage timing). A pays for this with 12-18 months to a first paid pilot, $8-12M seed, and a shrinking, cost-cutting buyer pool. That cost is what keeps this a close call.
h2h:C03:C06:ab.reasons:
Neither idea is likely to reach $100M. Both second-round critics put that case at 1-2%, so the choice depends on which realistic business is likelier to work and worth more if it does.

B is faster and cheaper to test, and its timing is better. Shops have open requisitions, freight is recovering and the technician shortage is documented. B's problem is the business as designed. The bill rate has to be about 1.9x the wage when the nearest comparable implies roughly $34-39 for experienced techs. The customer's all-in cost ($14k including the premium) exceeds its direct-hire-and-train alternative ($8k). Free conversion after about 1,000 hours cuts tenure and pushes EBITDA toward zero. The WIOA subsidy is likely ineligible for staffing, and Michigan-style licensing complicates deployment. Several independent assumptions have to hold at once, and the evidence leans against some of them. The moat is also nil.

A is slow and its demand is unproven, but the objections are mostly about access and unproven willingness to pay, not demonstrated impossibility. The spend is mandated, rivals have outsourced HCBS operations, and the category supports large outcomes. If R1 and R2 land, they are stickier and higher margin than anything in B, and automation is a plausible cost lever. Valuation conditional on success is roughly 2-3x B's.

I pick A on quality-adjusted odds, with B close because it costs far less to be wrong.
h2h:C03:C06:ab.a_biggest_risk: No non-Elevance, non-UnitedHealth plan pays a fixed, non-contingent fee to a new unaffiliated vendor. Plans insource, buy from CareBridge or insist on savings-only, and a contracting buyer pool stretches the 12-18 month sales cycle past the runway.
h2h:C03:C06:ab.b_biggest_risk: Shops will not pay a staffing-style bill rate of about $50 or more per hour (a 93% markup) for six-week-trained entrants when they can hire directly at $24-28 and train. Even where they do, conversion mechanics and attrition push margin to roughly zero.

decisive_factors: Capital at risk versus outcome: A needs about $30M equity with at most $15M of matched-book exposure, and it can start as fee-only brokering. B needs $60-75M of sponsor-style acquisition capital for a 5-8% margin business, so even its upside returns only about 1.4-2.1x.

B's own arithmetic undermines it: buying at 1.0x revenue with a 5-8% EBITDA margin means paying 12-20x EBITDA. The median case is effectively a capital loss, and the only public cost data show the sector losing about 12.5% at competitive prices.

Demand reality: A sells into a documented shortage (128-160 week lead times) where dealers already earn 12-15% spreads. A new dealer-financier therefore has a plausible base case even without a moat. B's open-market premium segment is unsized, its cost side is unverified, and funded sponsors (H.I.G., General Atlantic) compete for the same targets.

Tail risks: B carries policy risk (federal and state cuts to self-direction, fraud crackdown) and liability (IRS 3504 joint-and-several tax exposure, wage-hour class actions such as the $162M Calderon settlement), neither of which diversification fixes. A's main tail is price normalization as OEM capacity lands in 2027-29, which caps its upside but is survivable because inventory is short-duration and matched-book.

Test quality: A's 14-day test measures live demand, dealer response and willingness to pay, and it can kill the idea cheaply. B's test only checks whether sellers will talk, and sellers with good books are probably already being shopped to sponsors.
h2h:C04:C02:ab.reasons:
Both ideas are mediocre after refinement, so this is a choice between two small outcomes. A is the better bet because its failure modes are cheaper and its base case rests on a real market.

A is a dealer and financier in a transformer shortage. Competitors such as JCL, Maddox and Giga show the spread exists, and Giga reports infrastructure sales above $150M. A new entrant can plausibly reach a $20-30M-revenue profitable desk by brokering first and taking principal risk later, on modest equity of about $30M. The upside case is overstated: the fees are padded and the true margin is nearer 7-10%. But the downside is capped, the test is quick, and acquirers such as Sunbelt/TJC, Quanta and the OEMs are natural exits. The real weakness is no moat. Supply for the reserved and cancelled-unit tiers is unevidenced, and the premium compresses once new OEM capacity arrives in 2027-29.

B is structurally worse. It is a roll-up of thin-margin Medicaid fiscal agents, and its own figures contradict each other: it buys at about 1.0x revenue while projecting a 5-8% margin. That means paying about 12-20x EBITDA to hold a business that, in the only public cost data, loses money at competitive prices. It needs $60-75M of capital. It faces sponsor-backed bidders (H.I.G., General Atlantic) for the same targets. It also carries policy risk (cuts to self-direction, the fraud crackdown) and tax and wage-hour liability. Its median case is effectively a capital loss, and its upside is a joint event of several low-probability conditions.

A has a plausible small-business outcome, while B's most likely outcomes are failing the gate or earning below its cost of capital.
h2h:C04:C02:ab.a_biggest_risk: No durable edge or supply access. OEMs resell freed slots themselves, cancelled units rarely fit another buyer's spec, and existing dealers already deliver warranted units fast. The premium therefore collapses to a thin spread of about 5% as OEM capacity lands in 2027-29.
h2h:C04:C02:ab.b_biggest_risk: Qualified small fiscal agents may not be buyable at about 1.0x revenue with healthy margins. The sector loses money at competitive-bid prices, funded sponsors bid up the good targets, and the only available ones are sick. Capital is then deployed at 12-20x EBITDA into a business with 5-8% margins.

decisive_factors: Severity of objections: all three first-round critics rated A fatal (incumbent dealers already in stock, unit economics, capital and timing), while all three rated B only serious.

Durability of the demand window: A's premium depends on a transformer shortage that Rystad and new OEM plants say is fading by 2027-29. B's succession wave (about 54,000 planned closures against 49,000 handovers over two years) is structural and lasts a decade or more.

Downside and capital at risk: B stages EUR 4M, EUR 10M and EUR 16M and pays half the price only if customers stay. A needs about $30M equity plus a $50-60M warehouse line, first-loss on price, bought near peak pricing.

Floor outcome: B's median is a real service group with positive EBIT (about EUR 0.8M). A's median is roughly break-even dealer gross profit, and its supply side (assignable cancelled slots) has no evidence at all.
h2h:C04:C09:ab.reasons:
Both ideas ended up weak after refinement, so this is a close call between two small-outcome businesses. Each upside is about 2-5% likely and neither has a real moat. The difference is in the median and the downside.

Idea A concedes its original premise: Maddox, JCL, Giga and Sunbelt Solomon already stock or ship units in this size range. What is left is a 7-13% dealer spread on pass-through units. The median case is about $30M of revenue and roughly break-even. The supply side, third-party-assignable cancelled or in-production slots, has no source, and an OEM can simply resell a freed slot itself. The timing contradicts itself: the thesis needs the shortage to last through 2029, but new OEM capacity lands in 2027-29. The test also checks demand and dealer quotes only, not whether any OEM will cooperate. A bad outcome costs real capital: inventory price risk and a thin-margin warehouse line.

Idea B is a less exciting capital-allocation business, but it rests on a structural flow of sellers. Contingent pricing protects against the book shrinking. It can start on about EUR 4M, and its median is a real if modest cash-generating service group. Its weak spots are real. The 19% contribution and the recurring-revenue share are invented, the incumbents are well funded, the German-speaking operator requirement is a hard constraint, and the upside capital (EUR 28-30M of no-exit equity) is unlikely to be raised. But it fails cheaply and early, and A does not.

Overall B has a better probability-weighted outcome, with a higher floor and less capital at risk.
h2h:C04:C09:ab.a_biggest_risk: The advertised gap is not real: incumbent dealers and OEM-direct channels already deliver in a similar window. The cancelled or reserved slots the plan depends on have no evidence of being assignable. The scarcity premium also fades as new capacity arrives in 2027-29, which leaves a thin 5-10% dealer spread.
h2h:C04:C09:ab.b_biggest_risk: The unit economics rest on unproven inputs. Closing owners may mostly hold consumer-heavy, owner-dependent books that do not hold 70% retention at 0.25-0.4x. The invented 19% contribution on absorbed crews may also fail, as crews are free to leave in a labor-short market. Then no hub reaches the roughly EUR 1.55M break-even or the EUR 3M+ scale that makes a Meister pay, and the business stays a loss-making micro-firm collection that investors will not fund.

decisive_factors: Existence proof: transformer intermediaries (Giga at $150M+ infrastructure sales, Ayr at $500M+ in orders on about $25M raised, plus JCL, Maddox and Sunbelt Solomon) already reach $100M+ revenue on tens of millions of capital. B has no US precedent of a non-national operator that a hospital chose over cash and kept past year 3.

Demand and willingness to pay are better evidenced in A. Lead times are 128-160+ weeks, buyers are documented paying 3-15% for speed, and individual deals are about $2M. B's price only works if a startup with no route density beats the hospital's own cost by 17-24%, and that baseline is unbenchmarked.

A's first stages are cheap and quick to falsify or monetize: dealer quotes plus buyer calls in 14 days, then fee-only brokering with no inventory. B's stand-up and sales cycles are long (hospital CFO and board, 5-year terms, 90-180 day payer enrollment), and its test needs hospital executives to hand over cost data.

B has a documented customer rejection (Kootenai fired the closest analog, PAML) and stacked legal tails: CMS 1833(h)(5)(A) wholly-owned billing, 42 CFR 424.73 and EKRA. B's neutrality claim also conflicts with its own hub and JV upside layers. A's regulatory tails (DPA hoarding, EO 14420 provenance, tariffs) are more manageable.
h2h:C04:C11:ab.reasons:
Both ideas are weak and both critics left them wounded. Each has a median case near break-even (A about $30M revenue at 11-13% gross margin and a 25-person team; B about $7-8M after correcting its own inconsistent funnel). Each has an upside of roughly $8-12M EBITDA at 2-8% probability. So the choice turns on which is more likely to produce a real, modestly profitable business and which fails faster and cheaper if wrong.

A wins on that. The shortage it addresses is documented, with lead times of 128-160+ weeks and premiums for speed that buyers have actually paid. The deals are large, around $2M each, so a few fee or principal transactions already matter. Direct peers (Giga, Ayr, JCL, Maddox) show the intermediary model scales on modest capital. Even if the date-certain premium collapses, a brokerage or dealer business with real gross profit is a plausible fallback. A's open question is supply access. The two-week test doesn't cover it, but fee-only brokering in months 3-12 does, and it needs no inventory.

B has a worse structure. A hospital's best alternatives are cash from Quest or Labcorp, doing it in-house, or advice from Mayo, ARUP or Chi. Its one real analog failed and the customer left. Cost advantage, neutrality demand and the 33% win rate are all unsupported guesses, and the regulation (Medicare billing, EKRA, state rules) is heavier. Its upside is mostly pass-through revenue, and the hub and JV layers undercut its only moat.

A's chief weakness is that it has no moat. The shortage could also fade in 2027-29, but that risk is known and priced into A's matched-book design.
h2h:C04:C11:ab.a_biggest_risk: No defensible edge and no proven supply: dealers (JCL, Maddox, Giga, Sunbelt Solomon) already stock or quote fast units, OEMs have no reason to give a newcomer slots, and the cancelled-unit supply is unevidenced. As new OEM capacity lands in 2027-29 the speed premium could compress to a roughly 5% dealer spread.
h2h:C04:C11:ab.b_biggest_risk: No stayer health system signs a 5-year open-book contract with a startup instead of taking a national's management offer, using Mayo/ARUP/Chi advice, or keeping the work in-house. The required 17-24% cost advantage is unproven, the one documented customer of this model fired its operator, and the structure carries Medicare billing, EKRA and 42 CFR 424.73 risk.

decisive_factors: Floor vs. ceiling: B buys existing cash-flowing, recurring-revenue businesses, so even a failed thesis leaves an owned operating asset, while A's median case is roughly break-even on $30M of revenue and its premium may not exist.

Failure mode severity: all three of A's critics rated their objections fatal (competition, pricing, capital/execution), and the supply side (assignable cancelled units, OEM slots for a newcomer) is unevidenced and untested. B's critics rated theirs serious, and the main unknown (the price sellers accept) is directly testable.

Time-limited vs. durable demand: A depends on a transformer shortage that Rystad, new OEM capacity in 2027-28, and the plan's own pre-mortem say is easing, so it is structurally a peak-scarcity trade. B rides a multi-year family-succession wave with no expiry.

Capital and expected value: B needs about $10-14M of anchor equity, deal-by-deal, with proof of funds and a kill rule. Its modeled outcomes are 1.5x median and 3.5x at 21% IRR in the upside. A needs about $30M of equity plus a $50-60M warehouse for 7-10% gross margins and a 2-3% unconditional upside.
h2h:C04:C16:ab.reasons:
Both ideas are weak, and neither would get my money unconditionally. The question is which has the better expected outcome and the less fatal objections.

A, after being rebuilt, is a dealer-financier. The original fleet is withdrawn. Its own refined numbers give a median of $30M revenue at about 11-13% gross margin, roughly $4-5M gross profit, about break-even after a 25-person team. The second-round critic argues the blended margin is nearer 7-10% and the $120M upside is overstated by $10M or more. The upside is about 2-3% likely unconditionally. The 'nobody holds stock' gap was false, so the premium has to survive JCL, Maddox, Giga, Sunbelt Solomon, Ayr and FluxCo. Supply depends on OEMs or cancelled-order holders handing slots to a newcomer, and nothing shows that is assignable. The moat is none. The scarcity rent is also fading as new OEM capacity lands in 2027-28.

B is a conventional buy-and-build, but it is a real one. It buys cash-flowing, contract-based businesses, with no timing cliff and a succession wave behind it. Entry at 5.5-6.5x is roughly the going lower-middle-market sponsor price, which makes closing deals plausible. The downside is bounded: an owned laundry at 3.0-3.5x leverage, not a stranded inventory bet. Median returns are mediocre (1.5x, about 8% IRR), but the upside (3.5x, about 21%) has a concrete mechanism in margin synergy and scale multiple expansion. The main risk is price discipline, and the owner-call test measures it directly.

B has a higher floor, a more durable market, less fatal critiques and lower capital needs.
h2h:C04:C16:ab.a_biggest_risk: The premise that buyers will pay a durable premium for date-certain delivery is probably false or short-lived. Dealers already stock and quote comparable units, OEMs have no reason to give a newcomer slots they can sell directly, and new capacity compresses the spread toward a 5% dealer margin. The business then sits at about break-even with no moat.
h2h:C04:C16:ab.b_biggest_risk: Family owners may not sell to a new, unproven vehicle at 6.5x or below. Strategics and PE platforms with the same rollover offers set the price at 8x or more. Entry at 7.5x cuts the base-case IRR to about 12.5% and the median to about 4%, so the business then fails or reduces to a generic roll-up with adverse selection.

decisive_factors: Demand evidence: A rides a shortage that is documented in many sources (128 to 160+ week lead times, buyers prepaying, a 3.4% premium paid to save years). B has no evidence that any owner wants a growth cap and would pay for it, and its own pass test selects the cases where the prime loses money.

Time to revenue and capital at risk: A can book fee-only brokered deals within weeks, then take at most $15M of matched-book risk on about $30M of equity. B cannot earn until spring 2028 and first needs a sponsor, a surety line and references, plus $20-25M of retained fixed-price risk.

Payoff shape: A's upside is a $8-12M EBITDA dealer-financier that an acquirer would plausibly buy for $80-150M. B's upside is $4-7M EBITDA, and its median ends as a $20-40M sale to an ISP, with a negative-skew tail (a rotor failure on early package 3 can wipe out capital).

Fatality of the objections: A's biggest holes (existing dealers, OEM slot assignability) are testable cheaply and early, and a pass leaves a small but real business. B's biggest holes (no-reference entrant fails scored RFPs and 100% bonds, thin or negative margin against ISPs at 0.85-0.90x OEM, an unverifiable insurer wrap) are structural and cannot be fixed by the founders alone.
h2h:C04:C01:ab.reasons:
Both ideas are weak. Each has about a 2-3% unconditional chance of the roughly $110-120M revenue upside, a median of about $30M revenue at break-even, and no moat for years. I picked the one with the better expected outcome for the capital and time it needs.

A is a trading and brokerage business in the middle of a well-documented physical shortage. Its demand side is the strongest evidence in either file, and the downside is bounded by matched-book rules, a 25% cap on unsold units and a $15M early exposure limit. Early cash is available from fee-only brokerage while the company learns whether OEMs will assign slots. If it works, the result is a dealer-financier with $8-12M EBITDA that has several natural acquirers. The risks are real. Dealers already stock and quote units. The supply tiers are unevidenced. The 2028-29 capacity wave may collapse the premium. The model has no moat and the margin is thin.

B is a fixed-price, risk-bearing prime with no hardware and no references, selling to buyers who score references over price. The Austin RFP shows this directly: the winner scored 61, and an unreferenced entrant would top out near 39. Its demand gate and its unit economics pull against each other, because the pass test requires 10% or more cost growth while the margin only works if growth is 9% or less. At the ISP price level, margin is about 3-4% before bond premiums. It also depends on a sponsor, a surety and an insurer wrap that no one has produced evidence for, and it cannot earn before 2028. Even its upside yields only $4-7M EBITDA. A is risky but has the larger and faster payoff, and B's most likely failure points cannot be tested in two weeks.
h2h:C04:C01:ab.a_biggest_risk: The supply side: nothing shows that an OEM will assign cancelled or in-production units, or accept a newcomer's pooled-deposit reservation. Existing dealers (Maddox, JCL, Giga, Sunbelt Solomon) may already deliver new, warranted units fast enough. If so, the business is a thin-margin broker with a premium that compresses as new OEM capacity arrives in 2028-29.
h2h:C04:C01:ab.b_biggest_risk: Qualification and unit economics. A no-reference entrant loses scored RFPs and cannot get 100% bonds without a sponsor. Where owners can switch, they already have ISP turnkey offers at 0.85-0.90x OEM price, so the cap is priced at a 3-4% margin. Meanwhile the company holds $20-25M of fixed-price scope-growth risk, with the shops that control rotor slots as its own competitors.

decisive_factors: Median outcomes: A is a modestly profitable, capital-light regional business (about $20M revenue, 0-7% EBITDA, a few million of capital). B's own median burns $28-60M, reaches roughly $17M revenue and breaks even only around year 8-9. B's author says the median is 'not a good business'.

Falsifiability and time cost: A's make-or-break variable (will shops pay $50 or more an hour) can be tested for under $500 in two weeks with real order forms. B's riskiest assumption (owners release the money, 5-6% realized against 20% targeted) takes about 12 months to observe. The 14-day test only measures stated intent from friendly contacts.

Core value proposition: A sells a scarce input (technicians) against a real open requisition that earns the shop $149 an hour. B asks a CFO to pay about 1.1-1.3x a year of savings for capital and authority the CFO already owns. B's own claim is 'parity with DIY', and Redress, in-house teams and renegotiation sit at lower cost.

Capital and structure: A has no funded engineering, receivables are weekly-billed, and customers are small shops that decide fast. B funds $1M or more of engineering per client up front, needs E&O insurance, SOC 2 and a lender, and faces 9-18 month enterprise cycles. Its 36-month annuity and revenue cliff make growth hard to sustain.

Tails are similar and both poor: about 1-2% for A and 2-4% for B to reach $100M. B's tail is slightly fatter, but it sits behind much more capital and a negative-value median, so it does not offset the base case.
h2h:C06:C13:ab.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded and neither has a believable $100M path. The question is which has the better expected outcome net of capital and time.

Idea A is a hire-train-deploy technician staffing business. Its main objection is price. A 93% markup against a 35-45% staffing norm is probably wrong. LAUNCH's postings imply a bill rate of about $34-39. The tenure and conversion math also contradicts itself, and the WIOA subsidy is likely unavailable. Those are serious, and the price objection may well be fatal. But they are cheap and fast to learn: a $500, two-week test of 40 shops with order forms. If the test fails you lose almost nothing. If it passes, you hold a real if low-margin business. It sells into a documented shortage, and the shop earns about $149 an hour on the labor it buys. It needs no vans and no funded engineering. At a median of about $20M revenue it is plausibly profitable with a few million of capital.

Idea B is outcome-priced IT run-cost retirement. It faces several correlated objections at once. Realization was 5-6% against a 20% target. It is unclear why a CFO would pay for execution the CFO already owns. Alternatives are cheaper, such as Redress at 25% once, in-house teams, and renegotiation. The fee equals about 1.1-1.3 years of savings. Insurance, SOC 2 and lender terms are unresolved. The author's own median burns $28M or more, with negative EBITDA until year 8-9. Learning whether it works takes about a year, not two weeks. The upside needs five or six assumptions to hold together.

An early kill limits B's downside. But the conditional-on-success median is still a poor business, so A has the higher expected outcome.
h2h:C06:C13:ab.a_biggest_risk: Shops will not pay a roughly 1.9x markup (about $50 or more an hour against a $27 wage). They hire directly at $24-28, or the market only supports the $34-39 staffing norm. In that case unit economics break near $47.50, and tenure and conversion leakage push EBITDA to about zero even if they do pay.
h2h:C06:C13:ab.b_biggest_risk: Realization. After a CFO backs the program, business owners do not release enough identified run spend, so invoice lines do not fall and the fee base never exists. The evidence is 5-6% realized against 20% targeted. Compounding this, the CFO has cheaper alternatives (Redress, in-house, renegotiation) and the company funds the engineering, so low realization means heavy cash burn with little revenue.

decisive_factors: A's central risk (will shops pay about $50/hr) can be tested in two weeks for under $500, and revenue pilots can start within months. B's central risks need a winter-long controlled trial (about 20 months) before capitation revenue is even plausible.

A sells a familiar product, hourly staffing plus a training-to-hire conversion, into a documented shortage with a known buyer (the shop owner with an open requisition). B asks a risk-averse landlord to carve out its worst homes and take outcome risk. Two critics rated B's go-to-market and procurement as fatal, no precedent was found, and buyers are bundling and insourcing instead.

The downside floors differ. If A's $52 bill rate fails, it can fall back to a smaller training-and-placement or dealer-academy business with real cash flow. If B's concentration or persistence test fails, or the buyers never appear, the company has nothing to sell, and its fallback of fix-only subcontracting to primes pays prime-level margins.

Capital and geography: A needs little before its 90-day gates and its cost per head is known. B needs about GBP1M before the trial result, then GBP6-10M equity, then a GBP30-60M fund. It also depends on UK procurement law, FSMA perimeter questions and a category that does not yet exist.

The probability-weighted tails are comparable (both critics put $100M at about 1-2% or less), but A's middle outcome of $10-25M of revenue is much more probable than B's median, which only applies after clearing a 30% data gate and a trial.
h2h:C06:C15:ab.reasons:
Both ideas are long shots at the headline $100M, and both second-round critics put that tail at about 1-2% or lower. So the decision rests on the probability of a decent mid-size outcome, how fast the cheap tests resolve, and what happens if the key assumption fails.

A is a conventional hire-train-deploy labor business. Its main flaw is thin economics: a 93% markup against a 35-45% norm, a break-even bill rate near $47.50, tenure and conversion assumptions that contradict each other, and WIOA subsidy that is probably unavailable. Those are serious, but they are the kind of pricing and retention risks that a two-week outreach to 40 shops and a 90-day pilot will settle. The shortage is real. Temp-to-hire technician staffing already exists, and Tradesmen International shows skilled-trades staffing can pass $100M. If the full markup fails, the business can still run at lower scale as a trained-entrant placement or academy-for-dealers company.

B has a clever core idea and honest self-critique, but it stacks sequential dependencies. The 5-8% of homes must be concentrated and persistent, a landlord must hand over its ledger, and a randomized trial must show a cut of 40% or more through a winter. The trial also collides with Awaab's Law, and the pricing basis was shown to be internally inconsistent. After that, a new outcome-priced contract category has to appear, capital has to be raised, and primes have to subcontract. Procurement turnover tests exclude a newco. Wates and Mears already sell adjacent bundles, and buyers are insourcing. First real revenue is years away, and blended EBITDA is only 8-12% on pass-through works.

A fails faster and cheaper, and it has more ways to land a $10-25M outcome. B's expected value rests on a category that may never form.
h2h:C06:C15:ab.a_biggest_risk: Shops and dealers will not pay a staffing-style bill rate of about $50/hr (a 93% markup over a $27 wage, with break-even near $47.50). They can hire direct at $24-28, and a comparable temp-technician competitor appears to bill around $34-39 for experienced techs. Conversion that becomes free after about 1,000 hours would also push tenure toward 6 months, which roughly doubles the graduates needed and takes EBITDA to about zero.
h2h:C06:C15:ab.b_biggest_risk: No landlord buys the product. There is no precedent for a capitated or outcome-priced carve-out of a landlord's worst homes. Buyers are bundling whole-stock deals and insourcing, the incumbents (Wates, Mears) can add a gain-share schedule at no cost, and a newco fails the procurement turnover and D&B tests. Even if the data gate passes, revenue depends on a category that does not yet exist and on a winter-long trial.

decisive_factors: Capital at risk before the fatal objection is tested. A's make-or-break assumption (a shop pays $50 or more an hour) is a $500, two-week test. B's equivalent (small fiscal agents that earn margin and sell near 1.0x revenue) is cheap to test, but if it passes the thesis needs about $25M for the median case and $60-75M for the upside.

Median-case economics. A's median (about $20M revenue, 7% EBITDA, a few million dollars of capital) is a plausible regional business. B's median (about $25M revenue at 5-8% EBITDA on about $25M invested) implies 12-20x EBITDA paid, a probable capital loss, so it is really a bear case.

Sector fundamentals. Medicaid fiscal agents lost 12.5% in aggregate in Wisconsin at competitive prices, face policy and fraud-crackdown risk, and carry tail liability (Section 3504 joint liability, a $162M wage-hour settlement). A's demand is a documented technician shortage, and it has fallback paths (placement fees, employer-funded training) that still earn something.

Competitive structure. B must buy small targets while H.I.G. and General Atlantic pay about 10x for the same kind of asset, and its upside is a joint event of several low-probability conditions. A's refined model sidesteps the PE-funded mobile-PM incumbents and sells open requisitions rather than a share of a fleet's PM wallet.
h2h:C06:C02:ab.reasons:
Both ideas were wounded in the second critique round, and both $100M cases are unlikely. The earlier critics put A at 1-2% and B at 8-10% or less, and B's own arithmetic makes its upside a joint event. So the decision rests on the median outcome, the capital needed, and how cheaply each can fail.

A is a staffing-plus-training business with a demand signal that is real: roughly 20% of technician slots are unfilled, shop labor bills at $149 an hour, and Level-1 techs earn about $27. The critics' hits are real. The 93% markup is unproven, the conversion economics contradict the tenure assumption, the WIOA subsidy is likely unavailable, and the Michigan supervision rule is a constraint. But the bill-rate question can be answered for under $500, and a pass leads to small pilots, not an acquisition. If $52 an hour fails, there is a credible fallback in placement fees or employer-funded training. The median is a $10-25M regional business at roughly 5-7% EBITDA, and it needs only low single-digit millions in capital.

B is a financial roll-up that needs a seasoned co-founder and a sponsor. Its unit economics are thin: Wisconsin's four fiscal agents lost 12.5% in aggregate. Its margin thesis depends on an unsized premium segment, and its buy price is internally inconsistent: 1.0x revenue is not 6x EBITDA at 5-8% margins. Even if the $103M upside hits, the return is about 1.4-2.1x over seven years. Policy and liability risk are large and cannot be diversified away.

A has a lower ceiling than hoped but a much better risk-adjusted outcome.
h2h:C06:C02:ab.a_biggest_risk: Shops will not pay a staffing-style bill rate of $50 or more an hour (about 1.85x the $27 wage, against a 35-45% norm) for six-week-trained Level-1 techs, because they can hire direct at $24-28 and conversion becomes free after about 1,000 hours. That would break the unit economics, since break-even is about $47.50.
h2h:C06:C02:ab.b_biggest_risk: The acquisition thesis fails on price and margin. Small non-sponsor fiscal agents either do not earn the assumed 15-20% margin at $110 or more per participant per month, or they will only sell at a multiple (above 1.5x revenue) that PE buyers like H.I.G. and General Atlantic already set. The company then pays 12-20x EBITDA for a business that loses money at competitive-bid prices.

decisive_factors: Cost and speed of learning: A's decisive unknown (will shops pay about $50 an hour) is testable for under $500 in two weeks, with first revenue in months. B needs a sponsor, a surety line, insurer indications and two reference awards before first revenue, realistically spring 2028.

Capital at risk and tail shape: A's early losses are small payroll and cohort costs, and a failed pilot costs little. B carries a fixed-price tail, with $20-25M of retained-risk capital needed before event 1 and a bad early loss able to wipe the company.

Fixability of the fatal objections: A's fatal critiques mostly kill the $100M thesis and leave a $10-25M regional business. B's three fatal critiques hit the core mechanism: scored RFPs and bonds a no-reference entrant cannot clear, an insurer wrap that is probably uninsurable, and an incumbent that can copy the clause.

Optionality and adjacent pivots: if Level-1 bench pricing fails, A can still sell experienced-tech temp-to-hire (LAUNCH precedent), placement fees, or employer-paid training, in a documented labor shortage. B's fallback is a crowded, bond-gated plain independent contractor.

Quality of the profit pool: both are thin and mostly pass-through (A 5-12% EBITDA, B about $4-7M EBITDA at $100M revenue). The edge goes to the one a normal capable team can actually staff and execute, since B also needs deep power-industry credibility and a financial sponsor outside the founders' control.
h2h:C06:C01:ab.reasons:
Neither idea is attractive in absolute terms. Both were wounded by their own refinement, both put the real chance of $100M at 1-3%, and both have mediocre median outcomes. A median is about $20M revenue at 5-7% EBITDA, roughly $1-1.5M. B's median is a subscale break-even company that might sell to an independent service provider (ISP) for $20-40M. So the question is which has the better probability-weighted outcome per dollar and year at risk, and that favors A.

A's weakness is a single, falsifiable assumption: shops will pay about $50 or more an hour for six-week-trained Level-1 technicians. The evidence is not kind. LAUNCH's pay and conversion terms imply a bill rate of roughly $34-39 for experienced techs. The conversion fee and tenure are internally inconsistent, and WIOA on-the-job-training subsidies likely exclude hire-out structures. But the company can learn this in two weeks for under $500 and before any capital is committed. It operates in a real, documented labor shortage with proven analogs (Tradesmen International, LAUNCH). If the Level-1 price point fails, there are adjacent pivots.

B is slow and gated on things the founders do not control. It needs a $15M or larger sponsor, a surety willing to bond a start-up, an insurer view that contradicts the New York no-fortuity opinion, and shop slots in a casting squeeze where ISPs serve their own customers first. Its own pass condition (as-found growth of 10% or more) selects the cases where margin falls to about 3-4%. Hanwha can copy the cap. Buyers scored references over price in the Austin RFP. Its 18 months of overhead before first revenue and its fixed-price tail make a bad outcome expensive, while the upside is only $4-7M EBITDA.

A has the higher chance of becoming a real business, a cheaper way to fail, and more pivots.
h2h:C06:C01:ab.a_biggest_risk: The core price assumption fails: shops and dealers will not pay a staffing-style bill rate of $50 or more per hour (about 1.9x the Level-1 wage) for six-week-trained technicians when they can hire direct at $24-28. Evidence from LAUNCH implies $34-39 for experienced techs. Below about $47.50 the unit economics break, and rational early conversion of workers to the customer's payroll makes even the median roughly break-even.
h2h:C06:C01:ab.b_biggest_risk: A no-reference start-up cannot qualify to sell the product: buyers' scoring (50 of 100 points on technical plan and track record) and 100% performance bonds screen it out, while the insurer wrap is probably uninsurable. The company therefore depends on an outside sponsor, a surety and shop slots it does not control, and carries uncapped scope-growth risk on a thin 10-12% margin.

decisive_factors: Demand-side proof: A has a documented, acute shortage and real analogs (Penske's six-week program, LAUNCH TransTechs, Tradesmen at $100M+). B has no US precedent of a health system choosing a non-national operator over cash or a national's offer, and its one documented customer (Kootenai) fired the operator.

Fatal-objection quality: A's pricing assumption ($50+/hr) is untested and could fail, but it can be repriced or restructured. B stacks unresolved structural risks (Medicare 1833(h)(5)(A) wholly-owned rule, EKRA, 42 CFR 424.73, OIG, state laws) on a cost-advantage claim that needs about 20% savings from a startup with no route density.

Sales and capital shape: A sells to many small buyers in weeks and falls back to a $10-25M regional business that consolidators would buy. B needs about 10-15 five-year CFO contracts with slow cycles and a lab-industry insider founder. Its $110M upside needs $70M+ of outside capital and sponsor decisions, and its realistic floor is a $2-6M advisory boutique.

Testability and downside: A's $500 test of 40 shop calls gives a hard price signal in two weeks. B's test needs 20 hospital finance leaders to share cost data and a counsel opinion, and passing it proves little about a 5-year contract.
h2h:C06:C11:ab.reasons: Both ideas are wounded and both have roughly 1-3% odds of hitting $100M revenue, so the call turns on probability of a good-enough outcome, floor, and capital. A is a thin-margin staffing and training business. Median EBITDA is about 7%, and about 0% if the tenure and conversion contradiction holds. Its enterprise value at scale is modest. Even so, it addresses a real, measured pain (ATRI 65.5% of shops understaffed, 19.3% of slots unfilled). The training model is proven in production at Penske. The buyers are thousands of small shops, so each sale is quick and the idea is cheap to falsify. If $52/hr fails, the same academy can pivot to a lower-bill-rate plus placement-fee or employer-funded model. The floor is a $10-25M regional business, and PE-backed consolidators like Amerit and True North are active buyers of exactly that pipeline. B is a more elegant but more fragile concept. Its viability rests on a legally contested structure, a 20% cost advantage that nobody has benchmarked, and a startup winning 5-year contracts against Quest, Labcorp, Orion, TriCore and Mayo/ARUP/Chi advice. Its value-if-it-works is similar to A's, but it comes through three stacked layers needing sponsor capital. The one operator precedent (PAML) ended in acquisition by a competitor, and Kootenai insourced after leaving the model. The expected outcome favors A.
h2h:C06:C11:ab.a_biggest_risk: Shops and dealers will not pay a roughly 93% markup (about $50-52/hr against a $27 wage; break-even about $47.50) for 6-week Level-1 trainees when they can hire direct at $24-28. Free conversion after about 1,000 hours also shortens tenure, and WIOA subsidies likely exclude hire-out staffing. Together these push margins to about zero.
h2h:C06:C11:ab.b_biggest_risk: No non-selling health system has been shown to sign a 5-year open-book operating contract with a startup at a price at least 8% below its own cost, rather than insourcing, buying advice from Mayo/ARUP/Chi, or taking a national's management deal. That demand-plus-cost-advantage claim is unbenchmarked and has no precedent, and the structure is also exposed to Medicare 1833(h)(5)(A) and EKRA.

decisive_factors: Capital and time to find out: A's key assumption (a shop pays at least $50/hr for pre-trained Level-1s) can be falsified for under $500 in two weeks, and a failed pilot costs little. B needs a $100-175M equity partner plus a proven casting operator, and about a 35% chance of closing even a first deal.

Fatality of the objections: A's two fatal critiques are scoped to the $100M thesis, and a $10-25M regional business survives them. B's three fatal critiques hit its existence: no precedent for OEM prepay to a non-incumbent, a sources-and-uses gap, and a customer value proposition near nil, since the customer could sign the same deal with the plant's current owner.

Return quality if it works: B's own upside gives about 1.8-3.3x gross and low-to-mid-teens IRR, which may not raise the equity at all. Its unconditional median is $0, and the likeliest failure (no sellable asset at a sane price) is out of the founder's control. A's success case is small but real, and the training bench can be retargeted to dealers or off-highway.

Probability-weighted payoff: B's conditional payoff is larger (about $55M revenue and $10M EBITDA at the median) but the odds are about 3-5% and the founder holds a minority promote. A has roughly 10-20% odds of a modest business with thin 0-7% margins, plus a 1-2% tail. Expected dollars are close, so cheap falsification and capital-lightness break the tie.
h2h:C06:C05:ab.reasons:
Neither idea is attractive. This is a close call between a thin, cheap, testable staffing-plus-training business and an expensive, structurally doubtful acquisition platform.

B has the larger payoff if it works: about $55M revenue and $10M EBITDA conditional at the median, and possibly $200M revenue. Its keystone, an OEM paying a multi-year reservation with make-whole to a non-incumbent owner, has no precedent. The Doncasters model the idea imitates is not take-or-pay. The unanswered question is why an OEM would route its capex funding through a new owner when it can sign the same deal with the current owner. Sources and uses do not close at the low end. The author's own upside gives mediocre equity returns of about 1.8-3.3x gross, which makes raising $130-175M of equity doubtful. The target pool is being consolidated by GE/CPP, Pursuit, Arcline and Doncasters, and the founder would probably end up as a deal originator with a small promote. All three first-round critiques were fatal, and the structural ones are not fixable by narrowing.

A is probably a low-margin business, and it is shakier than its author admits. The 93% markup over wage is unproven. The temp-technician competitor LAUNCH implies bill rates of $34-39 for experienced techs. WIOA on-the-job-training subsidies likely exclude hire-out staffing. Free conversion after about 1,000 hours contradicts the assumed tenure, which pushes median EBITDA to roughly zero. Even so, the realistic outcome is a $10-25M regional business, the fatal critiques were scoped to the $100M claim, and the failure mode is cheap and fast to detect. The bench and academy assets can also be pointed at dealers, off-highway equipment or consolidators. That optionality is worth more than B's fixed, binary structure.

On probability times value, weighed against capital and time, A edges B narrowly.
h2h:C06:C05:ab.a_biggest_risk: The bill rate: shops and dealers will not pay a roughly 93% markup ($50-52/hr on a $27 wage) for 6-week trainees, since they can hire directly at $24-28. That breaks the unit economics, which break even near $47.50, and tenure and conversion pricing push median EBITDA to about zero.
h2h:C06:C05:ab.b_biggest_risk: No non-captive OEM will fund a line at a qualified caster owned by a non-incumbent. They can do the same deal with the current owner or buy the caster themselves, so the capital stack never closes and no sellable target is left at a sane price. Both outcomes leave a $0 unconditional median.

decisive_factors: B's core mechanism is a proven playbook (buy family firms at 5.5-6.5x, sell a scaled platform at 8-10x) with real transactions and funded buyers, so its main risk is price discipline. A's core mechanism, a roughly 93% markup on trainee labor, is unproven and contradicted by the file's own staffing benchmarks.

A's own author says the unconditional median outcome is a failed pilot. Its critic's arithmetic puts median EBITDA near zero or negative once conversion and tenure are reconciled. B's median is a mediocre but real operating business with a modest positive return.

B has an asset floor and a graceful fail mode. If sellers will not accept 6.5x or less, the founders simply do not buy and little capital is lost. A's thin-margin staffing model has no asset floor and no moat, and its WIOA subsidy and Michigan licensing assumptions are both shaky.

B's upside tail (about 10% chance of $130M revenue and 21% IRR) creates much more value per unit of probability than A's about 1-5% chance of a $100M, 5-10% EBITDA staffing company. A's credible ceiling is a $10-25M regional business.

B's weaknesses are real: no track record, adverse selection, and a first-time sponsor needing deal-by-deal equity. They keep the call close, because A is cheaper to start and easier for an operating team to execute.
h2h:C06:C16:ab.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded, so I weighed which fatal objection is more likely to land. A rests on one unproven number: shops will pay about $52 an hour for a six-week trainee they could hire directly at $24-28. That is a 93% markup against a 35-45% staffing norm. The only temp-technician competitor evidence points to a bill rate of roughly $34-39 for experienced techs. The model also contradicts itself. Conversion is free after about 1,000 hours, so rational shops convert early, and the critic's arithmetic then puts median EBITDA near zero or below. The WIOA subsidy is likely ineligible for hire-out staffing. Michigan's licensing rules threaten the labor model. Rivals Amerit, Ryder and Penske are PE-backed or already train in-house. A's own author calls the unconditional median a failed pilot, and the plausible ceiling is a $10-25M low-margin business with no moat.

B is a proven buy-and-build in a sector with a real succession wave and active lenders and capital. Its risk is that a new, unproven vehicle cannot buy at or below 6.5x, because strategics and PE platforms set prices. That failure mode is mostly "do not buy", not "lose everything". When it works, the returns come from standard multiple arbitrage plus 3-4 points of synergy. The median is poor (about 8% IRR), but the 21% IRR upside at 10% probability creates far more value than A's tail. The founders also get an asset-backed business with recurring revenue. B's real weakness is adverse selection and the first-time-sponsor capital hurdle. That keeps this a close call, since A needs less capital to test.
h2h:C06:C16:ab.a_biggest_risk: Shops and dealers will not pay a staffing-style bill rate of about $50 an hour or more for six-week trainees when they can hire directly at $24-28. Combined with free conversion after about 1,000 hours, this pushes median EBITDA to roughly zero or negative.
h2h:C06:C16:ab.b_biggest_risk: A new, unproven vehicle cannot buy family laundries at or below about 6.5x EBITDA, because Alsco, Wildman and PE platforms win the good targets at strategic prices. What remains is adverse selection, and returns fall to roughly 12% IRR at 7.5x entry (about 4% median).

decisive_factors: Capital and time to resolve the keystone risk: A's make-or-break question (will buyers pay a speed premium, and can dealers already deliver?) is answerable in 14 days for about $0, and fee-only brokering can earn revenue in weeks 3-12 with no inventory. B needs $100-175M of outside equity plus a proven casting operator before it can test its keystone.

B's keystone behavior has no precedent: no OEM prepay or take-or-pay to a non-incumbent owner was found by the researcher or any critic. B's own dossier calls it dead as a founder-led startup, and the customer-side value proposition is close to nil, since the same funding can go straight to the incumbent. A's demand is better evidenced (3.4% paid to save 2-3 years, 128-160 week lead times, Ayr and Giga scaling as intermediaries).

Founder economics: B is a PE-style capital allocation whose own numbers give about 1.8-3.3x gross, roughly mid-teens IRR, at entry multiples that GE, Arcline and Pursuit can outbid. The founder ends up as deal originator with a small stake, and the unconditional median is $0. A is a thin but real small business with a plausible floor (about $30M revenue, near break-even to modest profit) and a cheap kill.
Both have weak moats and ugly upside odds (A about 2-3% to $120M, B about 5-12% to $100M+), so the lower cost of being wrong and the faster feedback loop break the tie.
h2h:C04:C05:ab.reasons:
I would back A, but only narrowly, because neither idea is attractive on expected value.

A, in its refined form, is a thin dealer-financier. Gross margin is realistically 7-10%, the median case is roughly break-even at about $30M of revenue, and the $120M upside is about 2-3% likely and partly overstated. The competition critique is largely correct: Maddox, JCL, Giga, Sunbelt Solomon, Ayr and FluxCo already work this space, and the supply of cancelled or assignable OEM slots is unevidenced. Still, the market is real. Lead times run 128-160 weeks, buyers do pay for speed, and intermediaries have reached $100M or more of orders on tens of millions of capital. The decisive point is that A's biggest risk can be tested in two weeks for almost nothing. It can start earning brokerage fees without inventory, and it can scale its capital at risk in steps after that.

B is more likely to be fatal. Its keystone is an OEM prepayment with make-whole to a non-incumbent owner, and nobody found a precedent for it. The money Doncasters, Howmet and Chromalloy already get shows customers pay incumbents, not a new sponsor. The target-acquisition prices rest on a non-comparable deal, and qualified assets trade at 6-8x revenue. B needs $130-175M of equity and a proven operator, and its own numbers give mid-teens returns. The founder ends up as originator with a small stake, and the unconditional median is $0. Even if everything lines up, B mostly earns a capital return, not an operating edge. A's cheap, fast, mostly reversible path wins on risk-adjusted outcome, though only by a small margin.
h2h:C04:C05:ab.a_biggest_risk: The speed premium and slot supply are unproven. Existing dealers and intermediaries (JCL, Maddox, Giga, Sunbelt Solomon, Ayr, FluxCo) may already deliver warranted units fast enough, and no source shows OEMs will let a newcomer assign cancelled or reserved slots. That would leave only a roughly 5-8% spread boutique with no moat.
h2h:C04:C05:ab.b_biggest_risk: The capital stack never closes. No OEM has been shown to prepay with make-whole to a non-incumbent owner, and the same customer money goes to Doncasters or Howmet instead. Qualified casters are also priced far above the assumed 2x revenue and are being bought by better-capitalized bidders (GE, Arcline, Pursuit, Doncasters).

decisive_factors: A's core unit economics are contradicted by its own materials: a 93% staffing markup against a 35-45% norm, free conversion after ~1,000 hours that rational shops will use at 6-12 months, and training cost that cannot be amortized over that tenure. The critic's recomputation puts median EBITDA at about -5% to 0% instead of +7%.

A's demand evidence is misapplied, since the shortage is of qualified technicians, not Level-1 slots. Penske, Love's and Ryder insource the same 6-week model, shops can hire a $16-28 entry tech directly, and no evidence was found that anyone buys temporary trainee technicians at scale. WIOA subsidy is likely ineligible for hired-out staffing.

B's market is validated by real transactions: HomeServe Deutschland, Konzmann, Builtech and VINCI show Handwerk roll-ups reaching EUR 100M+ of revenue. Seller supply is structurally abundant (about 54,000 planned closures against 49,000 handovers, with a record 4,950 insolvencies).

B's deal design limits downside. Books are bought at 0.25-0.40x of retained revenue with 40-50% contingent, and the targets are real customers, crews and vans. The failure modes (sellers refuse, books are consumer-heavy) are caught by a two-week ledger test and a month-12 gate, and the fallback is a small, self-funded regional group.

A and B have similar median size ($20M vs $27.6M revenue) and similar thin median profit, and both reach $100M with only about 1-3% probability. So the call turns on which has the higher chance of working at all. A's likely-fatal flaw is arithmetic and market-structure. B's flaws, capital and the invented 19% contribution, mostly cap the upside rather than kill the median.
h2h:C06:C09:ab.reasons:
Both ideas ended wounded, with a credible $100M probability of only about 1-3% and thin median profit (A about $1.5M EBITDA at best, B about EUR 0.8M group EBIT). So the decision turns on which is more likely to work at all, and which objections are more likely fatal.

A's central objections look structural. The business sells a 6-week-trained Level-1 technician at a 93% markup. Its own materials show the break-even bill rate is about $47.50, and LAUNCH's experienced-tech postings imply a bill of only $34-39. The pricing makes conversion free after about 1,000 hours, so rational customers convert early, tenure drops to about 6 months, and training cost per FTE-year roughly triples. The second-round critic's arithmetic puts median EBITDA at about -5% to 0%. The demand figures measure a shortage of qualified techs, not Level-1 slots. The biggest employers (Penske, Love's, Ryder) insource this exact model. WIOA subsidies are likely off the table for hired-out labor. It is also a 1,000-head W-2 staffing business with workers' comp and negligent-training exposure. It is cheap to test, but I think it is more likely to fail the test than pass it.

B's objections are serious but mostly cap the upside. The buy-side market is proven by actual deals, and seller supply is abundant and growing. Contingent pricing and acquiring real customers, crews and vans give structural downside protection. The model ties to standard roll-up route-density logic, and the failure modes are caught early by a ledger-based test, so a small self-funded regional group is a plausible floor. Its flaws are real: no identified anchor LP, an invented 19% contribution figure, adverse selection among sellers, Meister and HWK constraints, and crowded competition. These mostly constrain scale rather than kill the median case.

B is slightly more likely to produce some real business, so I pick B, though it is a close call.
h2h:C06:C09:ab.a_biggest_risk: Shops and dealers will not pay a staffing-style bill rate of about $50 an hour (a 93% markup) for 6-week-trained Level-1 technicians when they can hire direct at $24-28. Even at that rate, free conversion after about 1,000 hours erodes tenure, so training costs are never recovered and EBITDA falls to about zero or below.
h2h:C06:C09:ab.b_biggest_risk: Not enough owner-led Elektro/SHK firms have retainable B2B service books and will accept the contingent 0.25-0.40x formula, because adverse selection leaves the owner-dependent, consumer-heavy books. The invented 19% contribution and 70% retention then fail, and no anchor LP funds the EUR 10M+ follow-on tranche, so the business stays at roughly breakeven scale.

decisive_factors: Objection severity: B drew two 'fatal' critiques (no evidence anyone buys a capitated carve-out; a newco cannot clear procurement, turnover or D&B tests). B's own dossier says 'weak, leaning kill'. A's critiques were all 'serious' and its dossier says 'not dead'.

Demand evidence: A sells into an existing category (contingency, savings-share and decommissioning services such as Redress, SoftwareOne, PRGX and ProsperOps), to US CFOs with their own budgets. B has no carve-out precedent, and buyers are bundling and insourcing.

Entry and fallback: A starts with a paid $75-150k X-ray, so cash arrives in months 2-4, and it has a smaller capital-light fallback. B's first step is a free x-ray, its capitated rung needs GBP20-40M of risk capital, and its fallback is a commodity fix-only contractor against Wates and Mears.

Testability and market: A's riskiest assumption (owner follow-through) can be tested with exports from 3 companies in 14 days, and its US market is larger. B is a single-country market with slow procurement, FSMA and Awaab's Law complications, and a key causal result that needs a full winter (about 20 months).
h2h:C13:C15:ab.reasons:
Neither idea is attractive. Both median cases are about $17M of thin-margin services revenue, and both $100M upsides sit near 2-4% by the authors' own numbers. The question is which one is more likely to die early.

B has the more dangerous objections. Two of its three critics called it fatal, and the objections are about buyer behaviour and the procurement door, not about tuning the model. Landlords are bundling whole-stock deals and insourcing. Winchester and Livin set turnover and D&B tests that a newco cannot pass. Wates already sells Healthy Homes. The signer's gain is under 0.5% of turnover while the landlord keeps the statutory duty. No capitated carve-out precedent exists. The realistic end state is subcontracting to primes at prime margins, with mostly pass-through revenue at 8-12% EBITDA. The causal proof also needs a full winter, and randomised controls collide with Awaab's Law.

A's weakness is the 'why pay us' parity problem, owner follow-through (5-6% realized against 20% targeted), and median burn of $28M or more. But the demand is real. Savings-share and decommissioning services already sell to CFOs. A paid X-ray gives early cash. The invoice-drop rule removes the baseline fight. A capital-light version, with co-funding and low-engineering lines, is a plausible $5-15M profitable business. The US market is larger, and the kill gates are cheap and fast. A's risks are mostly about margin and differentiation, which are survivable, while B's are about whether any buyer exists, which is more likely to be fatal.
h2h:C13:C15:ab.a_biggest_risk: Business owners do not release the identified retirable spend, so realization stays near 25-30% (5-6% was seen against a 20% target). The fee base then barely exists, and the CFO's cheaper alternatives (Redress, in-house, renegotiation) are at parity with this offer.
h2h:C13:C15:ab.b_biggest_risk: No landlord will buy a capitated carve-out of its worst homes from a newco, because buyers are bundling and insourcing, procurement gates exclude new entrants, and Wates and Mears already hold the scope. That leaves a small subcontract or fix-only niche at prime margins.

decisive_factors: A has no structural legal blocker; B has to clear several regulatory hurdles at once (Medicare referral-lab billing, the billing-agent pay rule, EKRA, OIG, state transaction laws). Each one can kill it or make it heavier than its margin supports.

A's fee is metered by a third party (the vendor invoice line falls or it doesn't). B's price rests on an unbenchmarked cost advantage, since the operator must come in 17-24% below a hospital's own cost with no route density, and the dossier found no published cost data.

A's market is broader: about 700 reachable payers across industries and three event-driven channels (M&A, sponsor exits, end-of-support). B has about 160 target systems and roughly 15 winnable ones. The buyer's real alternatives there are cash from Quest or Labcorp, doing nothing, or Orion, TriCore and Mayo. No US case exists of a non-national operator renewing past year 3.

A's median is a mediocre business (about $17M revenue, break-even around year 8-9). Its gates are cheap and fast, though: a $0 14-day test, a paid X-ray, and a kill rule at month 12. B's median is about $7-8M revenue, its stated odds of signing a second client are about 55%, and its $110M upside is mostly pass-through revenue at roughly 8% EBITDA.
Both upsides are long shots (A about 2-4%, B about 1-3%). A's upside is real profit at 52% contribution, while B's is mostly pass-through revenue. That leaves A ahead on expected outcome.
h2h:C13:C11:ab.reasons:
Both ideas survived adversarial rounds as "wounded", and both have a tail probability of roughly 1-4% for $100M. So the choice rests on the median case, the odds of getting there, and how many independent things must go right.

A is a thin-margin services business at median, with about $17M revenue and break-even around year 8-9 if it funds engineering heavily. It has no statute or regulator standing between it and revenue. Its fee base is auditable: no invoice line drops, no fee. It sells to any enterprise with $40M or more of external run spend, through several channels, and starts with a paid $75-150k X-ray that brings in cash early. Its biggest weakness is that its own evidence shows only 5-6% realized against 20% targeted. But that can be tested in 14 days for about $0, and the plan has hard kill gates. The CFO-vs-Redress pricing objection also hurts, since parity with doing it yourself is a weak reason to buy.

B's rebuild gives up the venture-scale structure to stay legal. Its price depends on an unproven 8% cost advantage, from a startup with no density. Its buyers have three better alternatives: cash from the nationals, a national's management offer, and regional operators like Orion and TriCore. Its legal path needs counsel to clear five regimes. Its own authors give 45% odds of never signing a second client and put its median below the $20M bar. Its upside needs a hub, a JV and $50-60M of sponsor money, which undercuts the neutrality pitch.

A's problems are about whether it converts. B's include whether it is permitted to exist and whether anyone wants it.
h2h:C13:C11:ab.a_biggest_risk: Realization: even with CFO backing, business owners don't release the identified spend, so invoice lines don't fall and there is no fee base. The evidence is 20% targeted and 5-6% realized. A related risk is that CFOs cap the share near 15-20% or choose Redress or an in-house program instead.
h2h:C13:C11:ab.b_biggest_risk: Demand and price: a non-selling health system won't sign a 5-year open-book contract with an unproven startup at a price at least 8% below its own cost, rather than taking a national's offer, a regional operator, or doing it in-house. The cost advantage is unbenchmarked, and the structure also has to clear the Medicare referral-lab, billing-agent pay and EKRA rules.

decisive_factors: Capital at risk is staged for A. The first gates are a 14-day test, paid X-rays by day 60 and a signed agreement by day 120, and they cost founder time rather than tens of millions. B has to put real acquisition capital to work, and its own refined pitch puts the full plan at $60-75M.

A's upside is a real business, with 20-50% contribution margins and $20-44M of EBITDA at $100M revenue. B's upside is $100M of revenue at 5-8% margin, which the critic calculates returns only 1.4-2.1x on capital over about 7 years. A 9% chance of a roughly break-even payoff is worth less than A's 2-4% chance of a large payoff.

B's median case is effectively a capital loss. About $1.3-2M of EBITDA on roughly $25M invested is 12-20x paid, against an 8-10x exit. A's median is also poor, but its kill rules stop it before the $28M burn is spent.

The market B sits in is structurally weak. The fee is about 2% of program spend, Wisconsin operators lose 12.5% in aggregate, and the best operator makes only +2%. The sector faces a federal fraud push, state cuts to self-direction, joint-and-several payroll-tax liability and a $162M Calderon-type wage-hour tail. The why-now is mostly spent. A faces a go-to-market problem, but its underlying economics (pay a share of a verified invoice drop) are sound.
h2h:C13:C02:ab.reasons:
Both ideas were wounded in the second round and neither is attractive, so this is a close call between two weak options. I weighed expected value against capital and time.

B is a roll-up of small Medicaid fiscal agents. It needs $60-75M of sponsor-style capital to buy operators in a sector where the only public cost data shows a combined -12.5% margin. The pitch's own median case earns $1.3-2M of EBITDA on about $25M invested. The critic's arithmetic puts that at 12-20x paid, so the median is a capital loss. Even the 8-10% upside returns about 1.4-2.1x over roughly 7 years. On top of that sit a federal and state push against personal-care spending, an active DOJ case, Section 3504 joint-and-several tax liability, and funded competitors (H.I.G., General Atlantic at about 10x) buying the same small targets. No FMS deal price has been found, so the thesis rests on an unobserved number.

A is a funded-retirement shrinker paid per invoice line that drops. It is also poor at its median: a roughly $17M services business that only breaks even around year 8-9. Its odds of $100M are an honest 2-4%. But it deploys money only after gates (paid X-rays, a signed program agreement, an E&O quote, first audited invoice drops), with an explicit instruction to stop rather than shrink. If it works at the upside, it is a 20-40% EBITDA business, and the unit economics improve as AI makes retirement engineering cheaper.

A's most likely fatal flaw is "why would a CFO pay 26-30% for something he could do himself or buy from Redress at 25% once." Realization is also a large risk, at 5-6% realized against 20% targeted in the evidence. But A fails cheaply and early. B can fail after the capital is spent.
h2h:C13:C02:ab.a_biggest_risk: Realization and the "why pay us" gap. Business owners may not release the identified spend (the evidence is about 5-6% realized against 20% targeted). Even if they do, the CFO can get most of the value through DIY, renegotiation or Redress at 25% invoiced once. In that case the fee base is zero, or the company is an undifferentiated $5M advisory boutique.
h2h:C13:C02:ab.b_biggest_risk: Unit economics and acquisition price. Small fiscal agents with healthy margins probably do not exist at a price the cash flow can carry, because sellers anchor on the 10x sponsor deals and the only sellable books are the money-losing ones. The thesis then needs $60-75M of capital to earn thin margins, with Medicaid policy and 3504/wage-hour liability tails stacked on top. The median is a capital loss and even the upside returns about 1.4-2.1x.

decisive_factors: Value per revenue dollar: A's upside path reaches $20-45M EBITDA at $100-120M revenue, while B's $110M upside yields only $4-7M EBITDA because revenue is mostly pass-through parts. At similar low odds (2-4% vs 3%), A's tail is worth several times more.

Severity of the objections: B drew three 'fatal' first-round critiques and its second-round holes (unit economics, no hardware behind the date guarantee, no moat) are structural. A drew 'serious' critiques, and its refined fee rule (no invoice drop, no fee) removed the baseline fight.

Dependencies outside the founders' control: B needs a $15-60M sponsor, a $10M-per-event surety line, scarce rotor and casting slots, and first revenue only in spring 2028. A gets cash in months 2-4 from a paid X-ray, and its gates can be run for near $0.
Downside shape: B retains scope-growth risk on fixed-price outages, and one bad early event can wipe out its capital. A's loss is bounded to funded engineering, with kill gates and liability caps.

Both medians are poor (A about $17M revenue at break-even in year 8-9; B about $30M and a small sale to an ISP). That does not separate them, so the upside quality and speed of invalidation decide it.
h2h:C13:C01:ab.reasons:
I weighed expected outcome as value if it works, times probability, against capital and time. Both ideas come out wounded and both put the odds of their upside at about 2-4%, so the difference is in what a win is worth and how cheaply a loser dies.

A's win is more valuable per revenue dollar. Fees are earned directly on measured invoice reductions, and contribution is 21-52% depending on account size. The upside reaches roughly $20-45M of EBITDA. B's $110M of revenue is mostly pass-through parts and shop labour. At par pricing its gross margin is 10-12%, and against an ISP alternative it is 2-5% before bonds. That leaves $4-7M of EBITDA at the top, and a median outcome of a $20-40M sale to an ISP.

B's objections are also closer to fatal. It has no references, so it cannot clear scored RFPs or 100% bonds. Hanwha can copy a pricing clause. The date guarantee has no hardware behind it. Selecting for owners who would accept a newcomer at price parity selects for the deals where the prime loses money. It needs a sponsor, a surety line and shop slots that the founders do not control, and first revenue is not before spring 2028. It also retains scope-growth risk, so one bad early package can wipe out its capital.

A's weakness is real: realization of 5-6% against 20% targeted, and the risk that CFOs cap the share at 20% or choose Redress or an in-house team. But A tests this in 14 days for about $0, collects a paid X-ray fee in months 2-4, and has explicit kill gates. A fails cheaply and B fails expensively.
h2h:C13:C01:ab.a_biggest_risk: Realization. Business owners do not release the identified retirable spend (the evidence is about 5-6% realized against 20% targeted), so third-party invoice lines never fall. The company would then have funded engineering with no fee base. CFOs capping the share at 20% or less, or choosing Redress or in-house work at roughly DIY parity, would make that worse.
h2h:C13:C01:ab.b_biggest_risk: The wedge is self-defeating. Owners willing to award a $5M outage to an unreferenced newcomer at price parity are the ones with an ISP alternative at 85-90% of the OEM price. That leaves a margin of about 3-5% while the prime retains scope-growth and schedule risk. It has no moat against Hanwha, and it depends on a sponsor, a surety and shop slots it cannot control.

decisive_factors: A's downside is bounded and cheap to learn. A 14-day test, then paid X-rays by day 60, with hard kill gates, means the team finds out within about 12 months at low cost. B's decisive proof (an OEM prepaying a non-incumbent) has never been observed, and B needs $130-175M of other people's equity plus a proven casting operator before it is real.

B's objections are structurally fatal, A's are mostly about size and price. All three critics called B fatal and the dossier calls it dead as a founder-led startup. The customer-side value proposition is close to nil, since OEM money can go straight to the incumbent (Doncasters, Howmet, Chromalloy). The edge over Pursuit, Arcline and CPP in buying scarce assets is thin. Even the upside returns only about 1.8-3.3x gross.

A's market is broad and the demand precedent is real. About 700 reachable payers, against 20-25 for B. Savings-share and recovery-audit models exist (PRGX, Redress, ProsperOps), and a paid entry product gives cash in months 2-4. B's unconditional median is $0.

A's own median case is poor, so it wins narrowly. Thin-margin services, about $17M revenue and break-even around year 8-9. The tail is only about 2-4% unconditional, and price parity with doing it in-house is unresolved. The close margin reflects B's higher value if it works (about $430-540M enterprise value in the upside case) against its very low odds of getting started.
h2h:C13:C05:ab.reasons:
Neither idea is attractive on its own numbers, so this comes down to which has the less fatal flaw and the cheaper, faster way to be wrong.

B (the foundry platform) is a PE-style buyout wearing a startup label. Its pitch value rests on an OEM prepaying a non-incumbent owner. No OEM has been found doing this, and the refinement adds no evidence for it. If OEMs fund 60-80% of a line anyway, they can sign with the current owner, as they already do at Doncasters and Howmet. So the sponsor mainly serves the seller. It would compete for scarce qualified assets against GE/CPP, Pursuit, Arcline and Doncasters. Equity returns on its own upside case are mediocre (about 1.8-3.3x gross). It needs $130-175M of equity and a proven operator, and the founder likely ends up as a deal originator with a small stake. Its unconditional median is $0, and the cycle may peak before capacity lands.

A (the Run-Base Shrinker) is also weak. It has no demonstrated edge over in-house work or Redress, realization could be as low as 5-6% of targeted savings, and the median case is a thin-margin $17M-revenue services firm.
