It does have a large addressable base, precedent for savings-share pricing, a paid entry product that brings in cash early, and a falsifiable test and kill gates that cap the loss. A capable team learns whether it works within months, for little capital. Because its objections concern size and price, not impossibility, it has the higher risk-adjusted expected outcome, though only narrowly.
h2h:C13:C05:ab.a_biggest_risk: Realization. Even with CFO backing, business owners may release only a small fraction of identified retirable spend (evidence shows about 5-6% realized against 20% targeted). Then too few third-party invoice lines fall to support the success fee, the funded engineering never pays back, and the product is at best price parity with a client doing it itself.
h2h:C13:C05:ab.b_biggest_risk: No evidence that a non-captive OEM will fund capacity at a caster owned by a non-incumbent, and no clear reason why it would. Without that, the customer-funded expansion that justifies the equity case collapses. What remains is a first-time sponsor bidding for scarce qualified casters against better-capitalized buyers, at below-hurdle returns, with the turbine cycle possibly peaking.

decisive_factors: B's median outcome is a real cash-generating asset: about $45M of bought revenue at 15% EBITDA margin, financeable with ordinary senior debt. A's own median is a $17M-revenue services firm that burns $28-60M and reaches break-even in year 8-9, which the refinement itself calls 'not a good business'.

B's fatal objection is entry price. It is legible, testable in two weeks, and fails safe: if sellers want 8x or more, the team walks away without having put capital at risk. A's fatal objection is the 'why would the CFO pay us' question plus owner realization (5-6% realized against 20% targeted). Nothing in the dossier shows it is solvable, and the team bears execution risk without controlling the owners.

Demand and a market exist for B (many funded buyers, active deals, lenders, a succession wave). For A, the dossier found no RFP, tender or published contract for third-party share-of-savings run-cost reduction, and the closest comparators (Redress at 25%, DIY, renegotiation at 0%) cost the buyer less.

The upside tails are roughly equal and both low: A at 2-4% unconditional for $100M revenue, B at about 10% by its author, which the critic calls generous and which I would put nearer 3-5%. The tails therefore do not separate the ideas, so downside shape and the median decide.
h2h:C13:C16:ab.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded, and neither is a high-probability, high-profit business. This is close, and I pick B mainly on the shape of the median outcome and the downside.

A has a clever fee rule (no invoice line drops, no fee). But its own refinement says the median case is a thin-margin $17M firm that burns $28-60M and breaks even in year 8-9. It puts $100M revenue at 2-4% before gates and 35-45% on clearing the gates. The core 'why pay us' question is open: the CFO already owns the capital, and the pitch concedes rough parity with a do-it-yourself program at the 25-30% realization the evidence shows. I found no demand evidence, such as an RFP or a published contract. Renegotiation costs the buyer 0%, and Redress charges 25% once. Enterprise sales cycles, CFO share caps and owner follow-through all work against it. Its receivables are contingent and hard to finance.

B is a conventional roll-up with no durable edge. The author scores it 4/10, and the median IRR is 8%. But what you own is real: a route-based, recurring-revenue asset with EBITDA from the first deal, financeable at 3.5-4x. The make-or-break variable is entry price. It can be tested in two weeks, and the walk-away rule of 7x means the failure mode is usually 'no deal', not a loss. The main loss scenario is overpaying while leveraged, as with Kleen and Angelica. The capital is also more conventional. Even a shrunk B, one good laundry at a fair price, beats A's median.
h2h:C13:C16:ab.a_biggest_risk: Owners will not release spend, so invoice lines do not fall (5-6% realized against 20% targeted). Combined with the unanswered 'why pay us' question, the funded engineering becomes unrecovered cost, and the median business never earns enough to cover its burn.
h2h:C13:C16:ab.b_biggest_risk: A new, unproven buyer cannot source family laundries at or below about 6.5x EBITDA. Strategics and funded PE platforms set higher prices, and any seller who does accept is adversely selected. Without that entry price the returns collapse (12.5% IRR at 7.5x, and the median falls to roughly 4% with no synergy).

decisive_factors: B's revenue mechanism is already proven at scale (HomeServe DE, Konzmann, Builtech), while A needs a new contract category that no landlord has bought

B has abundant seller supply (about 54,000 planned Handwerk closures) with no buyer-side gatekeeper. A's customers are bundling and insourcing, and a newco is excluded by turnover and credit-score tests
A's decisive premise (concentration, persistence and a 40%+ causal cut) needs a full winter and a randomised trial that collides with Awaab's Law. B's core premise can be tested in about 2 weeks

Expected value is similar if each succeeds (a small, profitable specialist group), but B's probability of reaching its median case is materially higher and B's capital is staged against cash-flowing assets
A's critics rated two objections fatal (demand and procurement), and the rewrite never closed them. B's three were rated serious, and each has a stated mitigation
h2h:C15:C09:ab.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded and both have an upside case under about 5% likely, so the decision rests on which one more probably reaches a respectable median outcome. B does.

A is a new product category for a customer set that is moving the other way. Landlords are bundling whole-stock deals (Livin, Thurrock, Winchester) and insourcing (Teign, Basildon). A newco cannot pass the turnover and D&B tests, and the incumbents (Wates Healthy Homes, Mears) can answer by adding a gain-share schedule. Its own pitch contradicts itself: it claims control-based pricing, but the capitated rung uses a trailing baseline with an index. It also assumes a randomised waitlist control that Awaab's Law makes legally exposed. The core premise, that the top 5% of homes are concentrated and persistent, is unmeasured, and the causal proof needs about 20 months. Revenue is mostly pass-through works at 8-12% EBITDA. The cheap kill test is a point in its favour, but the survivor is a small niche.

B is a buy-and-build model with proven precedent and a large supply of forced sellers who have no better alternative. Its worst numbers (19% contribution, EUR 240k overhead) are invented, and it is crowded with HomeServe, MEISTEREHRE and GREENOX. But the model is capital-light early (EUR 4M), pays mostly on retained revenue, and leaves cash-generating assets behind if it stalls. The 2-week ledger test is direct and decisive. The median is a modest regional service group, but it is far more reachable than A's median.

B wins clearly, with the caveat that it needs a German-speaking operator with credibility in the trades.
h2h:C15:C09:ab.a_biggest_risk: No landlord actually buys an outcome-priced carve-out of its worst homes. Buyers are bundling and insourcing, a newco cannot pass the procurement tests, and the persistence and causal-cut premise is unproven until a full-winter trial, so the idea may never get past the sprint stage.
h2h:C15:C09:ab.b_biggest_risk: Adverse selection on the books bought. Owners who cannot sell may have owner-dependent, consumer-heavy, low-margin books. If retention falls below about 70% or contribution on absorbed crews falls below about 15%, hubs never reach break-even and the capital raise fails.

decisive_factors: B's market demonstrably clears: family laundries are being bought every few months by Alsco, Wildman, PE platforms and Cintas. A's dossier found no precedent for anyone paying for a cohort carve-out, and buyers are bundling or insourcing.

A's two fatal objections are structural and still open after the rewrite: no single budget owner, and a newco can't pass Procurement Act and D&B turnover tests. B's objections are serious but are price and credibility problems that one 2-week test can measure.

B's downside is a no-buy: if sellers insist on 8x, you don't buy and little capital is lost. A's downside is that no one buys capitation and the product shrinks to a fix-only niche worth low single-digit GBP millions.

B buys real cash flow on day one, with abundant deal-by-deal capital and lenders, so a competent execution has a real floor. A depends on an unrun concentration test, a winter-long RCT and category creation, which stack up to under 1% for the upside (per the critic).
A's one real edge is a cheap, fast kill test (about GBP25k, 8 weeks) and a genuine Awaab's Law tailwind. That does not offset a median of roughly GBP2M of EBITDA and a low-probability upside.
h2h:C15:C16:ab.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded, so the question is which is more likely to become a real, profitable business. I judge B.

A is a new-category bet. It needs a concentration premise that nobody has measured (the top 5% of homes carry 25% or more of spend and stay costly). It then needs a landlord to hand over ledgers, a randomized trial across a winter, and a new outcome-priced contract lot that doesn't exist. Meanwhile buyers are bundling into whole-stock deals (Livin, Thurrock, Winchester) or insourcing. Incumbents (Wates Healthy Homes, Mears) already sell the adjacent product and hold the data, vans and relationships. A newco is shut out of the tenders by turnover and D&B tests. The refined ladder is a smart way to cheaply discover whether anyone cares. Even if it works, the median is about $17M of revenue, mostly pass-through, at 8-12% EBITDA. The pricing also contradicts the claim of a concurrent control at the capitated rung. Taking the critic's figure of under 1% for the upside, expected value is small.

B is a conventional buy-and-build, and it admits that. Its returns hinge on one measurable number, entry multiple, and the market for it is proven: sellers exist, lenders and independent-sponsor capital are available, and acquired EBITDA exists on day one. The median is mediocre (about 8% IRR). The upside needs entry at or below 6.5x and an exit near 9-10x. But failure mostly looks like "we can't buy at a good price, so we don't buy", not a sunk build. The team is also unfunded and doesn't yet exist, which is a real hole.

I give B the edge on probability and on how much evidence it rests on. The margin is not wider because B's median is sub-hurdle, and A's kill test is cheaper.
h2h:C15:C16:ab.a_biggest_risk: Nobody buys it. The dossier found no precedent for a cohort carve-out, buyers are bundling or insourcing, and a newco can't clear procurement tests. Without that, the idea shrinks to a small fix-only niche, and the top-5% concentration and persistence premise is still unmeasured.
h2h:C15:C16:ab.b_biggest_risk: Entry price and seller preference. Strategics paying 2-3x revenue and PE platforms already offering rollover set the price. A new, unfunded vehicle can only buy adversely selected targets at 6.5x or below, and at 7.5x entry the IRR falls to 12.5% (median case about 4%).

decisive_factors: A's core premise (top 5-8% of homes carry 25%+ of spend and persist) is cheap to test, and its entry products are director-level purchases that avoid the procurement door. B's core premise is a hospital buying a 5-year cost-plus contract from a startup, and that cannot be tested cheaply.

A has a near-term statutory forcing function that pays for fixes now (Awaab's Law phase 2 on 30 Nov 2026, uncapped claimant costs, existing damp-and-mould budget lines). B's pressures (UHC tier, Elevance, PAMA) are ambiguous, and the dossier says they favour cash buyers.

B has the only documented customer outcome for its model: Kootenai fired the PAML-style operator and its EBIDA rose about $10M after insourcing. Nationals and regional operators (Quest, Labcorp, Orion, TriCore, Mayo/ARUP) already sell the same pitch.

B's price needs the operator to run 17-24% below the hospital's own cost, and the 15-18% baseline it rests on is unbenchmarked. A's economics depend on a causal cut that a controlled trial can measure, with a stated breakeven of about 25% when the landlord funds the fix.

B has three fatal critiques and a dossier verdict of 'trending dead'. A has two fatal critiques and one serious one, and its rewrite changes the product so those two no longer apply to the first rungs.
h2h:C15:C11:ab.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded, both carry about a 3-5% chance of the roughly $100M upside, and both have a $12-17M median that is probably overstated. The choice therefore rests on which is more likely to produce a real, modest business and which kill risks can be tested cheaply.

A is the better of the two. A's rewrite sells a free ledger x-ray, then a 50-home sprint below the services threshold paid from an existing damp-and-mould line, instead of a capitated carve-out. That is an ordinary director-level purchase driven by a hard statutory date. Its central uncertainty, whether concentration and persistence exist, can be killed or confirmed in 2-8 weeks for under GBP25k. If it passes, even the fallback of a fix-only and verification business is a viable niche. Its weaknesses are real: Wates Healthy Homes, Mears and the PfH frameworks, landlords bundling or insourcing, a newco that fails turnover tests, and about 5-12% contracting margins.

B's rewrite fixed the Medicare 'wholly owned' billing problem with a 100% hospital-owned LLC, but the commercial problems remain unanswered. The only observed customer of this model terminated it. The price needs an unproven double-digit cost advantage from a startup with no route density. The nationals can match the 'keep control' offer at cost, and regional operators already exist. The upside also needs a hub and a $50-60M sponsor JV, and that breaks the neutrality claim. It is a heavily regulated product with a 5-year lock-in, aimed at risk-averse CFOs who have a cash alternative. A has lower legal tail risk and an easier first sale, so A wins, but only narrowly.
h2h:C15:C11:ab.a_biggest_risk: No landlord will pay an outcome-priced fee for a carved-out hot-spot cohort. Buyers are bundling into whole-stock deals or insourcing, and primes such as Wates and Mears can add a gain-share schedule themselves. That leaves a low-margin fix subcontractor or analytics niche of a few GBP million. The kill test (top-5% share, persistence and ledger access) is also still unrun.
h2h:C15:C11:ab.b_biggest_risk: A non-selling health system will not sign a 5-year open-book operating contract with a startup that must show a price at least 8% below the hospital's own cost (17-24% below at operator cost), when it can do the work in-house, buy advice from Mayo, ARUP or Chi, or take a national's or regional operator's management offer. The one documented customer of this model terminated it.

decisive_factors: Capital at risk before proof: A needs about GBP15-25k to the 8-week gate and about GBP1M to the winter trial read, with fix capital deferred until a controlled effect of 40% or more is shown. B needs about $25M of acquisition equity to reach even its median case, and $60-75M for the upside.

B's own median case is a capital loser. The critic's arithmetic gives $1.3-2M EBITDA on about $25M invested, which is 12-20x paid against an 8-10x exit. A's median is small but is not bought with sponsor-style capital.

B's thesis depends on exogenous, unfixable forces: federal and state pressure on Medicaid personal care, a roughly 2% fee on spend, and a sector that lost 12.5% in Wisconsin at commodity prices. A has a regulatory tailwind (Awaab's Law phase 2 starts 30 Nov 2026), and the landlord keeps the legal duty.

A's fatal critiques hit the original capitated carve-out, and the refined plan routes around them: a sprint below the procurement threshold, paid from an existing damp-and-mould line, with prime-channel and fix-only fallbacks. B's roll-up faces the same buyers (H.I.G., General Atlantic at about 10x), and the dossier found no deal price to buy against.

A's gate, a ledger-based concentration and persistence test, kills it cheaply if the premise is false. B's two-week test is also cheap, but a pass only leads to a capital-heavy roll-up. B's stronger point is certain, mandated, government-paid demand, which A lacks.
h2h:C15:C02:ab.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded and neither is a good venture bet. The question is which has the better expected outcome per unit of capital and time.

B has real, mandated, signer-backed revenue and an acquired book that produces cash on day one. But the refined plan concedes the commodity price is unprofitable. The 5-8% median EBITDA is also inconsistent with the 6x entry multiple, so the median case is effectively a capital loss. The $100M case needs about $60-75M of sponsor-style capital, 1.6x GT's footprint, and a New York slot that may never open, and it returns about 1.4-2.1x even if everything works. The buy side competes with funded sponsors, no deal price has been found, and the policy risk is large and cannot be diversified away.

A is a long shot. The upside is likely under 1-5%, and the realistic residual is a specialist niche worth low single-digit GBP millions. Pricing is also internally inconsistent: the capitated rung cannot have an untreated control once the cohort is handed over. But the structure is a stage-gated option. A free x-ray is both the sales hook and the kill test, the first real money is about GBP1M, and fix capital is deferred until a controlled effect is measured. The fix-only and prime-channel fallbacks sell into existing budget lines, in the Awaab's Law window. Awaab's Law phase 2 starts 30 Nov 2026. The weak points are that the concentration premise is unmeasured, and the Camden hotspotting trial shows regression to the mean can erase apparent savings.

A has the better expected outcome per pound at risk. B's demand certainty counts for less when the economics and the capital needs are this poor, which is why the margin is narrow.
h2h:C15:C02:ab.a_biggest_risk: The premise and the buyer both fail. Costly homes may not carry 25% or more of spend persistently, since savings can be regression to the mean. And even if they do, landlords are bundling and insourcing and have shown no sign of buying an outcome-priced carve-out, so the business collapses into low-margin fix-only work for primes.
h2h:C15:C02:ab.b_biggest_risk: Buying the qualification ticket at a price the cash flows can carry may not be possible. Sellers anchor on 10x-EBITDA deals by sponsors (GT, TEAM). The sellable operators are the money-losing ones. At 5-8% margins the median case is a capital loss, and Medicaid personal-care policy and fraud pressure can shrink the participant base.

decisive_factors: Capital and downside shape: A needs about GBP1M to reach the winter trial read, and the landlord funds the fixes until a 40%+ effect is proven. B needs a $15-25M sponsor by month 18, a surety line, and $20-25M of retained risk capital, and one bad early package could wipe it out.

Unit economics: B's 12% margin depends on a 0.77x cost basis, but independent shops charge about 0.85-0.90x OEM. At that price margin is about 3-4% before bonds, bid costs and liquidated damages, so the buyers who pass the demand test are the ones where the prime loses money. A has a margin table showing 17-29% at a 40-50% cut with landlord-funded fixes, and its breakeven is stated.

Fallback floor: if A's capitation never gets bought, it still sells paid damp-and-mould root-cause diagnosis and fix work (existing GBP2-3M-a-year lines at Wigan and InCommunities) to DLOs and primes under Awaab's Law. B has no floor, because its median is break-even and a small sale to an ISP.

Timing and fatal-flag count: Awaab's Law phase 2 starts 30 Nov 2026 and only about 4% of landlords say they are very prepared. A drew two fatal critic flags (both aimed at the capitation scale-up) and one serious. B drew three fatal flags (competition, buyer scoring and qualification, insurer wrap) with no cheap pivot, and its date guarantee has no hardware behind it in a casting-constrained market.
h2h:C15:C01:ab.reasons:
Both ideas are badly wounded, and neither upside is believable. Both have about a 3% chance of the $100M case, and in both the real profit pool at that scale is single-digit millions of EBITDA. So the choice comes down to which has the better median outcome, which is cheaper to be wrong about, and which objections are more likely to kill it.

B's problems are structural. The core promise is a hard return-to-service date, but the prime owns no rotors or casting slots, and ISPs allocate scarce slots to their own customers first. Margin only works at a cost basis independent shops do not offer. The refined pitch aims at owners who buy OEM transactionally, who are the least likely to hand a $5M outage to an unreferenced newcomer at price parity. The business also needs a sponsor, a surety and references at the same time, and each depends on the others. Its median is break-even and ends as a small sale to Hanwha or Allied. One rotor failure on an early package can consume the retained capital.

A's objections mostly threaten the scale-up, not the first business. Capitation and a new contract category are probably unachievable, and primes can copy the idea. But the early rungs are director-level purchases from existing damp-and-mould lines, priced below the procurement threshold. The first kill decision costs under GBP25k and lands in 8 weeks. Concentration of repair cost in a few persistent, physically caused problem homes is plausible, and the Thurrock data points that way. Risk is staged, with no uncapped tail and no fix capital before a controlled result. The causal-effects library is a modest real asset. The expected value is lower than the headline, but the capital at risk is small relative to B, and the median is positive.

I would back A at the cost of a small seed and 8 weeks. I would not back B without a committed sponsor, which is unlikely before it has references.
h2h:C15:C01:ab.a_biggest_risk: Nobody buys outcome-priced capitation. Landlords are bundling into whole-stock deals and insourcing, and primes can add a gain-share clause. The business then shrinks to a fix-only specialist niche of low single-digit GBP millions, and the concentration and persistence of the costliest homes is still unmeasured.
h2h:C15:C01:ab.b_biggest_risk: The economics and credibility do not work for a newcomer. Margin falls to about 3-4% once independent shops are priced realistically. It cannot qualify or bond without references or a $15M+ sponsor. The firm date guarantee has no hardware or slot control behind it, so a single early loss kills the company.

decisive_factors: Capital at risk vs. prize: A needs about GBP25k to reach its first kill decision and about GBP1M before the 20-month trial read, with every rung paid. B needs $130-175M of other people's equity plus a proven casting operator, and its own refined pitch says it is not a startup.

B's keystone behavior has zero precedent. Four independent searchers found no OEM prepay to a non-incumbent owner. The critic's structural point also stands: a customer funding 60-80% of a line can sign with the current owner, so the sponsor adds almost nothing for the buyer. A's thesis (concentration and persistence of cost in the worst homes) can at least be tested with public FOI data and landlord ledgers.

B's returns are mediocre even if it works: about 1.8-3.3x gross, low-to-mid-teens IRR, entry assumed at about 2x revenue against qualified comps at 5.9-8x, sources and uses that do not close, and cycle-peak risk. Most of the value created accrues to the capital providers, not the founders.

A's prize is much smaller, and that keeps this a close call. Its credible outcome is a low single-digit GBP-million-revenue niche at 8-17% margin. The $107M upside is under 1-5%. B's conditional payoff is roughly 4x larger in profit ($10M+ median EBITDA versus $2-3M).
h2h:C15:C05:ab.reasons: Neither idea is a high-probability business, so this comes down to which objection kills it first and how much it costs to find out. B has the bigger prize: a real shortage, 18-22% margins, and a conditional median near $10M EBITDA against about $2-3M for A. But B's prerequisites are the problem. It needs $130-175M of outside equity and a casting operator. Its central behavior (an OEM prepaying a non-incumbent owner) was found by no one. Its edge over GE-backed CPP, Pursuit, Arcline and Doncasters is, in its own words, not technological. The customer value proposition is close to nil, because the same OEM money can go to the current owner. The assumed entry price of about 2x revenue sits against 5.9-8x comps. Even the upside returns about 1.8-3.3x, so the founders hold a small stake in a capital-heavy, cycle-exposed deal. A's objections are also serious. Buyers are bundling and insourcing, the procurement door is hard for a newco, and the 2-3% upside odds are honest. But the refined plan removes the carve-out and sells a sprint from an existing damp-and-mould budget line, below the procurement threshold. The core thesis can be tested with FOI data and landlord ledgers for about GBP25k in 8 weeks. Capital is staged and nothing is risked on fixes until a controlled trial shows a 40%+ cut. Its expected value is modest, but it has a much better expected value per dollar and per month at risk, plus a real Awaab's Law catalyst. A edges B narrowly.
h2h:C15:C05:ab.a_biggest_risk: The premise is unproven: the costliest 5-8% of homes may not carry 25%+ of spend persistently, and buyers show no appetite for outcome-priced or capitated cohorts. They are bundling into whole-stock deals and insourcing, and a newco is shut out of procurement. Even if the thesis holds, the credible outcome is a small niche. The company would be a subcontractor or fix-only vendor to primes such as Wates and Mears.
h2h:C15:C05:ab.b_biggest_risk: No non-captive OEM will fund a line at a non-incumbent-owned caster, and there is no sellable qualified asset at about 2x revenue. Customers can sign Doncasters-style deals with incumbents, or buy casters themselves as Siemens Energy did. A first-time sponsor then loses auctions to better-capitalized bidders. In that case the $130-175M equity never gets raised, or it is deployed at cycle-peak prices for mediocre returns.

decisive_factors: Profit per dollar of revenue: A's upside reaches about 52% contribution and $20-45M EBITDA on $100-120M revenue. B's upside is about EUR 6M EBIT on EUR 94M revenue. At similar low odds (A 2-4%, B 3-5% by the authors, 1-2% by B's critic), A's right tail is worth roughly 3-5x more.

Capital efficiency and gating: A's peak burn is $32M for the upside, and its fees are paid only when an invoice line falls. The kill gates (two-week test, paid X-ray at day 60, first audited drop by month 12) cap the loss at a few million before the large burn. B needs about EUR 40M peak funding, with EUR 26-30M of no-exit equity from LPs not yet identified, to reach EUR 6M EBIT.

Direct competition: B's model (buy owner firms, keep management, central back office) is already executed by HomeServe/Brookfield, VINCI, Konzmann and Builtech, plus micro-tier rivals on the same HWK channel. The neighbour-absorbs-the-book objection also undercuts the hub. A's exact slot (funded execution paid per invoice drop) has no direct occupant, only adjacent players such as Redress, Flexera and in-house teams.

B's median is more robust: a small profitable regional group of about EUR 0.8M EBIT on little capital. A's median is a trap (about $17M revenue, break-even in year 8-9 after $28-60M burned). That trap is exactly what A's gates are built to avoid, and it is why this is a close call.
h2h:C13:C09:ab.reasons: Both ideas are wounded, and both authors put the venture-scale tail at low single-digit odds, so the choice depends on what the tail is worth and how cheaply each can be killed. A's tail is much richer. At $100M revenue it earns about $20M EBITDA in year 7 and $33M in year 8, and it is financed by receivables that clients pay only after a third-party invoice line falls. B's best case is about EUR 6M EBIT on EUR 94M of bought revenue. It is a capital-allocation business that needs about EUR 40M peak funding for a roughly 15% pre-tax yield, with no exit by design. B's own probabilities are weak, and its key economics (19% contribution, EUR 240k hub overhead) are invented and reverse-fitted to produce viable hubs. Crew attrition is unmodelled, and the same sellers are being courted by better-capitalised rivals running the same model. A's biggest objection (realization of 5-6% against 20% targeted, plus the question of why a CFO pays 26-30% for work Redress or in-house teams could do) is real and could be fatal. But it can be tested with a paid X-ray and one audited invoice drop within about 12 months for a few million dollars, while B's capital objection only shows up after tranche B is sought. A's pitch also opens an unoccupied slot and has software and data optionality (the ledger, the outcome statistics). B's median is the safer small business, but it has almost no upside beyond that. A wins on expected value, narrowly, because the downside is gated and the tail is several times larger.
h2h:C13:C09:ab.a_biggest_risk: Realization: business owners do not release the identified spend, so third-party invoice lines do not actually fall. The evidence is 5-6% realized against 20% targeted. CFOs also cap the share at 15-20% or choose Redress or an in-house team, which leaves a funded-engineering business with no fee base. The median then burns $28-60M for a break-even services company.
h2h:C13:C09:ab.b_biggest_risk: Unit economics and capital together: bought books come from owners who could not sell, so retention (assumed 70%) and the invented 19% contribution on absorbed crews likely fail. Even if they hold, no no-exit LP funds a first-time operator's EUR 26M+ later tranches against HomeServe/Brookfield-type rivals. The result is a small regional service group earning under EUR 1M.

decisive_factors: Staged, cheap-to-kill capital path: A's first proof point is a roughly $3-10M asset purchase gated by a no-capital two-week seller test and a month-6 LOI gate. B needs a $60-140M first acquisition plus $130-175M of equity before anything is proven.

Feasibility of the core behavior: A rests on buying small owner-operated businesses, which is ordinary roll-up behavior with live precedents (H.I.G./GT, General Atlantic/TEAM). B rests on an OEM prepaying a non-incumbent owner, which no source or critic found, and the refined pitch gives customers almost no reason to route that money through a new owner.

Severity of unresolved objections: all three of B's critics were rated fatal and the rewrite adds no new evidence for the keystone assumption. A's critics were rated serious, and its worst flaws (SLA, statewide RFP wedge, Kentucky) were conceded and removed from the base case.

Both have low absolute upside, but B's founder is likely a deal originator with a small stake. B's equity return is only 1.8-3.3x even in the upside case, and its unconditional median outcome is $0. A's downside is bounded and its demand is mandated, government-signed Medicaid spend.
h2h:C02:C05:ab.reasons:
Neither idea is good, so I weighed which one's objections are more likely to be fatal and how much capital each needs before it learns whether it works.

B has the bigger prize on paper. Gas-turbine and aeroengine casting is in a real shortage, margins are 18-22%, and the upside is a roughly $200M-revenue foundry. Everything depends on one behavior nobody has evidenced. That behavior is a non-captive OEM signing a dollar-denominated, make-whole capacity reservation to fund a line at a qualified caster owned by a non-incumbent. The three critics rated their objections fatal. The refined pitch concedes the greenfield plant, the consortium, the take-or-pay and the neutrality premium, and keeps only an acquisition platform. The second-round critic's structural point is unanswered: if customers fund 60-80% of a line anyway, they can sign that deal with the plant's current owner, so the sponsor offers them close to nothing. The sources and uses do not close. Mid-size targets are being bought by CPP/GE, Pursuit and Arcline, who have more capital. Even the upside returns only about 1.8-3.3x on $130-175M, and the unconditional median is $0.

A is a thin-margin, politically exposed roll-up. Its critics were rated serious, and its original pitch (SLA, statewide RFP wedge) is already dead. What remains is a standard small-operator roll-up with mandated, government-signed demand. Its first proof costs single-digit millions. A kill test could end it cheaply, and a signed LOI plus an equity partner gate the next capital. The acquisition-math inconsistency cuts both ways. If sellers really earn 15-20% margins, the 5-8% median is too pessimistic.

A's EV is small, roughly $10-20M, and B's EV may be larger in absolute dollars. A wins narrowly on probability, bounded downside and capital efficiency.
h2h:C02:C05:ab.a_biggest_risk: The economics of the acquired asset. No small fiscal-agent operator is shown to earn 15-20% margin at $110+ per participant-month, and none is shown to sell at about 1.0x revenue. The sector lost 12.5% in Wisconsin. The premium-fee segment is unsized and partly mis-specified (Minnesota fees are participant-paid and tiered, and Colorado is a closed-award market). Sponsor-backed buyers with more capital (H.I.G., General Atlantic) chase the same tail, so the median case could be a capital loss.
h2h:C02:C05:ab.b_biggest_risk: The keystone customer behavior has no precedent. No OEM has been found prepaying or signing a make-whole reservation to a non-incumbent-owned caster. Customers can sign the same deal with the plant's current owner, or buy the caster themselves, as Siemens Energy did with CIC. Without that money the roughly $340M capital stack fails to close, and mid-size qualified targets are being taken by better-funded buyers.

decisive_factors: Capital at risk versus median outcome: A's median ($25M revenue, $1.3-2M EBITDA) needs about $25M of acquisition capital, which works out to 12-20x EBITDA paid and a capital loss at an 8-10x exit. B's median (about EUR 0.8M EBIT) needs only EUR 4-10M, staged behind gates.

Quality of the objections: A's flaws are structural. The 'qualification ticket' is free in open-enrollment Texas and locked in awarded Colorado. Sponsors buy at about 10x. The only public cost data show the sector losing money at $77. B's flaws are unproven parameters (19% contribution, retention) that a cheap seller-ledger test and a EUR 4M Phase 1 can falsify.

Entry price and mechanics: B buys books and crews at 0.25-0.40x revenue with 40-50% contingent on retention. That is a familiar small-ticket route-density roll-up, with a claimed hub payback near 2 years. A has no FMS deal price anywhere in the evidence and competes against H.I.G. and General Atlantic.

Tail and policy risk: A carries Section 3504 joint liability, a $162M wage-hour settlement precedent, a DOJ receivership suit, a federal fraud crackdown on personal care, and revocable state rate cards. B's tails (Sec. 613a, warranty, Meister/Betriebsleiter rules) are smaller and mostly handled by deal structure.
Upside is weak for both. A's upside is a joint event of five conditions and returns only 1.4-2.1x. B's is 1-5% and needs a hard-to-find anchor LP. The median-case gap therefore decides it.
h2h:C02:C09:ab.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded roll-ups with small expected outcomes, so this is a close call. The deciding question is which failure mode is cheaper and which median case is more real.

A's economics are the problem. Its refined plan concedes the original pitch and keeps only the claim that qualification is the scarce asset. That claim does not hold up. Texas lets anyone in, so there is no ticket to buy. Colorado is locked to awarded vendors. New York and statewide RFPs need past performance and a $100M credit line that a roll-up built on tiny operators won't have. The plan's own numbers give about $1.3-2M of EBITDA on roughly $25M invested, which is a capital loss at a normal exit. The second-round critic is right that the median case is really a bear case, and that the 8-10% upside (1.4-2.1x if hit) is the only success path. A also faces sponsor competition at about 10x, uncertain premium-segment margins, thin spreads, and liability and policy tails: Section 3504 joint tax liability, the $162M Calderon settlement and the DOJ and fraud scrutiny.

B is also speculative. The 19% contribution and EUR 240k overhead are invented, the model is reverse-fitted, and falling Handwerk demand, seller adverse selection, crew attrition and HomeServe's entry are real. But the buy price is low (0.25-0.40x, half contingent), the first capital is only EUR 4M with explicit gates, and the median case does not need an outside anchor LP. The kill conditions are cheap to test. If the unit economics hold, a modest business emerges for a fraction of A's capital. If they fail, the loss is small and early.

I pick B on capital-adjusted expected outcome, with low confidence.
h2h:C02:C09:ab.a_biggest_risk: The acquisition price and margin mismatch. No FMS deal price exists in the evidence, sponsors buy at about 10x, and cheap targets are the money-losing ones. If the premium-segment margin is not 15-20%, the plan pays 12-20x EBITDA and the median case loses capital.
h2h:C02:C09:ab.b_biggest_risk: Unit-economics and seller-quality risk. The 19% contribution on absorbed crews and 70% book retention are unsourced, and sellers who can't find a buyer skew toward owner-dependent, low-profit books. If hub contribution is 15% or less, or B2B repeat revenue is under 40%, there are no viable hubs and no basis to raise capital.

decisive_factors: Asset quality: B buys real, contracted, cash-generating laundries with about 15% EBITDA margins, financeable at 3-4x leverage. A buys fiscal agents in a sector that lost 12.5% in aggregate at competitive prices, where the best operator earned +2%.

Median outcome: B's median is a mediocre but positive roughly 8% IRR (1.5x). A's median is about $1.3-2M EBITDA on about $25M invested, so it is a capital loss at any normal exit multiple. The critic is right that A's real success probability is the roughly 8-10% upside tail.

Capital and gating: B starts with a roughly $10-14M anchor equity check using deal-by-deal independent-sponsor capital. A needs $60-75M of sponsor-style capital to reach scale and no FMS deal price has ever been found.

Risk profile: A has a policy and liability tail that B lacks. Section 3504 joint and several payroll-tax liability, a $162M wage-hour settlement, a DOJ fraud suit, federal and state pressure on family-caregiver self-direction, and revocable one-year rate cards. B's risks (environmental, leverage, integration) are known, diligence-able and priced by an established PE playbook.

Upside mechanics: B's return is driven by entry multiple discipline plus a platform-scale multiple (6.5x in, 9x+ out), a well-trodden path with abundant exit buyers. A's upside needs five conditions to hold at once, including a New York slot, two statewide RFP wins as a first-time bidder, and $150 PMPM fees that the evidence does not support.
h2h:C02:C16:ab.reasons:
Both ideas were wounded in their own refinements, so this is a choice between two weak bets. I took the one whose failure is less likely and less costly.

Idea A rests on buying the "qualification ticket" cheaply, yet no FMS acquisition price exists in any file. The sector loses money at the $68-83 prices states actually pay. The premium-fee segment that is supposed to carry the margin is mis-specified: Minnesota's fee is participant-paid, Colorado is a closed award, and Texas has free entry, so an acquired book is non-sticky. By the second-round critic's arithmetic the median case is a 12-20x EBITDA purchase that returns less than it costs. Add the payroll-tax and wage-hour liabilities, the fraud and caregiver policy shocks, sponsor competition (H.I.G., General Atlantic), and a one-contract-per-year auction market. Even the upside returns only about 1.4-2.1x over seven years.

Idea B is a conventional, thin-edge roll-up, and the refinement says so honestly. Its fatal question is the price sellers will accept, and the 2-week owner and adviser test can answer that cheaply. It still has things A lacks. The underlying businesses are real, recurring, profitable and financeable, with a diversified customer base. Starting capital is small, and the downside is owning functioning plants rather than a political asset. The exit market is deep. Median returns are mediocre (about 8% IRR), but positive and recoverable. If entry holds at or below 6.5x, the upside gives roughly 3x and 21% IRR with a probability of around 10-25%.

Expected value is therefore higher for B. Its probability of at least a modest positive outcome is meaningfully higher, its capital at risk is smaller, and its tail is less political.
h2h:C02:C16:ab.a_biggest_risk: The cheap-ticket premise fails. Small fiscal agents either do not exist at 15%+ margins with a sellable price near 1.0x revenue, or the only sellable books are the money-losing ones. The economics also collapse at a median of 5-8% margin, and policy and liability shocks (caregiver restrictions, fraud crackdown, payroll-tax exposure) can shrink the participant base 20-30%.
h2h:C02:C16:ab.b_biggest_risk: Entry price and seller preference. Family owners may choose Alsco, Wildman or PE platforms at strategic prices (8x or more, up to 2-3x revenue) over an unproven new vehicle at 5.5-6.5x. Past about 7.5x entry, the model's IRR drops to about 12%, or about 4% with no synergy, and the business is not worth doing.

decisive_factors: B's core mechanic already happens routinely: family laundries sell, lenders and deal-by-deal capital exist, and the anchor equity check is about $10-14M. A needs $130-175M of equity, a proven casting operator and an OEM behavior no one has found a precedent for.

A drew three fatal critiques that the rewrite did not answer. The customer-side value proposition is close to nil, since an OEM could sign the same deal with the plant's current owner. Its acquisition comp is stale (Precicast closed 2026-09-30). Its sources and uses do not close. B's critiques were serious but not fatal, and B conceded and deleted its weakest pieces (price lock, FTC remedy, blind pool).

A's own unconditional median is $0, with 5% to 12% odds of reaching $100M revenue. B's failure mode is a mediocre return (about 8% IRR at the median) rather than total loss, so its probability-weighted outcome is higher even though its upside is smaller.

B's riskiest assumption (entry at or below about 6.5x EBITDA) is testable in two weeks with 25 owner calls and 3 adviser calls, then a 60-day gate of signed IOIs. A's test requires winning trust from OEM procurement teams that already fund incumbents.
h2h:C05:C16:ab.reasons:
Both ideas are weak, so the question is which is more likely to produce anything. I pick B.

A is a capital-allocation bet dressed as a startup. Its refined version needs about $340M of uses, $130-175M of equity and a proven casting operator. It also needs a non-captive OEM to sign a multi-year reservation with make-whole to a non-incumbent owner, and no critic or researcher found a precedent. The critics' structural point stands: if customers fund 60-80% of the line anyway, they can do it with the plant's current owner, so the sponsor's value to the customer is near nil. The acquisition price rests on a Precicast comp that has already closed and that has no disclosed revenue, while qualified assets trade at 5.9x to 8x revenue against bidders like GE, Pursuit and Arcline. Even the optimistic case gives about 1.8x to 3.3x gross, and the unconditional median is $0.

B is a plain buy-and-build in a market that clears every year. It is crowded, with Alsco, Wildman and about ten funded buyers, and it has no real moat. But the check is small, the independent-sponsor path exists, and the revenue arrives on day one. The median is mediocre, with an IRR of about 8% and $45M of revenue. Its main risk is entry price, which is the one thing the 2-week test measures. If the price holds, a flat-to-moderate outcome is plausible. If it fails, the team loses little time and money.

Probability times payoff, relative to capital and time, favors B.
h2h:C05:C16:ab.a_biggest_risk: The keystone behavior is unevidenced. No OEM has prepaid or signed a make-whole reservation with a non-incumbent owner, and the customers already funding Doncasters and Howmet may buy casters themselves. Without that money the roughly $340M capital stack does not close, and a qualified target is unlikely to be bought at a sane price against GE, Pursuit and Arcline.
h2h:C05:C16:ab.b_biggest_risk: Sellers will not accept about 6.5x normalized EBITDA with rollover from an unproven, newly financed buyer. Strategic prints of 2.3x to 3.3x revenue and the PE platforms that also offer rollover set the price. That leaves adverse-selection targets, and at 7.5x entry the IRR falls to about 12.5% (about 4% in the median case).

decisive_factors: A buys revenue that already exists, from mandated state or plan payers. B has to persuade skeptical health-system CFOs to sign 5-year contracts, and no one has shown that demand exists.

A's exit is proven. H.I.G. (GT Independence, Nov 2025) and General Atlantic (TEAM, about 10x EBITDA, Apr 2026) are paying for exactly these assets. B's only independent precedent, PAML, ended with Labcorp buying it.

B's critics rated all three first-round objections fatal. The Medicare billing rule, the price that works for neither side, and the incumbents who already sell the pitch each threaten the whole business. A's three were serious and mostly about price and timing.

A's upside is the better prize. Its probability is about 8-10%, and the author's 1-3% critic haircut applies to B, whose upside is about 5% by the author's own number. A's roughly $100M of revenue carries more margin and a real multiple. B's $110M is pass-through revenue at about 8% EBITDA, and it needs a hub and a JV that undercut B's own neutrality pitch.

Both ideas are cheap to test and stage-gated. A's single binary question is whether small operators exist that earn real margins and will sell at about 1x revenue. B has stacked unknowns: an unbenchmarked cost advantage, legal structure, and a startup winning against Orion, TriCore, Mayo/ARUP/Chi and the nationals.
h2h:C02:C11:ab.reasons:
Neither idea is attractive in full. The question is which has the better risk-adjusted outcome, and I think that is A.

A is a gated roll-up of a real, mandated, state-paid market. The fee pool is about $0.7-0.9B a year, and there is no free substitute outside California. The business buys operating cash flows, so go-to-market risk becomes deal-sourcing risk, which a capable team can work on directly. The 2-week test and the month-6 LOI gate keep most capital out of the failure branch. If the test passes, the playbook is familiar: buy owner-operated books near 6x EBITDA, add measured operations, and sell to sponsors who are visibly paying about 10x.

A's weak points are real. The median case (about $25M revenue at 5-8% EBITDA) is arguably a capital loss on its own arithmetic, the premium-fee evidence is partly mis-specified, and the tail is contested by funded buyers. But its upside has comps and an exit.

B has three fatal first-round critiques and a dossier verdict of "weak, trending dead." The rebuild survives by becoming a cost-plus service contract that must beat its own customers' costs by 8% or more, with no benchmark. It competes against Quest and Labcorp, which already sell "keep control" management deals, and against advisers such as Mayo, ARUP and Chi. No independent operator has been shown to win and renew a contract. The upside (about 5% by the author, 1-3% by the critic) is largely pass-through revenue at about 8% EBITDA. B is cheaper to start, but it is more likely to end as a $2-8M boutique.
h2h:C02:C11:ab.a_biggest_risk: Acquisition economics: small, non-sponsor-owned fiscal agents may not exist at a price their cash flow can carry. Sellers may anchor on the GT and TEAM headlines, the only sellable books may be the money-losing ones, and H.I.G. or General Atlantic may buy the same tail first. In that case the roll-up thesis fails or buys sick assets at 12-20x actual EBITDA.
h2h:C02:C11:ab.b_biggest_risk: Demand and cost advantage together: a non-selling health system must sign a 5-year open-book contract with an unproven startup at a price at least 8% below its own unbenchmarked commercial-function cost. Its alternatives are doing it in-house, buying advice from Mayo, ARUP or Chi, or taking a national's management offer. No precedent exists of an independent operator winning that choice and renewing.

decisive_factors: A buys going concerns: revenue and cash flow arrive in year 1, and the buy side has live strategic exits (H.I.G., General Atlantic at about 10x). B has no revenue until spring 2028, and then only if five stacked gates all clear.

A's pivotal unknown (seller multiples and margins) is observable data that a 25-seller outreach can settle in 2 weeks with a pre-written kill rule. B's gate is stated-preference calls, and the critic notes that passing its growth threshold selects the cases where the prime loses money.

B's margin is structurally thin and its risk is uncapped. The honest margin is about 3-4% after bonds, and $100M of revenue yields only $4-7M EBITDA. The company retains scheduled-scope variance that cannot be insured (the NY fortuity opinion), and it has no hardware in a casting squeeze where ISPs serve their own customers first. A's downside is bounded by what you pay for each book.

The probability-weighted upside favours A (about 5-8% to reach $80-100M of revenue, with a median that is a real if small business) over B (about 3% to reach $110M, with a median that is a break-even subscale firm). B also fails the scored-RFP and reference test and faces a copy-ready Hanwha. A's equivalent competitor, H.I.G., is only a price-bidding risk.
h2h:C02:C01:ab.reasons:
Neither idea is strong. Both critics landed serious hits and both refined pitches shrank. The question is which has the better risk-weighted outcome and which objections are more likely to be fatal.

B's objections go to demand and structure. The product is risk transfer (a price cap, a date guarantee and a bond) sold by a company with no references, no hardware, no insurer wrap and no surety line. Its own critics call competition, go-to-market and insurability fatal. The rewrite answers the insurance problem by moving the uninsurable scheduled-scope tail onto the founder's balance sheet. It also admits that moat arrives in years 4-6 and that the first-mover window is 18-24 months before Hanwha copies it. Even a full success yields $4-7M EBITDA on $100M of pass-through revenue. The odds of that are about 3%, and the median is a subscale break-even firm. The test relies on stated preference, which the pitch itself calls weak.

A's objections are mostly about price and policy, not existence. The market is mandated Medicaid money with a named payer. Real buyers are paying 10x for scale assets. A roll-up of small owner-operated books is a known playbook, with multiple arbitrage and a bounded downside, because you walk away if sellers' asks or margins fail the written thresholds. The critic's point that the median case implies 12-20x EBITDA paid is real. It is conditional, though: if the test passes, the acquired books earn 15%+ margins and the median is understated. If it fails, the idea dies at a cost near zero. A's weaknesses are real: thin sector margins, policy risk to self-direction, H.I.G. competing for the same targets, and $25M or more of equity before the first buy. They are fixable or testable, which makes A the better expected outcome.
h2h:C02:C01:ab.a_biggest_risk: Acquisition price versus quality. No FMS deal price has been found, so the only sellers who accept about 1.0x revenue may be the money-losing books (Wisconsin's four operators lost 12.5% in aggregate), or H.I.G. and General Atlantic may anchor sellers at sponsor multiples. That would mean paying 12-20x real EBITDA for a 5-8% margin business and losing capital.
h2h:C02:C01:ab.b_biggest_risk: No product-market fit at a workable margin. Owners who would switch already have ISP offers at about 0.85-0.90x OEM, so the cap has to beat what ISPs already quote. Real margin is about 3-4% before bonds, LDs and site management. A newcomer with no references cannot win scored RFPs or get bonded. The prime keeps the scope-growth and supply-squeeze tail with no insurer behind it, and Hanwha can copy the cap.

decisive_factors: Size of prize if it works: A's upside is about $36M EBITDA, roughly $430-540M of enterprise value, and even the conditional median buys a real $45M-revenue plant at 18% margin. B's upside is only $4-7M EBITDA on $110M of pass-through revenue.
Probability-weighted value is higher for A even after heavy discounting. About 12% of a roughly $200M+ equity gain beats B's 3% of a roughly $50M outcome. A still wins if its odds are cut to 2-3%.

B's economics are structurally bad even when it works. Margin is 3-4% against ISP alternatives, the demand test selects for loss-making cases, there is no moat for 4-6 years, and the hard date has no hardware behind it. B also carries uncapped fixed-price tail risk.

A's failure modes are mostly cheap deal-sourcing failures that cost time, not capital. Its collapsed-premise fallback is still a plain qualified-caster acquisition in a documented, supply-constrained market. B's failure modes include real balance-sheet losses.

Both ideas have unevidenced core behavior, but A's demand and shortage evidence is much stronger (Doncasters, Howmet, Siemens, Rystad). The unproven piece is who owns the plant, not whether buyers pay for capacity.
h2h:C05:C01:ab.reasons:
The question is which idea has the higher expected outcome after weighing how likely each objection is to be fatal. Both are wounded, and neither has shown its core behavior in the market. A depends on an OEM prepaying a non-incumbent owner, and B depends on owners paying a newcomer to cap overrun risk. The difference is what is left if the central bet half-works, and how big the prize is.

A is a capital-allocation business. Its critics found real holes: the entry multiple is optimistic, sources and uses do not close at the low end, and the customer's reason to route money through a new owner is thin. Even so, the demand for dedicated hot-section capacity is documented, the shortage is real, and the assets are hard and cash-generating. If the prepay premise fails, the fallback is a standard acquisition of a qualified caster, with mediocre but positive returns. If it works, it is a roughly $400-500M enterprise with real cash flow. Using its own 12% odds, which are generous, the expected value is still several times B's.

B is a thin-margin, pass-through general contractor that takes fixed-price tail risk. Its own numbers show 3% odds, a break-even median, and $4-7M EBITDA even in the upside case. Passing the demand test selects for owners where the margin disappears, and the moat arrives after Hanwha can copy it. Cheap tests and lower capital do not fix a small prize that is unlikely to arrive.
h2h:C05:C01:ab.a_biggest_risk: The core premise is unproven: no OEM has ever prepaid or reserved capacity at a plant owned by a non-incumbent. The few qualified mid-size casters are also being bought by better-capitalized buyers (CPP/GE, Pursuit, Arcline) at multiples above the model's assumed entry price. If either holds, there is no asset at a workable price, or no anchor money to expand it.
h2h:C05:C01:ab.b_biggest_risk: The economics fail even if demand exists. Realistic gross margin is 3-4% once the price is held near par with ISP alternatives, and Hanwha or Allied can copy the guarantee in 18-24 months. A newcomer with no references, no owned hardware and no sponsor-backed bond line would be getting low-priority slots from the shops it competes with.

decisive_factors: Demand is verified for A and unproven for B. A sells into a documented shortage where OEMs already fund dedicated capacity, with Doncasters at up to 80% of capex and Howmet capex backed by customer contracts. For B, no US case was found of a health system choosing a startup operator over cash or a national, and the one documented customer (Kootenai) fired its operator.

A buys real revenue, approvals and EBITDA on day one, so it keeps a floor as an ordinary buy-and-build if the OEM prepay never appears. B has no floor. If the keystone fails, B collapses to a $1-3M advisory contract, and its unconditional median is about $7-12M of revenue at breakeven.

The value ceiling favors A. B's upside is $110M of mostly pass-through revenue at about 8% EBITDA, worth roughly $80-130M, at a probability the critics put at 1-3% and the author at 5%. A's upside is about $36M of EBITDA and $430-540M of enterprise value at about 12% with an operator and equity partner in hand.

B's price model needs an operator cost advantage of 17-24%, which is unbenchmarked and unsupported. Nationals and regional operators (Quest, Labcorp, Orion, TriCore) already sell the same pitch, and the structure carries stacked regulatory risk (CMS 1833(h)(5), 424.73, EKRA). A's problems are capital intensity and deal access, which are real but are the normal conditions of PE-style acquisition rather than a missing buyer.
h2h:C05:C11:ab.reasons:
Neither idea is good, and both dossiers say dead. The question is which fatal objection is more likely to bind.

A's objections are financing and access problems. No OEM has prepaid a non-incumbent. Sources and uses do not close at the low end. Mid-size qualified targets are scarce, with GE/CPP, Arcline and Pursuit bidding. Equity returns of 1.8-3.3x are mediocre. These are serious, but the underlying market is not in doubt. Castings are the binding constraint on a roughly 100 GW turbine and engine order wave, and buyers already pay to secure dedicated capacity. If the prepay keystone fails, a founder with an operator and equity partner can still own a profitable, furnace-limited, sold-out caster. The owner's value is roughly what was paid, plus expansion upside.

B's objections go to whether anyone wants the product. Cash sellers are excluded. Stayers have a free or cheap national or advisory alternative. The only documented customer of the model ended it. The price only works if the operator is 17-24% cheaper than the hospital, which nobody has benchmarked. Even full success yields a thin-margin, pass-through services firm worth about $80-130M. I put its chance of reaching $100M at 1-3%, and its median is near breakeven.

A needs far more capital and the founder likely holds a small stake. That is why this is a close call. B is cheaper to kill, but cheapness to kill is not value. A's expected value is several times higher and its demand risk is lower.
h2h:C05:C11:ab.a_biggest_risk: The keystone behavior is unevidenced: a non-captive OEM signing a multi-year, make-whole capacity reservation to fund a line at a non-incumbent-owned caster. It sits alongside the scarcity of qualified targets at a sane price (about 11x EBITDA or less) against better-capitalized bidders. Without both, the capital stack does not close and equity returns are mediocre.
h2h:C05:C11:ab.b_biggest_risk: Demand and cost advantage fail together. A non-selling health system must sign a 5-year open-book contract with a startup at least 8% below its own cost, rather than take cash or a national's management offer, do it in-house, or buy advice. The 15-18% commercial-cost baseline and the 17-24% operator advantage are unbenchmarked, and there is no US precedent of a non-national operator renewing past year 3.

decisive_factors: Size of the prize if it works: A reaches about $36M EBITDA (roughly $430-540M EV), while B's upside is only about EUR 6M EBIT. B's median is about EUR 0.8M of EBIT, a small regional group.

Failure is cheap and the test is a real discriminator: A's two-week test (3 of about 10 buyers naming $10M or more over 5 or more years) separates a large outcome from nothing, and a pass would be a meaningful signal. B's test only checks seller willingness and leaves the 19% contribution and 70% retention untested.

Margin quality and moat: A earns 18-22% EBITDA on qualified approvals that are bought on day one, in a documented, multi-year capacity shortage with real strategic buyers. B earns about 3.5% group EBIT on invented contribution numbers, has a weak moat, and its hold-forever structure removes the exit.
Both are wounded and both depend on other people's capital. A's objections can mostly be hit cheaply before money is committed, while B's unit economics only reveal themselves after capital is spent.
h2h:C05:C09:ab.reasons: Both ideas are really capital-allocation businesses with an operating edge, and both are wounded. My choice is a close one based on expected outcome. A's own odds are about 5-12% for $100M+ revenue, and its unconditional median is $0. The critics' structural objection is strong: if customers fund 60-80% of the line, they can do it directly with the plant's current owner, so the sponsor adds little for the customer. A first-time sponsor also has to win a scarce asset against GE, Arcline and Pursuit. But if the sponsor does close, it owns a real, qualified, cash-generating business in a shortage with 18-22% EBITDA margins. The value at the top end is large, with about $36M EBITDA against $130-175M of equity. The GE/CPP deal also creates a real reason for non-GE OEMs to back an independent, and possible forced divestitures. B's problems are different. The model is plausible, since HomeServe went from 8 to 24 firms and about EUR 100M of revenue in two years, but the pitch's economics are reverse-fitted: contribution, overhead and retention are all invented. The median outcome is about EUR 0.8M of EBIT, and even the upside is only about EUR 6M, with no exit under the hold-forever structure. Its odds of reaching the upside are 1-5%. So B is more likely to work at all, but the profit pool is roughly an order of magnitude smaller and the work is heavy: 22 or more deals a year and 25-30 central staff. A's expected value per unit of founder time is higher, and its test fails cheaply.
h2h:C05:C09:ab.a_biggest_risk: The keystone behavior has no precedent: no OEM has been shown to prepay a non-incumbent owner, and a first-time sponsor must also win a scarce qualified caster at a sane price and raise $100M or more of equity against better-capitalized bidders.
h2h:C05:C09:ab.b_biggest_risk: The unit economics are unproven: the 19% contribution on absorbed crews and 70% retention on books bought from owners who could not sell are invented. So the business most likely plateaus as a roughly EUR 1M-EBIT regional group, with no anchor LP for the staged equity.

decisive_factors: Floor and median: B's median is a real operating business (about $45M revenue, roughly $6-7M EBITDA, 1.5x MOIC) while A's own unconditional median is about $7-12M of pass-through revenue at breakeven, with a 45% chance of never signing a second client.

Demand evidence: B's sellers exist and deals clear routinely (20-25 a year, abundant capital). A has no US precedent of a hospital choosing a startup operator over cash, in-house, or a national's management deal, and its cost advantage (17-24% below the hospital's own cost) is unbenchmarked.

Fatality of objections: A took three fatal critiques, was rebuilt, and still has an unsupported price model, funnel arithmetic that contradicts its upside, and a heavy regulatory stack (CMS 40.1, 424.73, EKRA, OIG). B's objections are serious but are about price and edge, not legality or mechanism, and its pass/kill test is concrete.

Tail and capital: B's tail (about 10% at $130M revenue, 21% IRR) is more probable and larger in value terms than A's 1-5% tail at $80-130M EV. A is cheaper to start ($1-2M), but B's capital is deal-by-deal and non-recourse to the founders, so B's capital burden is lower than it looks.
h2h:C11:C16:ab.reasons: Neither idea is attractive; the question is which has the better expected outcome and the less fatal objections. B wins on probability-weighted value. B is a conventional buy-and-build, so its mechanics are known: sellers exist, deal flow is steady, and lenders and independent-sponsor capital are active. Its weakness is edge. It has no moat and faces adverse selection against Alsco, Wildman and a dozen PE platforms. But that weakness shows up as a mediocre return (median about 8% IRR), not a dead business. A competent team that holds entry price discipline (walk above 7x) can still land an anchor and build a $40-50M revenue, $6-7M EBITDA platform, and the downside is bounded because equity is raised deal by deal. A's problems are more structural. Its original design was legally barred, and the rebuild leans on an unbenchmarked cost advantage, a funnel that yields about 10 systems rather than the 15 its upside needs, and a buyer (a hospital CFO and board) with cheaper alternatives and no precedent of choosing a startup. Its own authors put the upside near 5%, and the critic puts it at 1-3%. Even the upside is mostly pass-through revenue at about 8% EBITDA, worth $80-130M of enterprise value, much of it in sponsor-owned JV economics. A's low capital need is a real advantage, but a cheap test cannot fix a weak distribution. B's tail is more probable and larger.
h2h:C11:C16:ab.a_biggest_risk: No non-selling health system signs a 5-year open-book contract with a startup at 8% or more below its own cost, because the operator's cost advantage is unbenchmarked and there is no precedent of a non-national operator winning or renewing against in-house, advisory or national alternatives.
h2h:C11:C16:ab.b_biggest_risk: The platform cannot buy sub-$25M family laundries at or below about 6.5x normalized EBITDA with rollover, because strategics and PE platforms set higher prices. A first-time team then faces adverse selection and cannot close an anchor deal or assemble deal-by-deal capital.

decisive_factors: Higher floor and better median: A's median is a profitable ~$27M-revenue service group (~3.5% EBIT, about $1M) built on real cash-flowing assets. B's honest median is $7-12M of mostly pass-through revenue at about breakeven, with a 45% chance of never signing a second client.

The destination is proven for A and unproven for B. HomeServe went from 8 to 24 German firms and about EUR 100M of revenue in roughly two years, and capital is actively chasing this sector. B has no US case of a non-national operator that a health system chose over cash and then renewed; its one precedent (PAML) ended in a sale to Labcorp.

B's core economics depend on an unsupported premise. Its price only works if a startup with 1-3 clients delivers 17-24% below the hospital's own cost, and its 15-18% baseline cost has no benchmark. A's weak spot (the 19% contribution) is also invented, but it can be checked quickly from seller ledgers, and the downside is a smaller hub, not a dead model.

Regulatory and policy exposure is much heavier for B: Medicare referral-lab billing (§40.1), 42 CFR 424.73, EKRA after the 9/25/2026 DOJ position, state transaction laws, and swings in PAMA and payer rules. A's legal issues (Betriebsleiter rules, §613a BGB, §25 HGB) are known and manageable by design, for example one hub per Meister.

A's capital is staged, and its early assets are real revenue and crews, so downside is bounded. B must sell 5-year contracts to hospital CFOs against Quest, Labcorp, Orion, TriCore and free Mayo/ARUP advice, and its upside layers (a company-owned hub and a sponsor-funded JV) undercut its own neutrality pitch.
h2h:C09:C11:ab.reasons:
Neither idea is a clean venture bet. Both second-round critics rated them wounded, both put the upside at roughly 1-5%, and both have unvalidated core economics. The upside cases are similar: about $108-110M of revenue and about $6-9M of EBIT or EBITDA. So the choice rests on the median outcome, the odds of reaching it, and how likely each set of objections is to be fatal.

A wins on those three. Its median is a modest but positive-return regional service group. It is a roll-up whose end state is already proven at scale by well-funded incumbents. It buys real cash-flowing revenue at 0.25-0.4x, with half of the price contingent on customers staying, so price risk shifts to the seller. Capital arrives in stages with explicit gates, and the Phase 0 test is cheap and falsifiable. Its biggest problems are threats to the upside: HomeServe and others can lower their size floor, and it may never raise the EUR 26M or more of no-exit equity. Neither problem makes the median business impossible. If the equity never arrives, A stays a small profitable group.

B's rewrite fixed the Medicare billing structure, but it left the pricing and customer problem open. The price needs an unproven 20% or larger cost advantage over a hospital's own commercial functions, delivered by a startup with no route density. Buyers are conservative CFOs who can say no, insource, take free advice from Mayo or ARUP, or accept a national's management offer. The upside also needs 15 systems to sign when its own funnel yields about 10. The hub and JV layers weaken the neutrality edge, which is its only differentiator. Its median is roughly breakeven on pass-through revenue.

On expected value, A's higher floor and proven destination give it a clear but not overwhelming edge.
h2h:C09:C11:ab.a_biggest_risk: Not enough sellers with retainable B2B service books exist, or they will not accept the 0.25-0.40x contingent price. Related to this: the 19% hub contribution and 70% retention are invented numbers, and a funded rival (HomeServe/Brookfield, GREENOX, MEISTEREHRE) can bid above 0.5x for the same sellers. If either fails, there are no deals and no hubs, and the EUR 26M or more of no-exit equity for the upside never appears.
h2h:C09:C11:ab.b_biggest_risk: No health system that is not selling will sign a 5-year open-book contract with a startup at about 8% below its own commercial cost. That demand-and-cost-advantage bet rests on an unbenchmarked 15-18% cost baseline. The buyer's alternatives are insourcing, free Mayo/ARUP/Chi advice, or Quest/Labcorp/Orion/TriCore management offers, and no non-national operator has been shown to win and renew. EKRA and 42 CFR 424.73 add legal risk on top.

decisive_factors: Downside and capital shape: A is staged (about EUR 4M first, hub cash flows fund the median path, contingent pricing shifts retention risk to sellers). B needs a $15M+ sponsor, a bond line and $20-25M of retained fixed-price risk before first revenue around spring 2028, with ruin risk from one bad early package.

Unit economics: B's own demand test selects for the cases where the prime loses money (margin about 3-4% once costs are fully loaded, against a claimed 10-12%), and it has no hardware, no references and no moat. A's economics are invented but rest on route density, an analog with real precedent (HomeServe reached about EUR 100M in 2 years).
Median outcome: A's median is a small but real profitable service group (about EUR 0.8M EBIT). B's median is break-even or a loss and a hopeful sale to an ISP.

Testability and tail: both have roughly 3% upside odds and similar upside profit (about $5-7M). A's first test (ledgers, written non-binding yes, continuity letters) is more concrete than B's stated-preference calls, and A can close small deals within months.
h2h:C09:C01:ab.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded, and neither has better than about 3-5% odds of the $100M-plus upside, so this comes down to median and downside. Their upside profit is similar: A is about EUR 6M EBIT, B about $4-7M EBITDA.

A is the more conventional business. It buys customer books and crews at 0.25-0.4x retained revenue, with half of the price contingent on retention. The seller supply is structural: about 54,000 planned closures against 49,000 handovers. Capital is staged, and the first tranche (EUR 4M) is small. Its worst objections are unsourced inputs (19% contribution, B2B repeat share, adverse selection among sellers who could not sell). They are cheap to test, and a failure costs little. A's median is a modest profitable group. Its hold-forever wrapper caps founder upside, but it limits no downside.

B's objections are closer to fatal. The unit-economics contradiction is the worst: a prime priced at par to the OEM, with no hardware or references, earns about 3-4% after realistic costs. The demand test passes only where growth is high, which is where the prime loses money. It also needs a sponsor and surety before it has a track record, and Austin showed references beat price. The fixed-price tail can wipe out retained capital on an early package. The rotor and casting squeeze means ISPs serve their own accounts first. Hanwha can copy the cap in 18-24 months. Its median is break-even and an uncertain sale to an ISP.

A has the higher expected outcome, mainly because it has the lower variance of failure and a real median.
h2h:C09:C01:ab.a_biggest_risk: Seller and book quality, combined with an unproven hub contribution. Owners who cannot sell at 0.7x or more are adversely selected: owner-dependent, consumer-heavy books with weak retention. If retained B2B repeat revenue is under about 40-55% and contribution on absorbed crews is 15% or lower, hubs never reach EUR 3M+ and stay below break-even. HomeServe, MEISTEREHRE and GREENOX competing for the same sellers makes this worse.
h2h:C09:C01:ab.b_biggest_risk: A no-reference, no-hardware prime cannot both win awards at par pricing and earn a positive margin on a fixed-price cap. Real margin is about 3-4% against a claimed 10-12%, with no sponsor or surety in place. Allocation in a casting squeeze, Hanwha copying the cap, and one bad early package can all consume the retained capital before a moat exists.

decisive_factors: Size of outcome: B's median is about $45M of revenue at 15-18% EBITDA, and its upside is about $130M at a platform exit. A's median is about EUR 0.8M of group EBIT, and even its upside is only about EUR 6M of EBIT with no exit by design.

Proven playbook: B is a known buy-and-build with real lenders (3.5-4x), independent-sponsor capital and PE-secondary or strategic exits. A's model has no precedent, a capped-yield no-exit structure, no identified LP, and a legal wrapper that does not yet exist in statute.

Quality of the core assumptions: A's central economics (19% contribution, EUR 240k overhead, 70% retention, B2B-repeat share) are invented and reverse-fitted, and its own second-round critic says the hub test does not validate them. B's key unknown (entry multiple at or below 6.5x) is a single price variable that the owner calls and adviser comps can test in two weeks.

Probability-times-value: A's own odds are 3-5% unconditional (critic says 1-2%) for a small upside. B's are about 10% for a far larger one, and B's median is a mediocre but positive investment rather than a stall.

Founder dependency: A needs a German-speaking operator with Handwerk credibility, 6-7 Meister-partners a year, and HWK acceptance of mobile-crew hubs. B needs a US operator co-founder and sellers who accept the offer, which is more available and more conventional.
h2h:C09:C16:ab.reasons:
B wins on expected outcome, though neither idea is strong. The two ideas fail differently, and A's failure is worse.

B is a conventional lower-middle-market roll-up of a sticky, contract-based, high-margin industry. Its edge is thin, and the critics land real hits. Alsco, Wildman and a dozen PE platforms already offer rollover. Sellers say they chose Alsco for trust. Strategic bids run 2-3x revenue. Still, B has the structure of a financeable asset. Cash-flowing laundries with real estate retained, available senior debt, deal-by-deal equity and several credible exit buyers mean a failed price test is cheap to learn and a successful one scales. The median is poor (about 8% IRR) but positive. The upside is large: about $24M of EBITDA and a roughly $200M enterprise value. Weighted at about 10%, it dwarfs anything A can produce.

A's problem is the size of the prize, not just its odds. Even the winning case is a EUR 6M-EBIT service group under a hold-forever, capped-yield structure with no flip exit. The median is about EUR 0.8M of EBIT. The core economics are invented and fitted so a 25-technician hub works. The marginal-economics argument says any neighbouring firm with idle capacity absorbs a closing owner's book more cheaply than a new hub. The sellers it targets are adverse-selected, since owners who cannot sell hold the weakest books. It also needs Meister recruitment, HWK acceptance of mobile crews, an LP for a structure that is not yet statutory, and a German-speaking operator. Crew attrition is not modelled. Its own critic puts the probability at 1-2%.

Rough expected value created is several times higher for B.
h2h:C09:C16:ab.a_biggest_risk: The hub unit economics and the retained-book premise are unproven. Closing owners hold adversely selected, owner-dependent, consumer-heavy books. The 70% retention and 19% contribution are invented. Any neighbouring firm or HomeServe unit with sunk overhead can absorb the same books more cheaply. Without those, there is no profitable hub, no audited P&Ls, and no LP for the next tranche.
h2h:C09:C16:ab.b_biggest_risk: Entry price. If sellers will not accept 5.5-6.5x normalized EBITDA with rollover, and strategics or PE platforms (Alsco, Wildman, Falcon, ImageFIRST) set the price at 8x or more, a new unproven sponsor either loses the best targets or buys adversely selected ones. At 7.5x entry the IRR falls to about 12.5%, and with no synergy to about 4%.

decisive_factors: Probability of getting to a real, financeable operating business: A needs only sellers, a lender and deal-by-deal equity, all of which demonstrably exist (12+ funded buyers already doing it); B needs a sponsor, a surety line, scarce shop slots and references that a newcomer does not have, and B's own estimate is about 3% to reach its upside.

Unit economics of the surviving product: A buys real EBITDA at 5.5-6.5x with a known exit path (PE secondaries, Alsco, Wildman); B is pass-through revenue at 10-12% gross margin, and its own demand-test pass criterion (10%+ scope growth) selects the cases where margin falls to about 3-4%, while the upside is only $4-7M EBITDA.

Fatality of the objections: A's main objection is price and edge, which is testable in two weeks and fixable by walking away above 7x. B's objections are structural: unreferenced newcomer cannot qualify in scored RFPs, insurer wrap likely uninsurable, a hard return-to-service date with no hardware behind it, and Hanwha can copy the cap.

Floor of the downside outcome: A's median is a mediocre but positive roughly 8% IRR business with tangible assets and fee income to sponsors; B's median is break-even and a small sale to an ISP, with fat-tail loss risk on early packages.
h2h:C16:C01:ab.reasons:
