The R3 margin is asserted, the neutrality pitch was dropped, and the upside arithmetic has a gap. B's capital is cheaper to stage. Its failure mode is no sale at all, and the remaining generic BPO is a low-differentiation business.

A's weakness is real: thin sector margins, liability tail, policy and fraud-crackdown exposure, and sponsor competition for targets. It is still the likelier of the two to produce a modest positive outcome.
h2h:C02:C03:ba.a_biggest_risk: Cannot acquire a qualified small fiscal agent at a price its cash flow supports. Premium-market margins of 15-20% are unproven, sponsor-backed buyers anchor prices high, and the only cheap sellers are the money-losing ones. If so, the qualification ladder leads to statewide auctions at $68-83, where the sector loses money.
h2h:C02:C03:ba.b_biggest_risk: No non-Elevance, non-UnitedHealth plan will pay a fixed, non-contingent fee to an unaffiliated startup. They will insource, buy from CareBridge at a discount, or insist on savings-only, while shrinking plan budgets and long procurement cycles eat the runway. The labor-heavy coordination rung then has no demonstrated margin.

decisive_factors: Unit economics: A's own critics show realistic margin of about 3-4% once an ISP alternative at 0.85-0.90x OEM sets the price, and passing the demand gate (growth of 10% or more) selects the cases where the prime loses money. B has about 34% blended gross margin and about 14% EBITDA at scale, with R1-R2 as asset-light fee work.

Capital and tail risk: A needs a $40-60M sponsor, a surety line and retained fixed-price growth risk before or at the first package, so one bad early event can end it. B's R1-R3 carry no downstream risk, a seed round of $8-12M funds two paid pilots, and the failure mode is a smaller regional business, not a blow-up.

Severity of objections: all three of A's round-1 critiques were rated fatal (copyable by Hanwha, buyers score references and bonds, insurer wrap likely uninsurable). B's were rated serious, and its core objection (will a plan pay a fixed fee?) can be answered cheaply with 12 priced-offer calls.

Market and exit: B has a larger pool ($1.2-1.8B of plan spend) and a plausible sale to HHAeXchange, Maximus, Conduent or Evolent. A's realistic median is a break-even business sold to an ISP for $20-40M, and its upside is only $4-7M EBITDA at 3% odds.
h2h:C01:C03:ba.reasons:
Both ideas are weak and both documents say so, so this is a close call between two long shots. The question is which long shot has the better expected outcome and the less fatal objections.

A (Capped Outage) was rated fatal by all three round-1 critics. After the rewrite it is a fixed-price, bonded, date-guaranteed outage prime that owns no hardware, sells at about par to OEM and has no moat for 4-6 years. Hanwha can match the cap within 18-24 months. The economics contradict the demand test. The 12% gross margin needs a 0.77x cost basis, but a prime subcontracting shops pays about 0.85-0.90x, which leaves roughly 3-4% before bond premiums. So at $100M of revenue the profit is $4-7M EBITDA, at about 3% odds. The hard return-to-service date depends on rotor and casting slots that the ISPs hold and allocate to their own customers first. The business also holds retained fixed-price risk, needs a sponsor and a surety before event one, and realistically has first revenue in spring 2028.

B (HCBS Operations Utility) has a weak demand thesis: no evidence that neutrality sells, buyers are shrinking, and big plans insource. The rewrite responds by dropping neutrality and selling substitution of admin and coordination spend the plan already carries, priced at or below 95% of in-house cost. That is an ordinary business-process-outsourcing sale. It has higher margins, lower capital through year 5 and no risk licence until later. A bad outcome is a $5M boutique, not a loss on a bonded contract. The $100M case needs the labor-heavy R3 rung and is only about 1-8% likely, but the median of about $18M of revenue is comparable to A's, and a priced-offer call sprint can falsify it cheaply.
h2h:C01:C03:ba.a_biggest_risk: Margin and moat collapse: against ISP alternatives at 0.85-0.90x OEM, the prime's realistic margin is about 3-4% before bonding costs, Hanwha can copy the cap, and slot allocation in a casting squeeze means it cannot deliver the hard date. The result is a thin-margin, fixed-price-risk middleman that cannot qualify for bonds or sponsor capital.
h2h:C01:C03:ba.b_biggest_risk: No non-Elevance, non-UnitedHealth plan has been shown to pay a fixed, non-contingent fee to an unaffiliated vendor, rather than insource, buy from CareBridge, or insist on savings-only. Even if they do, the $100M case needs the caseload-ratio-bound R3 labor rung to earn 10-15% margin at 95% of in-house cost, which is unproven.

decisive_factors: Demand evidence: B has observed willingness to pay for speed (a city paying 3.4% for years saved, 12-15% middleman premiums) and intermediaries that reached $100M+ of orders on tens of millions raised (Ayr, Giga). A has no precedent of any landlord buying a cohort carve-out, and buyer behaviour (bundling, insourcing) points the other way.

Speed and shape of the proof: B's 14-day test plus a fee-only brokering fallback gives revenue within months. A's causal proof needs a full winter trial, about 20 months, capitation revenue starts in year 3, and its core premise (top 5% of homes carry 25% or more of spend and persist) has never been measured.

Market structure: B sells into a $1.5-3B a year class with a documented multi-year shortage and real, funded buyers. A's pool is money already routed through primes' bundled contracts, and about 20% of its revenue is pass-through works at 8-12% EBITDA that must be re-competed.

Fatality of the objections: A's objections are gatekeeping (procurement turnover tests, incumbent exclusivity, Wates and Mears already selling it), which can mean zero revenue. B's objections (existing dealers, thin spread, no moat) mean a smaller dealer business rather than no business, so its downside is better.
h2h:C15:C04:ba.reasons:
Both ideas survive only as wounded, much-reduced versions, and neither upside case ($107M or $120M of revenue) is believable. Both second-round critics put the upside at 1-3%. So the comparison comes down to which has the higher probability of becoming a profitable business of useful size, at what cost in time and capital.

B wins on that. Its pain is documented and current: 128 to 160-week lead times, buyers paying premiums, regulators pushing substation costs onto the large loads that cause them. Its competitors prove the market makes money. The refined plan concedes it is a dealer-financier with no moat. Even so, a matched-book broker and principal with a small team has a plausible path to $30M of revenue and several million dollars of gross profit. Its first test is nearly free and takes two weeks. If the premium holds, fee-only brokering can produce revenue in months.

A's premise is more novel and potentially more durable, but it is unproven at every step. The concentration data does not exist. The buyer must carve its worst homes out of bundled contracts it is simultaneously insourcing. The newco is excluded by procurement turnover and credit tests. An incumbent that already sells an adjacent product can add a gain-share schedule cheaply. Proof of causal effect takes a winter, so real revenue arrives in year 3 or later. Its capital need is lower, but its expected payoff is smaller and slower.

B's main weakness is that the shortage premium may compress as OEM capacity arrives in 2027-29, and supply access is unevidenced. That is a margin risk on a real business. A's risk is that no one buys at all.
h2h:C15:C04:ba.a_biggest_risk: No landlord will carve its worst homes out of bundled or insourced repairs contracts for a new outcome-priced entrant. Procurement turnover and credit tests exclude a newco, primes like Wates and Mears can add a gain-share schedule cheaply, and the concentration-and-persistence premise has never been measured.
h2h:C15:C04:ba.b_biggest_risk: Existing dealers (JCL, Maddox, Giga, Sunbelt Solomon) already deliver stocked or fast units, so the speed premium may be unavailable or collapse to a thin spread as new OEM capacity lands in 2027-29. Access to assignable cancelled or reserved slots is unevidenced, and the business has no moat.

decisive_factors: A's load-bearing economics contradict each other: a 93% markup ($52 bill on a $27 wage) against a 35-45% norm, plus free conversion after ~1,000 hours, which a rational shop uses at 6-12 months. The second-round critic's arithmetic puts median EBITDA near -5% to 0%, not +7.3%. The WIOA subsidy is likely unavailable for hired-out staffing.

A's demand evidence measures a shortage of qualified technicians, not open Level-1 slots. The only temp-tech comparable (LAUNCH) sells experienced techs at roughly $34-39 bill. Shops and dealers can hire a green tech directly at $24-28, and Penske and Torque already run the same training model in-house.

B sells a high-ticket product ($2M+ a unit) into an acute, documented scarcity: 128-160+ week lead times, and a premium sourced at 3.4% to 15%. Intermediaries have reached $100M+ of sales on tens of millions of equity (Giga, Ayr), so each deal carries meaningful gross profit and a small team can be viable.

B can start lean: fee-only brokering with no inventory, then at most $15M of matched-book risk, with a free 14-day test and explicit kill rules. A has no comparable lean floor, because it needs payroll float, workers' comp for brake and tire work, and hundreds of W-2 hires before economics show.

Upside tails are similar and both are low-probability (A is about 1-2% for $100M of revenue at 10-16% margin; B is about 2-8% for $120M of revenue and $8-12M EBITDA, worth $80-150M to an acquirer). B's exit buyers (Sunbelt Solomon/TJC, Quanta, United Rentals, OEMs) are more natural than A's.
h2h:C06:C04:ba.reasons:
Both ideas were wounded and both medians are roughly break-even, so the call turns on which fatal objection is more likely to hold and which business has the better floor and tail.

A's problem is structural, not just untested. The pitch sells a 6-week trainee at $52 an hour, but the shop's alternative is hiring a green tech directly at $24-28. The conversion mechanic breaks the model: if conversion is free after about 1,000 hours, a rational shop converts early. Tenure drops to months, training cost per FTE-year roughly triples, and EBITDA falls to about zero. The WIOA subsidy that cuts training cost is likely off-limits for hired-out staffing. The shortage data measure qualified technicians, and the one temp-tech comparable pays and bills far below A's assumed rates. Incumbents already run the academy model in-house. If the pricing assumption fails, nothing is left but a thin-margin training business. It would also need about 1,000 W-2 hires, workers' comp on brake and tire work, and liability exposure.

B's fatal risk is real: dealers (JCL, Maddox, Giga) already stock or quote fast, and cancelled-unit and slot supply is unevidenced. But B's fast tier is narrow (new, warranted, spec-matched 40-200 MVA units), the market is in a documented acute shortage, and deal sizes are large. Intermediaries have reached $100M+ of sales on small equity. B can start with fee-only brokering and capped matched-book inventory, and a free two-week test with clear kill rules decides it. If it fails, the cost is near zero. The risks are premium compression when new OEM capacity lands in 2028-29 and inventory mark-downs.

B has the slightly higher expected outcome. The edge is narrow because B's gap may already be closed.
h2h:C06:C04:ba.a_biggest_risk: The customer will not pay a ~93% markup ($50+/hr) for 6-week trainees when it can hire directly at $24-28. Free conversion after ~1,000 hours also shortens tenure and pushes EBITDA to about zero or below.
h2h:C06:C04:ba.b_biggest_risk: Existing dealers (JCL, Maddox, Giga, Sunbelt Solomon) already deliver warranted units of the right spec in ~20-35 weeks near a 5-8% spread. OEMs and cancellation sources would not hand a newcomer slots or assignable units, so there is neither a speed premium nor supply.

decisive_factors: Capital at risk and speed of learning: B has a roughly $0, 14-day demand test and a staged build (fee-only brokering first, at most $15M at risk in months 3-12, about $30M equity total). A needs $25M or more for the first acquisitions, and $60-75M for the upside case, before it learns whether sellers exist at a workable price.

Return on capital if it works: A's own critic computes about 1.4-2.1x over 7 years in the upside, and the median case implies about 12-20x EBITDA paid against 5-8% margins, which is a capital loss. B's upside is about 3-5x on a small equity base, and its median is roughly break-even rather than a loss.

Market evidence for new entrants: Ayr (about $25M raised, over $500M of orders), Giga ($150M or more of 2025 infrastructure sales) and FluxCo show capital-light intermediaries scaling quickly in transformers. In Medicaid fiscal agency no venture-funded entrant exists, every award went to a multi-state incumbent, and the Wisconsin operators lose about 12.5%.

Tail risk and durability: A carries sector-wide legal and political tails (Section 3504 joint liability, the $162M Calderon settlement, the DOJ suit against PPL, fraud and paid-family-caregiver crackdowns, state rate cuts) that cannot be diversified away, and its price anchor ($68-83 for statewide bids) loses money. B's main risk is cyclical: a fading speed premium after 2028, which matched-book inventory limits.

Unknown purchase price versus unknown premium: A's whole thesis rests on buying qualification cheaply, and no FMS deal comp exists while H.I.G. and General Atlantic pay about 10x. B's premium is also unproven, but B can test it directly in two weeks and has a real fallback (fee-only brokerage).
h2h:C02:C04:ba.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded. Neither upside case survives scrutiny, and both medians are small. The choice comes down to which has less capital at risk, which is more likely to produce a profitable operating business, and which has the less certainly fatal objection.

C02 is a roll-up of Medicaid fiscal agents. Its own second-round critic shows that the median case implies paying 12-20x EBITDA for assets earning 5-8% margins. That is a capital loss, so the only real success path is the 8-10% upside, and that upside returns about 1.4-2.1x over seven years on $60-75M of sponsor-style capital. The thesis needs a cheap seller. No deal comp exists, funded sponsors (H.I.G., General Atlantic) pay about 10x, and the cheap targets are the loss-making ones. The sector also sits under political, fraud, joint-liability and rate-cut pressure. It does have durable, mandated demand and a stable payer. But that demand is paid at $68-83 per participant-month in competitive bids, and the only public cost data show those prices losing money.

C04 is a dealer-financier of date-certain transformers. It is a thin-moat, dealer-margin business, and its competition and supply objections are serious. The customer is real, though: an acute shortage with 128-160 week lead times, and buyers who pay premiums. Entrants with tens of millions (Ayr, Giga, FluxCo) have reached hundreds of millions of orders or sales, which shows new intermediaries can scale in this market. The business is also staged and cheap to kill. A 14-day test, fee-only brokering and a matched-book principal phase mean most failure paths cost little. The median is about break-even and the upside is a 2-3% long shot. Its exposure is mostly the cyclical premium, not structural capital destruction.

On expected outcome, B wins narrowly. It has lower capital at risk, a faster path to first revenue and a real fallback, and it is not locked into buying overpriced assets in a politically exposed sector.
h2h:C02:C04:ba.a_biggest_risk: Cannot buy a qualifying fiscal-agent operator at a price its cash flow supports: sponsors pay about 10x, the only cheap sellers are the money-losing ones, and no FMS deal comp exists. Even if the buy succeeds, thin sector margins and Medicaid policy or legal shocks leave capital returns near or below cost.
h2h:C02:C04:ba.b_biggest_risk: The speed premium may not exist for a newcomer. Dealers (JCL, Maddox, Giga, Sunbelt Solomon) and Ayr may already deliver comparable units, no OEM may give a startup slots or assign cancelled units, and new OEM capacity in 2028-29 would collapse the premium to a plain dealer spread.

decisive_factors: B's objections are more likely fatal. All three first-round critics rated B fatal, and the rewrite mostly concedes them (no moat at launch, dealers already stock the product, supply side unevidenced). A's critics rated it serious, and the rewrite fixed several of them by moving the fee base from modelled rates to units with invoice proof.

Timing runs against B and with A. B sells a scarcity rent that its own sources say is plateauing (Rystad: prices and lead times stalled; new OEM capacity 2027-28). Its large commitments are timed for the moment the premium compresses. A's engineering cost falls as AI tools improve, and its demand triggers (M&A integration, sponsor exits, platform end-of-support) recur.

The upside is worth more for A. A's upside is about $100M revenue with 20-40% EBITDA from year 7. B's upside is $120M revenue at about 7-13% gross margin and $8-12M EBITDA, a dealer worth $80-150M. The author-estimated odds are similar (2-4% vs 2-3% unconditional), so the larger payoff wins.

The model has precedent and the downside is staged. Contingent fees on metered invoice drops have scaled before (PRGX, Redress, ProsperOps). The paid X-ray and kill gates cap early losses. The weakness is a poor median: roughly $17M revenue, breakeven around year 8-9.
h2h:C13:C04:ba.reasons:
Both ideas have mediocre medians and low-single-digit odds of a large outcome, so I compared fatality risk, durability and upside value.

B is a dealer-financier in a market that already has incumbents. Maddox, JCL, Giga, Sunbelt Solomon, Ayr and FluxCo stock or quickly deliver what B proposes. B's own rewrite concedes it has no moat at launch. Its dossier calls it "dead as a startup." The surviving margin is 7-13% gross, and the median is roughly break-even after a 25-person team. The supply side (OEMs giving slots to a newcomer, cancelled units being assignable) has no evidence and is not covered by the 2-week test. The shortage that justifies the premium is easing, and B's own plan times big commitments for 2028-29, when new capacity lands.

A has real problems. The "why pay us" question is unanswered. Realization is untested (20% targeted, 5-6% realized in the health-system panel). The median is a thin-margin business that breaks even in years 8-9. Even so, the pool is large and durable, the fee base is now metered by third-party invoices, and an adjacent pay-from-savings business (Redress) already exists. Falling AI engineering cost helps A. A paid X-ray and dated-event triggers give early revenue, and kill gates cap the loss. At scale the economics are far better than B's. A's weak median is also the likelier failure mode, and its gates are designed to catch it early.

A wins on lower fatality risk, a better time profile and a higher-value upside.
h2h:C13:C04:ba.a_biggest_risk: Realization: even with CFO backing, business owners may not release the identified spend (20% targeted vs 5-6% realized in the evidence). Then the fee base never materialises, the buyer's DIY or Redress alternative looks as good, and the business sits at the weak median or the boutique outcome.
h2h:C13:C04:ba.b_biggest_risk: The wedge may not exist. Established dealers and startups already deliver warranted units in the 30-160 MVA range on short lead times, and a newcomer has no moat or OEM slot access. New OEM capacity will compress the speed premium by 2028-29, leaving a thin-margin dealer spread.

decisive_factors: Durability of the tailwind: A rides a decade-long, demographic succession wave (about 54,000 planned Handwerk closures against 49,000 handovers, plus a demand trough that forces sellers). B rides a transformer scarcity rent that its own sources say is fading, with Rystad saying prices and lead times have stalled and new OEM capacity landing 2027-2028.

Quality of the downside and median case: A's median is a small but positive regional service group (about EUR 0.8M EBIT) funded in stages from EUR 4M, with contingent pricing that absorbs revenue loss. B's median is roughly break-even after a 25-person team, a dealer spread on pass-through units, with about $30M of equity needed and the thesis resting on an unevidenced supply side.

Severity of competition: A's incumbents (HomeServe, Konzmann, Builtech) have a structural size floor of about 20 staff, so the EUR 0.2-0.6M book tier is less contested. B's exact niche is already served by Maddox (stock to 160 MVA), JCL, Giga, Sunbelt Solomon, Ayr and FluxCo. All three first-round critics rated B's objections fatal, against serious for A.

Capital and structure: A's first tranche is small and gated, and the business can stay small by design. B's supply depends on OEMs assigning slots or cancelled units to a newcomer, which has no evidence and runs against OEM incentives, and it carries inventory price, tariff, EO and hoarding tail risks.
h2h:C09:C04:ba.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded and both have an unconditional upside probability of only about 2-5%, so this comes down to median outcome, how long the window stays open and which objections kill the idea.

B has the larger single-ticket profit pool. Its upside is $8-12M of EBITDA on $120M of sales. But its objections are the ones most likely to be fatal. The "nobody holds stock" premise is false. Maddox lists substation units to 160 MVA and JCL, Giga and Sunbelt Solomon ship fast, so the two-week test could kill it by showing dealers already quote 20 weeks or less at 8% or less above benchmark. Its supply side is not evidenced at all: no source shows cancelled or in-production units are assignable, and OEMs have every reason to resell freed slots themselves. The business is also a spread on a scarcity rent that is decaying as 2027-2029 capacity lands. The second-round critic's margin check puts the blended margin nearer 7-10% than 11-13%. The median is break-even.

A has weak economics in places. The 19% contribution and EUR 240k overhead are invented, and competitors such as MEISTEREHRE, GREENOX and HomeServe could pursue the same sellers. But it sits on a structural, multi-year seller glut. Its price is contingent on retained revenue, which transfers risk to sellers. Its first tranche is small and gated, and its median is a profitable small group. The roll-up pattern is proven in Germany, and its failure modes (sellers refuse the formula, books are consumer-heavy) are cheap to find out about in about two weeks. That makes its expected value modest but real, and its path to the downside less catastrophic.

A is the better expected-outcome bet, though neither is a great business.
h2h:C09:C04:ba.a_biggest_risk: Adverse selection on the seller side. The owners who accept 0.25-0.40x of retained revenue, with half of it contingent, are the ones who cannot sell elsewhere. Their books skew owner-dependent, consumer-heavy and low-margin, which breaks the unsourced 70% retention and 55% B2B-repeat assumptions and the invented 19% contribution that makes a hub profitable.
h2h:C09:C04:ba.b_biggest_risk: The speed premium does not exist or does not last. Incumbent dealers (Maddox, JCL, Giga, Sunbelt Solomon) already ship or quote fast units. OEMs have no reason to give a newcomer assignable slots or cancelled units. New transformer capacity in 2027-2029 compresses the premium to a plain 5% dealer spread, leaving a thin-margin trading business.

decisive_factors: A's objections are about edge and price discipline in a mechanism that demonstrably works (family laundries are bought and sold every month by funded buyers). B's objections hit the mechanism itself: dealers already stock and ship, and no source shows cancelled or in-production OEM units can be assigned to a third party.

Downside and capital at risk: A is deal-by-deal with about $10-14M of anchor equity and independent-sponsor economics, so the loss is time and deposits. B needs about $30M of equity plus a $50-60M warehouse line, with inventory marked to a transformer price that is up 77% since 2019 and likely to mean-revert.

Durability of the why-now: A's succession wave is evergreen and its entry price (5.5-6.5x) sits in the observed GF Data band for $10-25M EV deals. B's scarcity premium is fading as Rystad reports prices and lead times stalling and as new OEM plants open in 2027-29, which is also when its upside needs leverage over OEMs.

Expected-outcome arithmetic: B's $120M upside is only 2-3% likely unconditionally, its EBITDA is $8-12M on a business with no moat, and its median is about break-even after a 25-person team. A's median is mediocre (8% IRR) but it owns real cash-generating assets and has a plausible 10% path to a platform worth 3x or more.
h2h:C16:C04:ba.reasons:
Neither idea is attractive; both dossiers score them at 3-4/10 and both second-round critics call them wounded. The question is which objections are more likely to be fatal.

A's main objections are that Wildman, Alsco and about ten funded PE buyers already do this, that strategics outbid on synergy, and that a new vehicle is the least credible bidder. These are real, but they bear on edge and price. The business itself is proven. Sellers exist, lenders are active, capital is abundant relative to deal quality, and the target entry multiples (5.5-6.5x) fall inside the going lower-middle-market range. The structure also limits regret. The founders write no cheque until a capital partner and lender sign at the LOI, and the 2-week owner test is a clean kill gate. Even a bad outcome leaves them owning a cash-generating laundry. The median return is poor, about 8% IRR, but the upside (about 3.5x and 21% IRR at roughly 10% probability) is a realistic roll-up outcome.

B's objections are fatal on mechanism. Dealers (Maddox, JCL, Giga, Sunbelt Solomon) already stock and ship 30-160 MVA units, and the pass-through spread is thin. The supply side, meaning assignable cancelled units and OEM slots for a newcomer, has no evidence behind it, and the 2-week test does not cover it. The scarcity premium is fading, and the upside's own timing assumptions contradict each other. The upside is about 2-3% likely and its fee line is overstated. The original dossier calls the idea "dead as a startup." A's thin edge is a smaller flaw than B's missing gap.
h2h:C16:C04:ba.a_biggest_risk: The team cannot buy at or below about 6.5x normalized EBITDA. Sellers who have Alsco, Wildman or PE platforms bidding 8x or more will not pick a new, unproven vehicle, so the only sellers who accept are adversely selected. No anchor closes, and the median economics fall to about 4% IRR.
h2h:C16:C04:ba.b_biggest_risk: The 'date-certain, 20 weeks or less' gap is already served by incumbent dealers. The supply of discounted cancelled or slot-reserved units is unevidenced, so the business collapses to a roughly 5-8% pass-through dealer spread with no moat and a fading scarcity premium.

decisive_factors: B has observed willingness to pay: buyers already pay 3.4% to 15% premiums for speed against 128 to 160 week lead times. A has no hospital on record saying it would buy the offer, and its price needs an unsupported 17-24% cost advantage.

B's key objection (dealers already stock units, premiums fade as OEM capacity lands in 2027-29) can be tested in 14 days for about $0, using dealer quotes and buyer calls. A's test needs counsel plus access to hospital CFOs and still leaves a 5-year contract and EKRA/billing structure unresolved.

B degrades gracefully: matched-book, at most $15M at risk, and fee-only brokering as a floor. A's failure shows up after 12-24 month hospital sales cycles, and the only documented precedent (PAML/Kootenai) ended with the customer firing the operator.

Upside is similar (about $110-120M revenue, $8-12M EBITDA, 1-3% unconditional), but B has a clearer buyer set (Sunbelt Solomon/TJC, Quanta, United Rentals, OEMs) and a larger median ($30M against about $7-8M revenue).
h2h:C11:C04:ba.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded, and both upside cases are roughly 2-3% unconditional with about 8% EBITDA, so the choice rests on which objection is more likely to be fatal, and how cheaply and quickly each can be found out.

A's core problem is structural. The customer is a risk-averse hospital whose alternatives are cash from Quest or Labcorp, doing it in-house, or free advice from Mayo or ARUP. The price only works if a startup with no route density beats the hospital's own commercial cost by at least 8% after adding 10-12% markup. That is a 17-24% cost advantage, resting on a cost baseline nobody has benchmarked. The one documented case of this model ended with the hospital firing the operator. The refined plan also admits a 45% chance of never signing a second client. Sales cycles are long, the legal structure needs counsel clearance on several fronts (Medicare billing rule, agent pay, EKRA), and no US non-national operator has been shown to renew past year 3.

B's problems are real: dealers already hold stock, there is no moat, supply access is unevidenced, and the premium fades as OEM capacity arrives. But demand is observed and current, with lead times of 128-160 weeks and buyers already paying premiums. Capital at risk is staged and matched-book. The kill test is cheap and fast, and a dealer-financier outcome is the floor. B's upside is not better than A's, but its probability of a real business is higher.
h2h:C11:C04:ba.a_biggest_risk: Hospitals will not sign a 5-year open-book contract with a startup at a price below their own cost. The operator cost advantage is unbenchmarked and probably unattainable without route density, and the hospital's alternatives (cash from a national, in-house, Mayo/ARUP advice) are all easier to choose.
h2h:C11:C04:ba.b_biggest_risk: The speed premium disappears or was never capturable by a newcomer. Dealers like JCL, Maddox and Giga already ship stocked units, OEMs will not give slots or cancelled units to a startup, and new capacity in 2027-29 compresses margins to a plain 5% dealer spread. That leaves a break-even brokerage.

decisive_factors: A buys revenue, OEM qualifications and an operating team on day one, so it still has an asset-backed floor if the anchor-prepay mechanism never appears. B has no assets, no moat and no qualified positions.

B's expected value is close to zero. Its realistic gross margin is 5-10% rather than 11-13%, its median outcome is break-even, and its upside is an $8-12M EBITDA dealer worth $80-150M at 2-3% odds. A's conditional upside is about $36M EBITDA and $430-540M of enterprise value at roughly 5-12% odds.

B's thesis is time-limited and already contested. Maddox, JCL and Giga hold stock, Rystad says prices and lead times have stalled, and new OEM capacity lands in 2028-29, exactly when B would scale. A's demand runs to about 2030 and rests on qualification barriers that last years.

A's capital and operator needs ($130-175M of others' equity plus a proven casting operator) are heavy and push the odds down. This is the main reason the call is close, and it is why A's founder-level payoff is only about on par with B's.
h2h:C05:C04:ba.reasons:
This is a close call between two flawed ideas, and I give it to A narrowly. Both survive only as different businesses from the original pitches. Both have a core behavior no source shows happening. Both are likely to die at their cheap two-week test.

On expected outcome, A's upside is much larger. Its own case is about $36M of EBITDA and $430-540M of enterprise value at roughly 5-12% odds, which I would haircut to about 5-8%. B's own case is $8-12M of EBITDA at 2-3% odds, and the second-round critic shows even that is overstated. Fee revenue is inflated by about $10M, and the gross margin is more like 5-10% than 11-13%. B's median is about break-even.

B's moat problem is worse than A's. Its whole thesis, a speed premium over dealers, is the claim the dealers contradict. Maddox lists stock to 160 MVA and JCL ships the same week. The supply of cancelled or reassigned units is unevidenced. The window closes in 2028-29 as OEM capacity lands. A buys what incumbents have: approvals, furnaces and staff. It earns 18-22% EBITDA in a shortage that runs toward 2030.

A's real weaknesses are capital and acquisition. The sources and uses do not close at the low end. Equity returns are only 1.8-3.3x unless the exit multiple expands. A first-time sponsor competes against GE, Arcline and Pursuit. The customer-side value proposition is thin. Even so, A can degrade into a plain PE-style operating deal without anchor prepayment. B degrades into a boutique broker.

A wins because it has the larger and more defensible expected value. B is the easier idea to start, but its ceiling and moat are weak.
h2h:C05:C04:ba.a_biggest_risk: The capital stack and customer behavior do not materialize. No OEM has been shown to prepay a non-incumbent owner, so the anchor funding that cuts the equity need has no precedent. A first-time sponsor also has to win and finance a qualified target at a sane price against GE/CPP, Arcline, Pursuit and Doncasters.
h2h:C05:C04:ba.b_biggest_risk: The speed premium does not exist or gets competed away. Dealers such as Maddox, JCL and Giga already ship stocked units, and OEM-sourced supply from cancelled or reassigned units is unproven. New OEM capacity in 2028-29 would compress any premium to a 5% dealer spread with no moat.

decisive_factors: A has an internal economics contradiction. Demand passes only where as-found growth is 10% or more, but at a prime's real cost (about 0.87x OEM times growth) that is where it earns about 3-4% before bonds and liquidated damages, so success in the test selects for money-losing jobs.

B can earn revenue and get evidence in weeks through fee-only brokering and a matched-book design (title only with a buyer PO and deposit, at most $15M at risk). A needs a sponsor, a surety line and shop slots before its first package, so first revenue is spring 2028.
B's downside is capped by the matched-book rules. A keeps $20-25M of uninsured scope-growth risk after the insurer wrap was dropped, and a single bad early package can wipe that out.

B's market is bigger and has intermediary proof points (Ayr over $500M of orders and Giga over $150M of infrastructure sales on tens of millions raised). B's upside EBITDA of $8-12M (nearer $5-8M after the critic's corrections) beats A's $4-7M. B's 2-week test also collects hard dealer quotes and written indications, where A's test is mostly stated preference.
h2h:C01:C04:ba.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded, with about 3% odds of the upside and a median case near break-even at $30M of revenue. Neither is a venture-scale margin pool, so the call is about fatal-objection likelihood and the cost of finding out.

A (Capped Outage) is a thin-margin general contractor with no cost edge, no moat for 4-6 years, and no hardware behind its date guarantee. Its sharpest flaw is that its own demand criterion (growth of 10% or more) sits where its margin is lowest. It also needs an unreferenced newcomer to win $5M outages at price parity against Hanwha, with 100% bonds, from owners who stay with the OEM for reasons other than price. A separate sponsor and surety are required that the founder cannot supply alone. With the insurance wrap gone, the business holds the volatile scope-growth tail itself. That tail is the worst part of the business, and it can end the company.

B (Time-to-Power Desk) has real weaknesses. Dealers already ship stock, supply from OEMs and cancelled units is unproven, and new OEM capacity in 2027-29 may compress the premium. But a buyer-PO-gated model limits what can go wrong. It starts earning in weeks, and it uses larger ticket sizes in a market with live demand evidence and active acquirers. Its kill test is a fast, hard-data test that settles the main question, whether dealers already close the gap. If B fails, the loss is small. If A fails, it fails late, after sponsor and surety effort.

The margin is thin because B's supply access may never exist, which would leave it a boutique broker.
h2h:C01:C04:ba.a_biggest_risk: The economics contradict the demand: owners who actually suffer 10% or more scope growth are the ones where a prime paying shops at about 0.87x OEM loses money at par pricing. An unreferenced, unbonded newcomer also cannot win $5M outages from OEM-loyal buyers or secure the surety and sponsor needed to start.
h2h:C01:C04:ba.b_biggest_risk: No durable supply edge. Dealers (JCL, Maddox, Giga) may already deliver warranted units quickly, and OEMs allocate slots to volume buyers and may not assign cancelled units. As new OEM capacity lands in 2027-29 the speed premium collapses toward a 5% dealer spread, leaving a fee-only boutique.

decisive_factors: B's fatal critiques attack only the $100M thesis, and its realistic floor is a $10-25M regional business in a form buyers already purchase (technician temp-to-hire staffing plus training). A's fatal critiques attack whether anyone buys at all.

A depends on creating a new contract category (outcome-priced hot-spot lots) in a market moving the other way: bundling into whole-stock deals and insourcing, with winners already awarded for 2026-31 and a newco shut out by turnover and D&B tests.

B's demand pain is documented (54-65% of shops understaffed, wage inflation) and can be tested in two weeks for under $500 in one metro. A's core premise (top 5% of homes carry 25% or more of spend and persist) is unmeasured, and the full proof needs a winter-long controlled trial, about 20 months, with revenue starting in year 3.

A's own model has internal contradictions (control-based vs trailing-baseline pricing; fee per home vs persistence gate), unresolved Awaab's Law and randomised-control conflict, and a legal tail. B's contradictions (tenure vs free conversion, WIOA ineligibility) are real but they hit margin, not existence, and B has fallbacks such as dealer-only focus or a placement-fee model.

Both are thin-margin (A about 8-12% EBITDA on mostly pass-through works; B about 0-7% on staffing), so the winner is the one with the higher probability of a working business and the faster, cheaper path to learning. That is B.
h2h:C15:C06:ba.reasons:
Both ideas end up as modest-margin services businesses once the critics are done with them. Each has a roughly 1-3% chance of reaching $100M, so the decision turns on the probability of a working business at the $10-25M scale and on how fast and cheaply each idea finds out.

B wins on that. Technician shortage is a documented problem, and staffing technicians into shops by the hour already exists. Temp-to-hire techs, perm recruiters and $100M-scale skilled-trades staffing firms are all real. B needs buyers to pay a premium for something they already buy: an extra pair of hands on an open requisition. The shop bills that labor at about $149 an hour, which makes the spread plausible. Its weak point is the $50+ bill rate against a typical 35-45% markup, and a $500 test in one metro settles that in two weeks. If staffing at that rate fails, there are fallbacks: dealer-only focus or a training-and-placement fee. The likely end state is a regional bench or training business that a consolidator would buy.

A needs a category that does not exist. No carve-out precedent turned up in about 26 searches. Landlords are bundling and insourcing, and the 2026-31 awards are done. A newco cannot meet the turnover and credit-score tests, and incumbents like Wates and Mears can answer cheaply. Its premise, that a small cohort of homes concentrates spend persistently, is unmeasured. The real proof needs a randomised winter trial that collides with Awaab's Law, and revenue starts around year 3. The pricing mechanism contradicts itself, and the fix capital and liability tail come later. Its credible outcome is a low-single-digit £M niche, below B's floor.

B is clearly the better bet.
h2h:C15:C06:ba.a_biggest_risk: No landlord will buy an outcome-priced, capitated carve-out of its worst homes. Buyers are bundling into whole-stock deals and insourcing, a newco is excluded from procurement by turnover and credit tests, and incumbents can add a gain-share schedule. The concentration and persistence premise is also still unmeasured.
h2h:C15:C06:ba.b_biggest_risk: Shops will not pay a staffing-style bill rate of $50 or more per hour (a 93% markup against a 35-45% norm) for six-week trainees when they can hire direct at $24-28. If the market clears nearer $38-45, or conversion and tenure behave rationally, the model drops to about zero or negative EBITDA.

decisive_factors: A buys revenue that already exists and is already paid for, with 40-50% of the price contingent on retention. B has to create a new buyer behavior (shops paying a staffing markup for trainees) that nothing in the file shows exists.

B's core economics contradict themselves: a 93% markup against a 35-45% norm, a conversion fee that is free after about 1,000 hours, a customer who pays more than the training cost it avoids, and a WIOA subsidy that is probably unavailable. A rational customer converts early and median EBITDA falls to about zero or below. A's weak spot is the invented 19% contribution, which is a parameter to measure, not a broken mechanism.

A degrades gracefully. If Series B capital never arrives, it stays a 10-12 hub regional group with positive EBIT, and contingent pricing caps losses on bad books. B's most likely outcome is a failed pilot or a thin-margin staffing shop that incumbents with the same labor cost structure can price-match or buy.

The critic severities differ. B drew two fatal ratings (competition and customer). A drew three serious ones, and its refinement answered them with structural changes: a different unit of purchase, a staged capital plan, and a veto-share legal wrapper.

The upside probabilities are about equal (1-5%), so the median and downside decide it. A's median is a roughly EUR 24M-revenue group with about EUR 0.8M EBIT, small but plausible. B's honest median is a $10-25M regional bench business with doubtful margin.
h2h:C09:C06:ba.reasons:
Both ideas have a 1-5% chance of reaching the $100M headline, so the median and downside decide this. On those, A is better.

A is a capital-allocation business built on existing cash flows. The seller supply is real: about 54,000 Handwerk firms plan to close against 49,000 planning a handover, and insolvencies are at a decade high. Customers already pay for the service. Contingent pricing at 0.25-0.40x retained revenue, with half paid only if customers stay, limits loss on any single deal. If the hub model's marginal economics hold, payback is about two years. The objections (HomeServe, the invented 19% contribution, adverse selection among sellers, Meister supply, no LP for the later tranches) mostly limit scale rather than kill the business. The two-week seller-ledger test can falsify the key assumption cheaply. The weaknesses are real: no moat, a flat 3-5% chance of the upside, and a low EBIT margin even at success.

B's central claim is that shops will pay about $52 an hour for six-week trainees when a direct hire costs $24-28. The file contains no evidence that shops or fleets buy temporary technicians at scale. The one comparable posting implies a bill rate of $34-39 even for experienced techs. The tenure and conversion economics contradict each other. The WIOA subsidy likely excludes hire-out models. The demand statistics measure missing qualified technicians, not open Level-1 slots. Two critics rated its competition and customer objections fatal. Incumbents with the same labor cost can price-match or acquire an entrant.

B's cheap $500 test is attractive, but a pass would only start the real work. A has the better odds of producing a positive, scalable outcome.
h2h:C09:C06:ba.a_biggest_risk: Seller adverse selection combined with unproven hub economics. Owners who can only close are likely to hold owner-dependent, consumer-heavy books, which weakens the 70% retention and 19% contribution that the model assumes. A hub below about EUR 1.55M of revenue loses money, and crews can leave. Capital for the scaled version has no identified LP.
h2h:C09:C06:ba.b_biggest_risk: Customers will not pay a roughly 90% staffing markup ($50+ an hour) for six-week trainees when they can hire direct at $24-28 and train. Nothing in the file shows that shops buy temporary technicians at scale. The conversion and tenure economics also break the margin even if the price holds.

decisive_factors: Even the conditional-median outcome is worth far more in A: a closed, qualified plant of about $45-55M revenue at 18-22% EBITDA is a real asset in a sold-out market. B's own median is $20M revenue at 7% EBITDA, and the critic's tenure/conversion math puts that at about 0.

A has downside floor and upside the other lacks. If A closes, the founder owns an operating business in a multi-year capacity shortage, even if the anchor-funding mechanism fails. B's failure mode is a staffing business that works but earns nothing.

B's core economics are contradicted by evidence in the files: a 93% markup against a 35-45% norm, temp-tech competitors implying about $34-39 bill rates, WIOA subsidy likely ineligible, free conversion after about 1,000 hours, and a $149 shop labor rate that makes a direct hire cheaper. B's probability of $100M is about 1-2%, and the likely end state is a roughly $1M-EBITDA regional business or a sale to a consolidator.

Expected value gap is roughly an order of magnitude. A is about 10-12% x a roughly $250M+ equity gain, or $25-40M, against B at about $2-5M. A's capital is large but is third-party equity and staged behind a cheap test, while B's thin-margin, labor-heavy model has weak moat and weak asset value.
h2h:C05:C06:ba.reasons:
Both ideas survived three fatal-grade critiques, so the question is which carries more expected value per unit of objection risk. I rate A higher.

A's problems are serious. No OEM prepay to a non-incumbent owner has been found. The sources and uses do not close at the low end. The entry price assumes 2x revenue against 5.9x and 8x comps. Pursuit, CPP and Arcline are better-capitalized bidders. And the customer value proposition is thin. But if A fails at the anchor-funding step, what remains is a leveraged buyout of a qualified caster in a market where hot-section capacity is the binding constraint, order books run to 2030, and independents earn 18-22% EBITDA. Strategics pay 18x or more for such positions, so multiple expansion at exit is plausible. Revenue and approvals are bought on day one, and the asset keeps value even if the thesis is wrong.

B's problems go to the unit economics. The whole model rests on shops paying about $52 an hour, a 93% markup, for six-week trainees they could hire directly at $24-28 and train themselves. The files give no evidence of that demand, and some contrary evidence: experienced temp techs bill about $34-39, the WIOA subsidy likely excludes hire-out models, and free conversion after about 1,000 hours makes rational customers convert early. That drives modeled EBITDA to about zero, and there is no moat. Even a success is a $10-25M staffing business, probably sold to Amerit or Ryder at a regional multiple.

A needs far more capital and has a low unconditional close rate. B's cheap test is a real advantage. On expected value, though, A is roughly 5-10x higher.
h2h:C05:C06:ba.a_biggest_risk: The keystone behavior is unevidenced and may not exist: a non-captive OEM funding a capacity line at a non-incumbent-owned caster. Qualified targets may also be unavailable at sane prices against Pursuit, CPP/GE and Arcline. Together these leave a first-time sponsor needing $130-175M of equity for a generic, mediocre-return buyout, with an unconditional median outcome of $0.
h2h:C05:C06:ba.b_biggest_risk: Shops and dealers will not pay a staffing-style bill rate of about $50 or more per hour (a 93% markup) for six-week trainees when they can hire directly at $24-28. Even if they pay it, the tenure/conversion contradiction pushes EBITDA to about zero. The business becomes a thin-margin, moatless staffing company that tops out at a $10-25M regional outcome.

decisive_factors: Capital at risk and speed of learning: B needs about $15-30M to reach $100M but can start in one metro for well under $1M, with a $500 two-week price test. A needs a $40-60M sponsor, a roughly $60M surety line and retained-risk capital, and does not reach first revenue until spring 2028.

Profit pool per unit of revenue: A's $100M of revenue is mostly pass-through with $4-7M EBITDA, and the critic's arithmetic shows 3-4% margin at realistic cost, so the demand-gate pass selects for money-losing deals. B's staffing-plus-training economics give 7% at median and 16% at upside, with about $14M of EBITDA at $100M even if the critic's haircuts apply.

Failure mode: A's tail is a rotor failure or casting-inflation hit on an early fixed-price package that wipes out retained capital, and the insurer wrap is probably uninsurable. B's worst case is a cheap failed pilot or a $10-25M regional staffing business.

Market structure: A sells to 200-300 units in a market where scored RFPs reward references the entrant cannot have, and Hanwha can copy the cap. B's buyer base is thousands of shops with a documented shortage, and PE roll-ups (Amerit, True North, Ryder) are natural acquirers.
h2h:C01:C06:ba.reasons:
Both ideas are weak, and neither is a strong pick. B is the better expected outcome because it is cheaper to be wrong about and has a more attractive residual if partly right.

A has three fatal critiques that interlock. Scored RFPs reward references a newcomer cannot have, and Hanwha can match a cap or a condition-priced contract in 18-24 months. The hard return-to-service date has no hardware behind it, since rotor and casting slots are held by the ISPs and OEMs it competes with. The insurer wrap is probably dead on arrival. The second-round critic's arithmetic is the most damning point. Price parity with a 0.87x subcontract cost gives about 3-4% margin, so passing the demand test selects for deals the prime loses money on. The author's own odds are about 3% for an upside that yields only $4-7M EBITDA, and the median is break-even. It also needs a sponsor, a surety and $40-60M of capital before references exist, and a bad early package could wipe out the retained capital.

B's core risk is also serious. Shops may refuse to pay about $52/hr when they can hire direct at $24-28, and the conversion and tenure mechanics contradict each other. The WIOA subsidy is probably unavailable to a hire-out model, and Michigan-style supervision rules apply. But that risk can be tested for under $500 in two weeks, and the capital at stake before the test resolves is trivial. If it works even partly, the result is a real $10-25M staffing business with a plausible acquirer set and a mid-single-digit EBITDA margin. Its upside also earns more profit per revenue dollar than A's.
h2h:C01:C06:ba.a_biggest_risk: The economics do not close at realistic prices. At price parity with an ISP alternative at 0.85-0.90x OEM, the prime's margin is about 3-4% before bonds and liquidated damages. The demand test selects for the deals that lose money, and the unreferenced newcomer, uninsurable cap and absent hardware leave it with no defensible position.
h2h:C01:C06:ba.b_biggest_risk: Shops will not pay a bill rate of $50 or more per hour, which is a 93% markup on a $27 wage, for 6-week-trained Level-1 technicians when they can hire and train directly at $24-28. Breakeven is about $47.50 an hour, and with a free-conversion clause the tenure math gets worse.

decisive_factors: A's asset class is proven and its median is positive. Family laundries are recurring-contract, cash-generating businesses that lenders fund and PE and strategics buy actively (ImageFIRST made 25 deals, Alsco 4 in 18 months). Even with no edge, the median is a roughly 8% IRR. B's median is a failed pilot or roughly 0% EBITDA after its own tenure and conversion contradiction.

Value if it works is larger for A. The median is a $45M-revenue business at roughly 15% EBITDA, and the upside is a $130M platform at a 9-10x exit with a stated 10% chance. B's median is about $20M of revenue at 5-7% margin (about $1.4M EBITDA), and its $100M upside is rated 1-3%.

B's core price assumption is unproven and contradicted. It needs a 93% markup (about $52 bill on a $27 wage) against a 35-45% staffing norm, and LAUNCH implies about $34-39 for experienced techs. The dossier found no evidence that shops buy temporary technicians at scale. Direct hire at $24-28 is a cheap substitute, WIOA on-the-job-training subsidies likely exclude hired-out staffing, and PE-funded Amerit and Ryder can match price or insource.

A's failure mode is more benign. The risk is price discipline (walk away above 7x) and a slow anchor, not a broken product. Capital is deal-by-deal and other people's, with fee economics for the sponsor, and the 60-day IOI gate and the 12-month anchor checkpoint limit the loss. B is cheaper to test ($500), but a cheap test does not make a small, low-margin outcome large.
h2h:C16:C06:ba.reasons:
Neither idea is attractive; the question is which has the higher expected outcome. A is a conventional buy-and-build with a thin edge, rated about 4/10 by its own author. B is a new staffing model whose price assumption is untested and contradicted by the evidence.

On value if it works, A wins clearly. Its median is a $45M-revenue, roughly 15%-margin platform worth tens of millions of dollars. Its upside is a $130M platform at a 9-10x exit, which the author puts at about 10%, and the critic calls that generous. B's median is about $20M of revenue at 5-7% EBITDA. The second-round critic argues that free conversion after about 1,000 hours pushes that margin to roughly zero. B's $100M upside is 1-3%.

On probability of working, A's objections are about price and adverse selection. A disciplined buyer still gets a positive-return median in a sector where deals clearly close. B's objections go to whether a product exists. The 93% markup has no market evidence, a direct-hire substitute is cheap, WIOA subsidies likely exclude hire-out staffing, and PE-backed Amerit and Ryder can price-match or insource.

B wins on capital and speed. Its test costs $500 and a full pilot needs little capital, while A needs a 9-12 month anchor process and equity partners. That option value does not make up for a much smaller payoff. A also uses deal-by-deal capital with stop points at 60 days and 12 months, and the sponsor earns fees along the way.
h2h:C16:C06:ba.a_biggest_risk: Sellers do not accept 5.5-6.5x with rollover from a new, unproven vehicle. Alsco, Wildman, PE platforms and strategics pay 7-8x or more, so the platform is left with adverse-selected targets or an entry price (7.5x) that drops IRR to about 12% and leaves the median near 4%.
h2h:C16:C06:ba.b_biggest_risk: Shops and dealers will not pay a staffing-style bill rate of about $50 an hour (a 93% markup over a $27 wage). They hire direct at $24-28 and train in-house, and tenure and conversion economics then push EBITDA to about zero. Break-even is already about $47.50 an hour.

decisive_factors: B's single load-bearing unknown (will shops pay $50+/hr for pre-trained Level-1s) can be settled in two weeks for under $500. A's equivalent unknown (will a hospital sign a 5-year contract with a startup at a price 8%+ below its own cost) takes 6 to 18 months and counsel spend to settle.

A's price model needs the operator to cost 17-24% less than the hospital's own commercial functions, with 1-3 clients and no route density. No benchmark exists for that, and the only documented precedent (PAML/Kootenai) ended with the hospital firing the operator.

A's addressable buyer set is only about 160 systems, of which about 11-22 value neutrality, and it has three independent kill risks (Medicare referral-lab rule, EKRA/424.73, national and regional rivals). B has thousands of small shop and dealer buyers and a fallback of a $10-25M regional bench-and-training business.

A's contracts are better if they land: sticky, recurring, about $4M per system. But the critics put A's upside at 1-3%, its median near $7-8M revenue at breakeven, and its upside revenue is mostly pass-through at about 8% EBITDA. B's expected profit is also thin, so the tie goes to the idea with the higher survival odds and the cheaper, faster test.
h2h:C11:C06:ba.reasons:
This is close, because both ideas are wounded and neither gives a high-probability large outcome. A's best case is better revenue: sticky 5-year contracts at about $4M per system. But it needs several unproven things to hold at once. A hospital has to pick a startup over doing it in-house, Orion/TriCore, Mayo/ARUP/Chi advice, or a national's management offer. The startup has to deliver a 17-24% cost advantage with no density. Counsel has to clear a structure that sits right next to the Medicare referral-lab rule, 42 CFR 424.73 and EKRA. There is no US precedent of a non-national operator being chosen over cash and renewing. The one documented model (PAML/Kootenai) ended with the hospital firing it and insourcing. The buyer set is about 160 systems, and a 10-20% neutrality-minded slice of the stayers is the only claimed edge. Even if it works, the revenue is mostly pass-through at about 8% EBITDA, and the unconditional median is about $7-8M revenue at roughly breakeven.

B's economics are thin and may be near zero if conversion is free. But the demand problem is real: 54% of shops are understaffed and shops bill $149/hr labor, so a $50 bill rate leaves them a spread. The key risk is binary and can be tested in two weeks for under $500. The buyer universe is thousands of independent shops and dealers, which gives many fast shots on goal. A realistic fallback exists in a $10-25M regional bench-and-training business, and the consolidators are also potential buyers. B's ceiling is low, with $100M at 1-2%. But its survival odds are higher, it costs less to find out, and it needs less rare founder expertise.
h2h:C11:C06:ba.a_biggest_risk: No non-selling health system signs a 5-year open-book contract with an unproven startup at a price at least 8% below its own commercial-function cost. That would need a 17-24% cost advantage the startup cannot have without density, and the only documented precedent (PAML/Kootenai) ended with the hospital firing the operator. h2h:C11:C06:ba.b_biggest_risk: Shops will not pay a bill rate of $50/hr or more (a 93% markup over a $27 wage) for 6-week-trained Level-1s. They can hire direct at $24-28, or buy experienced temp techs at an implied $34-39. decisive_factors: A's core product has no buyer evidence and buyers are moving the opposite way: critics rated customer and procurement objections fatal, landlords are bundling and insourcing, and the landlord's saving is under 0.5% of turnover. B has adjacent proof that buyers pay on share-of-savings (Redress at 25%, PRGX, ProsperOps, SaaS-buying share models, a sponsor case with $100M removed). A has no precedent for capitation or a carve-out after about 26 searches.

The market is bigger and the buyer richer in B: about 700 US payers with $40M or more of run spend, a CFO signer, and $2-5M a year savings per client. A is UK-only, slow, and sold to cash-squeezed, risk-averse landlords at 59% interest cover.

At scale B earns better margins (20-30% EBITDA in the upside) than A (8-12%, mostly pass-through works), so the same low-probability tail is worth more. A's realistic residual is a small damp-and-mould specialist contractor facing Wates and Mears.

A's advantages are real but not enough. Capital is light to the winter read (about GBP1M), the FOI test needs no cooperation, and Awaab's Law forces demand. B's median case burns about $28M for roughly break-even, but its gates (paid X-ray, kill if two of G2-G5 are missed by month 12) cap the downside.
h2h:C15:C13:ba.reasons:
Both ideas are badly wounded. Each author puts the chance of reaching about $100M a year at roughly 2-5%, and each has a median case near $17M of revenue. The choice therefore turns on which objections are more likely to be fatal, how large the realistic ceiling is, and what the capital costs.

A's problem is demand. Its critics found no evidence that anyone will buy a capitated cohort carve-out. Landlords are bundling whole-stock deals (Livin, Winchester, Thurrock) and insourcing (Teign, Basildon). A newco fails the turnover and D&B tests. Wates Healthy Homes and the price-per-property primes already sell the adjacent product. The signer saves under 0.5% of turnover while keeping the statutory duty. The randomised control design also collides with Awaab's Law. The refined plan retreats to a fix-only damp-and-mould contractor, a low-margin niche. The author concedes that A's upside needs category creation, which is "heroic". It also needs the unrun concentration premise to hold.

B's problem is realization and "why pay us". Realization ran 5-6% against a 20% target, and the CFO already owns the capital. B also has a revenue cliff and a median case that burns about $28M. But buyers already pay a percentage of savings (Redress, PRGX, ProsperOps). The invoice-line-drops rule removes baseline disputes, and a paid X-ray brings in early cash. The kill gates are explicit and the pool is large. If it works, margins are better.

I pick B, narrowly.
h2h:C15:C13:ba.a_biggest_risk: No buyer wants it. Landlords are bundling and insourcing, the incumbent primes already sell the adjacent product, a newco cannot clear procurement or turnover tests, and a less than 0.5%-of-turnover saving does not justify the signer's career risk. The business collapses into a low-margin damp-and-mould subcontractor.
h2h:C15:C13:ba.b_biggest_risk: Realization. Business owners do not release the identified spend, as in the health-system panel (20% targeted, 5-6% realized). CFOs then cap the share near 15-20% or use Redress or an in-house team, because the one thing B adds, execution backed by the CFO, is something the buyer already controls. decisive_factors: A's demand is mandated, government-paid and not in doubt (about $0.7-0.9B fee pool), so its failure risk collapses into one testable variable, namely whether small agents can be bought at a workable price. B has demand and pricing risk at its core.

B's core unit economics are self-defeating. Free conversion after about 1,000 hours, combined with a 93% markup over a 35-45% staffing norm, pushes median EBITDA to roughly zero. The WIOA subsidy is likely ineligible, and the nearest precedent (experienced temp techs) bills around $34-39 an hour against B's $52.
A has a clear, well-paid exit buyer set (H.I.G. and General Atlantic at about 10x EBITDA). B's likely end state is being acquired at a small regional staffing multiple.

Probability of a real business is higher for A. Its median band is about 45%, against B's own admission that the unconditional median is a failed pilot. B's cheaper test (under $500) is its main offset but does not outweigh this.
h2h:C02:C06:ba.reasons:
Both ideas are weak after their critiques. I pick A narrowly because its demand is real and its failure mode is concentrated in one testable unknown, while B has several independent structural flaws.

A sells into a mandated, state- or plan-paid market with a fee pool of about $0.7-0.9B. It also has an identifiable sponsor and strategic exit market (GT/H.I.G., TEAM/General Atlantic at roughly 10x EBITDA). Its fatal objection is a single unknown: whether owner-operated fiscal agents exist that earn real margin in choice and rate-card markets and will sell near 1.0x revenue. A no-capital seller-side test and a month-6 LOI and equity gate cap the downside before the large dollars go out. The weaknesses are serious. It has no structural edge over funded sponsors, needs $60-75M of capital, and its median case is close to a capital loss at realistic purchase prices. It also carries Section 3504 liability and policy tail risk.

B has no evidence that shops buy trainee labor at a 93% markup. The closest precedent, experienced temp techs, bills near $34-39 an hour. The conversion design is self-defeating: free conversion after about 1,000 hours shortens tenure, which pushes median EBITDA to about zero. The WIOA subsidy is likely ineligible, heavy-duty liability and state licensing add cost, and PE-funded incumbents can copy the model or buy it. Its author puts $100M at 3-5% and the critic at 1-2%, so the realistic outcome is a $10-25M regional business at near-zero margin. B is cheaper to try, but cheap failure is worth less than A's better odds of building a real asset.
h2h:C02:C06:ba.a_biggest_risk: Acquisition price and availability. No FMS deal price has been found, funded sponsors (H.I.G., General Atlantic) are bidding for the same small operators at about 10x, and the only cheap targets may be the money-losing ones. h2h:C02:C06:ba.b_biggest_risk: Shops will not pay a bill rate of $50 or more an hour, about a 93% markup, for trainees they can hire directly at $24-28. Even if they do, early conversion to the customer's payroll defeats the economics of the training spend.

decisive_factors: Return on capital: A's own critic shows the median case yields roughly 5-8% EBITDA on $25M revenue against $25M or more invested, about 12-20x EBITDA actually paid, and even the upside is only about 1.4-2.1x over 7 years. B's upside is a real operating-leverage outcome ($20-44M EBITDA by years 7-9) on roughly $30-60M of burn.

Cost of being wrong: B is gated by paid X-rays, an 18-month payback funding hurdle and kill gates by month 12, so a failed realization test costs little. A's real spend is $60-75M of sponsor-style acquisition capital, and the thesis depends on a deal price nobody has found.

Competitive structure: A competes for a thin supply of targets against H.I.G., General Atlantic (about 10x EBITDA) and incumbents who hold the qualification, while the only cheap sellers are the money-losing ones (Wisconsin -12.5%). B's rivals (Redress, Flexera, ISG, in-house teams) each cover a slice, but none funds and executes retirement to an invoice drop, and Redress's 25% and PE portfolio cases show buyers pay.

Structural downside: A carries Section 3504 joint-and-several tax liability (a $162M Calderon settlement), a fee of about 2% of spend, and state-budget and federal-fraud policy risk it cannot fix. B's risks (insurance, retirement breakage, vendor retaliation) are operational and mostly mitigable by design.
h2h:C02:C13:ba.reasons:
Both ideas ended round two wounded, and in both the median case is really a weak outcome. The decision therefore rests on the tail, the cost of being wrong, and whether the core risk can be tested cheaply.

A is a Medicaid fiscal-agent roll-up. It has a 2% fee on program spend, a sector that lost money in the only public cost data, and a thesis that rests on buying a "qualification ticket" at a price nobody has found. The author's own median is about $1.3-2M EBITDA on $25M or more invested, so a 10x exit returns less than the capital. h2h:C02:C13:ba.a_biggest_risk: Cannot acquire the multi-state qualification at a workable price and margin. h2h:C16:C13:ba.reasons:
Neither idea is attractive, so this is a choice between a mediocre but real business and a gated long shot. The tails are roughly equal in expected value, so the median case and the downside decide it.

h2h:C01:C13:ba.a_biggest_risk: Unit economics and defensibility. h2h:C01:C13:ba.b_biggest_risk: Realization. Business owners may not release the identified spend, so invoice lines never fall and there is no fee base. The only documented precedent (PAML/Kootenai) ended with the customer firing the operator, and no US case exists of a system choosing a startup operator. B's rests on realization, which is a behavioral risk, is selectable by owner sign-off, and can be tested before heavy funding.

Market breadth and incumbent fit: A's reachable pool is about 160 hospital systems, with 2-13 transactions a year and Quest, Labcorp, Orion and TriCore all competing. B's pool is about 700 payers (unsourced), and no one funds and executes retirement. Redress, ISG and Flexera only advise or identify, and contingent-fee comps (PRGX, ESCO, cloud savings share) have precedent.
h2h:C11:C13:ba.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded, with 2-4% odds of their stated upside and weak medians, so this is a close call. The difference is in what each looks like when it works and how cheaply it fails.

A started with three fatal critiques. The rewrite (100% hospital-owned LLC, vendor paid cost-plus) plausibly clears the Medicare billing problem, but it turns the company into a low-margin pass-through operator. Even a good outcome of about 15 managed systems earns roughly $10M of operating profit. The price model needs a 17-24% cost advantage that a startup with no density cannot have. The only observed customer of this model fired the operator, and every outreach exit went to Quest or Labcorp. A's bear case is a $2-6M boutique, and its median is breakeven at about $7-12M of revenue. Its regulatory risk (CMS 1833(h)(5)(A), EKRA, 424.73) is also never fully closed.

B's rewrite is more disciplined. The rule "no invoice line drops, no fee" removes the baseline fight, and the pool is broader. A paid X-ray puts cash in by month 2-4, and kill gates cap exposure. If the upside path works, margins are real (about $20-33M EBITDA at $100-121M revenue). Its median is poor: about $17M of revenue, breakeven in year 8-9, and $28-60M of cash needed. That is acceptable only because the gates should stop it first. B's weaknesses are real. Realization has contrary evidence (5-6% realized against 20% targeted), "why pay us" over Redress or DIY is thin, and the 700-payer count is unsourced. They are more testable and less structural than A's.

I give B a modest edge in expected outcome: higher value if it works, similar tiny odds, and no worse downside.
h2h:C11:C13:ba.a_biggest_risk: No workable price or buyer. A non-selling health system must sign a 5-year contract with a startup at least 8% below its own unbenchmarked commercial-function cost. The startup has no route or billing density, and the hospital can do nothing, use Mayo/ARUP/Chi advice, or take a national's management offer. The one documented precedent ended with the customer firing the operator.
h2h:C11:C13:ba.b_biggest_risk: Realization. Business owners may not release the identified spend, so invoice lines never fall. The company would then fund engineering for units that earn no fee and sit on a median profile of about $17M of revenue and breakeven in year 8-9 after $28-60M of burn. The CFO's alternatives (Redress at 25% once, in-house, or vendor renegotiation) price at parity.

decisive_factors: Conditional on working, A is a real asset with positive EBITDA from day one in a shortage backed by hard evidence (Rystad orders about 30% above delivery capacity, GE paying about 18x EBITDA for CPP, Doncasters at about 8x sales, Howmet capacity committed through 2029). B's own median case is a roughly $17M-revenue services company that does not break even until year 8-9.

B's median outcome destroys value. It needs $28-60M of capital for a business that contingent-fee comps value at about 1x revenue (PRGX sold for about $195M on about $165M of revenue). Its upside is a 2-4% tail.

B's riskiest assumption has contrary evidence (about 5-6% realized against 20% targeted), and the author concedes the offer is at 'parity' with doing it yourself and with Redress. The buyer would be paying for something it already owns, so the objection goes to demand itself.

A's fatal objection is narrow: the customer prepay to a non-incumbent has no precedent. That does not kill the base case, which is a conventional independent-sponsor buy-and-build of a qualified caster at roughly 1.5-2.5x revenue. Failure in A mostly means 'no deal closes', not 'we bought a bad business'. The exit-multiple gap between entry and the 5.9-18x comps leaves room for re-rating.

A's weakness is real. It needs $100-175M of other people's equity and a proven operator, it has a thin edge against Pursuit, Arcline and GE, and the founder ends up with a small stake. That is why this is a 1-point call, not a clear one.
h2h:C05:C13:ba.reasons:
I put rough numbers on each idea as probability x value, net of capital.

A. Its own odds are about 14% for closing a first deal (about 40% to have an operator and an equity partner, times about 35% to close). Add about 5% of reaching $100M revenue without those two in hand, 12% with them. If it closes, you own an approved-source superalloy caster with $8-10M of EBITDA on day one. That sits in the tightest part of the industrial economy, where comps clear well above any plausible entry price. A fair value created is $100M or more at the median, and $300M or more at the upside. Failure mostly costs time and deal expenses. Even if customer prepay never materializes, a conventional leveraged buy-and-build of a qualified caster is still a coherent path, just with a larger equity cheque. Three critics called it fatal, but their objections hit the novel financing mechanism and the lack of a customer-side edge more than the existence of a viable acquisition thesis.

B. About a 40% chance of clearing the early gates. After that, the author's own median is about $17M revenue, negative EBITDA until about year 8-9, and $28-60M of funding. A contingent-fee services company is valued at about 1x revenue, so the median branch is worth less than the capital it consumes. The gates stop the bleeding early, but they also mean B only pays in a 2-4% tail. The deeper problem is that the CFO who signs already owns the missing ingredient, and Redress and DIY are cheaper at roughly the same realized outcome.

A is a long shot with a real asset behind it. B is a cheaper long shot behind a mediocre median. A comes out ahead, narrowly.
h2h:C05:C13:ba.a_biggest_risk: No qualified mid-size caster can actually be bought at a sane price and financed. Pursuit, Arcline and GE/CPP are consolidating the few targets, a first-time sponsor cannot raise $100M or more of equity and recruit a proven operator, and no OEM has ever prepaid a non-incumbent owner, so the customer-funded capital stack may never close.
h2h:C05:C13:ba.b_biggest_risk: Realization. Business owners do not release the retirable spend (about 5-6% realized against 20% targeted in the one panel cited), so the invoice-line fee base never materializes. CFOs also will not pay 26-30% for 3 years plus a tail when the pitch is only at parity with doing it in-house or hiring Redress.

decisive_factors: B has a hard unit-economics wall. Break-even bill rate is about $47.50/hr against a 35-45% staffing markup norm ($38-47) and an implied LAUNCH temp-tech bill of $34-39. The conversion/tenure contradiction pushes median EBITDA to roughly zero, and the WIOA subsidy is likely unavailable. No evidence exists that shops buy temp technicians at scale.

A's success states are far more profitable. Contribution runs 27-52%, and partial successes ($70-85M revenue at 20%+ EBITDA) still create real value. B at scale is a 5-16% EBITDA staffing company with no moat and consolidator-exit multiples.

A's fee rule (an invoice line drops or no fee) is metered and has scaled precedents (PRGX, ProsperOps, Redress, ESCO-style M&V). Hard kill gates cap the pre-traction downside, and falling AI engineering costs help A's margins rather than hurt them.

Capital and time favour B. A's median case burns $28M (plan $45-60M) and breaks even only in year 8-9, and the first success-fee evidence arrives at month 9-15. B's riskiest assumption is testable for under $500 in two weeks. This is why the call is close.
h2h:C13:C06:ba.reasons:
Neither idea is attractive at the median, so the choice turns on which objections are more likely fatal and which has the better outcome if it works.

B's problems are structural unit economics, not execution. The business only clears break-even at about $47.50/hr, but the market price for trades temp-to-hire sits around $38-47, and the one comparable temp-tech operator (LAUNCH) implies a $34-39 bill. Even if shops pay the price, conversion is free after about 1,000 hours. That makes it rational to convert at about 6 months, so the roughly $8k training cost is not recovered and median EBITDA falls to about zero. Add a likely-ineligible WIOA subsidy, state supervision rules (Michigan), brake/tire liability, no moat, and no evidence that temp technicians sell at scale. Its realistic ceiling is a $10-25M thin-margin regional staffing firm that a consolidator buys at a low multiple.

A's problems are serious but more addressable. Realization is the single big one. The "why pay us" parity problem and adverse selection are real. However, the fee design is the cleanest of the two, the buyer is a CFO with budget authority, and partial wins are valuable at much higher margins. Gates kill it cheaply if realization is weak. A's weakness is capital intensity and a slow learning loop. That keeps this close, but the expected value tail and the lower odds of B's price wall tip it to A.
h2h:C13:C06:ba.a_biggest_risk: Realization: business owners do not release the identified spend (documented 5-6% realized against 20% targeted). Combined with the unanswered "why pay us" parity problem against DIY and Redress, the result is no invoice drops, so no fees. The funded engineering and a 9-15 month cash lag are then sunk.
h2h:C13:C06:ba.b_biggest_risk: Price: shops and dealers will not pay a roughly 93% markup ($52/hr on a $27 wage) when they can hire direct at $24-28 or buy temp techs at a 35-45% markup. Below about $47.50/hr the business loses money, and free conversion at about 1,000 hours leaves the training cost unrecovered.

decisive_factors: Demand certainty: A's sellers and capital demonstrably exist (Alsco closed 4 deals in 18 months, 10+ funded buyers, $100M is under 1% of the pool). B has no precedent for a buyer of an outcome-priced cohort carve-out after about 26 targeted searches, and landlords are bundling and insourcing.

Objection severity: A's critics rated the objections 'serious', and the dossier says the business is real but undifferentiated, so the main risk is price. B drew two 'fatal' ratings (customer and procurement), with a newco shut out by turnover and D&B tests.

Probability of a viable outcome: A needs one anchor closed at or below 6.5x, which is a sourcing problem with a known playbook. B needs concentration, persistence, a 40%+ causal cut, category creation and fund capital to all hold; the second-round critic puts overall odds of the upside under 1%.

Quality of the revenue base: A buys cash-flowing EBITDA at about 15% margin with a hard walk-away at 7x. B's revenue is mostly pass-through works at 8-12% blended EBITDA, and its likely end state is a subcontractor at prime margins of 5-6%.

Cost of being wrong: both have cheap kill tests, but A's deal-by-deal structure with partner capital caps the founders' downside. A's median (about 8% IRR) is weak, so the margin is clear rather than decisive.
h2h:C16:C15:ba.reasons:
